items.title: WorldMint
items.text:
WorldMint is a 3D game editor for Windows, designed to work with an AI agent. You describe your game in the Agent panel, with your own Claude or Codex account, and the agent builds it before your eyes in the scene: it places models, sculpts the terrain, activates game systems (health, combat, inventory...), writes the scripts and plays the game to check that it works. Every one of its changes is undone with Ctrl+Z, just like yours.

Everything the agent does, you can also do by hand: move an object with the mouse, change a setting in the Properties, paint a forest, choose the key of a control. The editor borrows the gestures of Windows File Explorer (double-click, right-click, F2, drag and drop) and everyday words. When you like your game, File > Export game... turns it into a folder with its own program, which anyone can run.

The screenshots in this guide show the editor in French; switch it to English with Help > Language.

items.title: Where to start
items.text:
• Installation and first launch: get the editor and open it.
  • Getting started: your first game, from creating the project to the Play button.
  • The agent: connect it to your account, and talk to it.
  • The editor: every panel, every button, every setting.
  • The Trigger, physics and zones, the game interface: make the game react without code, and give it its menus.
  • Reference: game systems, scripts and the agent's tools, taken straight from the code.
  • Frequently asked questions.

items.title: The agent
items.text:
The agent is an AI assistant that builds your game in the editor. You talk to it in the Agent panel, at the bottom of the right column; it acts on the open scene, before your eyes. "The agent changes this scene before your eyes, and you can undo everything."

It is your agent: Claude (Anthropic's Claude Code program) or Codex (by OpenAI), started by the editor with your own account. The editor never sees your credentials. The agent only has the tools the editor gives it: it can neither read your files nor run commands on the computer. The full list of what it can do is in What the agent does.

items.title: Signing in
items.text:
On the first launch, the panel shows Connect your agent.

  1. Choose the agent: Claude or Codex.
  2. If it is not installed, the panel says so ("First, install Claude Code, the Anthropic program that links the editor to your account."). Install runs the official installer of this program. See the installation page opens its page in the browser, and Check again looks for the program again. Codex requires Node.js to install.
  3. Choose how to sign in:

For Claude:

Choice For whom Claude subscription Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise. Anthropic's page opens in your browser. Anthropic Console account Billed by usage. Anthropic's page opens in your browser. Anthropic API key Billed by usage. Paste the key, then Use this key: it is kept encrypted for your Windows session. Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry Uses the configuration already on this machine, as in VS Code. Without a configuration, the panel says so: set the provider's variables, then restart the editor.

For Codex:

Choice For whom ChatGPT account Plus, Pro, Business or Enterprise. OpenAI's page opens in your browser. OpenAI API key Billed by usage. Codex keeps it itself, not the editor.

With a browser choice, the panel shows "Waiting for your browser…": finish signing in on the page that just opened, the panel updates by itself. The Undo button there gives up. If it fails, the panel says why, and Try again starts over.

items.title: Updating the agent
items.text:
A recent model often needs a recent version of the agent's program. The editor reads that version at each connection, and also recognizes it in the answer of a model that refuses a version that is too old. The panel then shows "Claude Code must be updated for this model.", with the version needed and the one installed.

  • Update runs the official update (for Claude, this is claude update; for Codex, its installation, which sets up the version checked by WorldMint). The panel shows that it is working, reads the version again, then reconnects the agent, without closing the editor. All that is left is to send your message again.
  • If it fails, the panel says what to do. Most often, the program's file is open somewhere else: close the Claude desktop app, VS Code and the terminals where Claude Code runs, then click Update again. You can also type claude update in a terminal.
  • Technical details shows the exact text of the problem and what the update wrote, to copy into a help request.
  • At connection time, Continue without updating keeps the installed version: models that need a newer one will refuse to answer, and the panel will offer the update again.

The known version Claude needs is kept in the config/agents.json file, next to the editor (minimumVersion). The editor also remembers the one the model asks for, even a newer one.

items.title: Talking to the agent
items.text:
Once signed in, the top of the panel shows the agent and your account (for example "Claude · Max"), with two buttons: + (New conversation) and the gear (Agent settings).

An empty conversation offers three ideas: "Which models are in my library?", "Describe what is in this scene", "What can you do in this editor?". A click sends one.

The input area ("Describe what you want to build…"):

  • Enter sends the message; Shift+Enter starts a new line. The round button, on the right, sends too (Send (Enter)).
  • While the agent works, this button becomes a square: Stop the agent. The answer is then marked "Stopped.".
  • Above the area, "Selection: Door" recalls what is selected in the scene: the agent knows it too. So you can say "make this one bigger".
  • Writing the path of a folder of your computer in a message adds it to the library, so the agent can use it.

In a project, there is a single conversation for the whole game: the agent goes from one scene to another without losing it, and it is kept when you close the editor.

items.title: Attaching files
items.text:
The paperclip (Attach an image, a PDF or a text (or drop it here)) offers:

  • A file from the computer…: an image, a PDF or a text;
  • A capture of the 3D view: what the view shows, to show the agent what you see;
  • The copied image (Ctrl+V in the input area): a screenshot, an image copied from a website.

You can also drag a file from File Explorer onto the Agent panel. Attached files show as thumbnails above the text; a thumbnail's cross removes it, a click opens it in full. Limits: ten attachments per message, a PDF of 20 MB at most, a text of 200 KB at most. Codex does not read PDFs: attach an image or a text instead.

items.title: Model and effort
items.text:
Under the input area, two discreet lists:

  • The model that answers: Default (the one your agent chooses), or for Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.1.
  • Reasoning effort: "the higher it is, the more the agent thinks before acting, and the slower it is". For Claude: Low, Medium, High, Extra high, Max; for Codex: Minimal, Low, Medium, High.

The change applies from the next message.

items.title: While it works
items.text:
• "Thinking… 12 s" shows that it is progressing, with the number of tokens of its reasoning.
  • Its actions show in folded groups, each as a short sentence: "Reading the scene", "Creating objects (5)", "Playing the game"... A click opens the group. A refusal stays visible without opening the group.
  • Its plan stays shown at the top of the conversation for a long job: the current step, and the number of steps done. A click shows all the steps, and the proof given for each.
  • If it gives no news for a while, the panel says so: it may still be working, and the square button stops it.

Under each answer: its duration, the number of actions, the cost if your account is billed by usage, and Undo these changes, which undoes at once everything the agent changed during that turn. Its changes are also undone one by one with Ctrl+Z.

Copy: drag over the text of a message to select it (a double-click takes a word), then Ctrl+C or right-click > Copy. The Copy message icon, on hover, copies a whole message. Links open with a click.

items.title: Agent settings
items.text:
The gear of the panel (or Agent > Agent settings). Back returns to the conversation.

Section What you find there Account The Claude / Codex choice, the signed-in account ("Signed in: ..."), Change connection, and Sign out (or Forget this connection), to confirm with Confirm sign out. Note: signing out applies to the whole computer, not only the editor. Model The model that answers. Reasoning effort The level of reasoning. "The change applies from the next message." Program The path of the agent's program. Empty: the editor finds it by itself ("Automatic detection: ..."). Agent rules "The agent follows the method that comes with the editor: a plan, a game playable at every step, and proof." Customize for this project creates an AGENT.md file in the project, which you can edit; then Open this project's rules opens it. See The agent's guide. Another agent "Another agent can connect to the editor from your terminal. It then keeps its own tools, so only do this if you trust it." Allow the agent opens the access; Copy the command copies the command to run in the terminal. It contains an access key: don't share it.

items.title: What it can do
items.text:
The agent builds worlds (terrain, water, vegetation, objects set on the ground), places the player and sets its animations, activates and sets game systems, writes scripts, creates and links scenes, plays the game without a window to check that it works, looks at the scene as an image, and exports the game. It follows a method: it presents a plan for a large request, keeps the game playable at every step, and gives proof.

  • The list of its tools: What the agent does.
  • Its method: The agent's guide.
  • What it knows about each system: the systems reference.

items.title: Animate and make cutscenes
items.text:
The timeline, at the bottom of the view, animates objects frame by frame, without code: a door that opens, a platform that rises, a drawbridge that lowers, a lamp that blinks. It also puts cutscenes together: cameras, characters who walk or wave, sounds, subtitles, while the player watches.

A timeline belongs to the scene, like its objects: it is saved with it, and every gesture is undone with Ctrl+Z.

items.title: Open the timeline
items.text:
• In the status bar, at the bottom of the window, click Timeline, next to Library.
  • Or, in the View menu, Animation timeline.
  • Or create a timeline straight away: in the scene list, + then Animation or Cutscene.

At the top of the timeline, the list chooses the open timeline; it also offers New animation and New cutscene.

items.title: Animate an object
items.text:
1. Select the object (the door), in the view or the scene list.
  2. New animation: it starts from the object as it is, with a first keyframe at 0 seconds (a diamond on its row).
  3. Move the playhead: click or drag on the ruler of seconds, at the top of the timeline.
  4. Move the object with the gizmo: move it, turn it, scale it. It does not move in the scene: it gets a keyframe at that moment.
  5. Play (the triangle, or Space with the mouse over the timeline): the view shows the animation live.

The Keyframe button sets a keyframe of the selected objects as they show, at the playhead: that is how you add another object to an animation. An object's children follow it: animating the door carries its handle.

Values are kept relative to the object's parent: moving the house later does not break its door's animation. A rotation from 0 to 360 degrees makes a full turn.

items.title: Set a keyframe
items.text:
A click on a diamond chooses it, and the row above sets it:

Setting What it does Linear, Smooth, In steps How the object goes to the next keyframe: at a steady pace, starting and stopping gently, or waiting then jumping. Visible Shows or hides the object from this moment on: a blinking lamp, a bridge that appears. Color The object's tint at this moment; it changes smoothly from one keyframe to the next. Remove the keyframe The object goes straight from the previous one to the next. Delete does the same.

Drag a diamond to move it in time. A right-click on a row offers Keyframe here and Remove this object from the timeline.

items.title: Playback
items.text:
Playback For Once A door that opens and stays open. Looping A blinking lamp, a turning wheel. There and back A platform that goes up and down, forever.

Length: the length of the timeline, in seconds. From the start of the game plays it as soon as the game starts: for a platform that comes and goes on its own.

items.title: Make a cutscene
items.text:
New cutscene opens a ten-second timeline, with its rows: Cameras, Characters, Sounds, Subtitles, Events, besides the objects it animates. A right-click on a row, Add here, sets a moment at that time; a click on it chooses it to set it.

Row A moment Its settings Cameras Show the game through a placed camera (see Create, Camera) The camera, or Player camera; Glide: it glides from the previous one; Fade to black: black centred on the change. A camera can also have its own row of keyframes, to move during the shot. Characters Play an animation, or Walk to an object The character, its animation (read from its model), Looping; for walking, the target, the Speed, and the animation once there. Sounds A sound from the library Music: it loops and replaces the one playing; Volume. Subtitles A text at the bottom of the screen The text, its Length. Events A name sent at that moment A Trigger rule (When an event happens) or a script can wait for it.

During a cutscene, the player has no control: black bars frame the picture. At the end, the camera from before comes back and the player gets control again.

  • World stopped: the rest of the game stops (enemies, physics, scripts); only the cutscene goes on, with its characters. Otherwise the world lives around it.
  • Can be skipped: Esc (or Start on a gamepad) skips the cutscene. Everything is set as at its end: objects at their last pose, characters arrived, the events left sent. The sounds left do not play.

items.title: Play it in the game
items.text:
• Without code, with the Trigger: Play an animation, Play a cutscene, Stop an animation. The At the end, send the event field chains another rule (When an event happens): the drawbridge is down, a chest appears.
  • From the start of the game, with nothing else.
  • In a script: game.play_timeline("door_opens"), game.stop_timeline(...), game.timeline_playing(...). The timeline's id is in its … menu. See scripts.

The game announces timeline.debut and timeline.fin (see Events).

items.title: With the agent
items.text: Just ask: "make the door open when I pull the lever", "an intro cutscene that flies over the village". The agent writes the timeline, links it to the Trigger, and checks it with pictures at several moments, then by playing the game. You see it in the timeline and touch it up with the mouse.

items.title: Game controls
items.text:
Controls are the game's keys: one control per player action. They are set in the Game tab, Controls section, and apply to the whole game.

Each control has:

  • a label, which the player sees ("Jump");
  • a name for scripts (jump): scripts and systems ask "is the jump control pressed?", never a precise key. Changing the key therefore breaks nothing;
  • a key (or a mouse button, or the wheel);
  • a gamepad button, optional.

When you hover over a label, the editor shows the name for scripts and where the control comes from: this game, the engine, or the system that added it.

items.title: Starting controls
items.text:
A new game has these controls. The first seven come from the engine; Attack and Use belong to the game, which can remove them.

Control Name for scripts Key Gamepad Move forward move_forward W (Z on an AZERTY keyboard) left stick Move back move_back S left stick Move left move_left A (Q on an AZERTY keyboard) left stick Move right move_right D left stick Run run Left Shift LT Jump jump Space A Pause pause Esc Start Attack attack Click X Use interact E Y

Keys are read by their place on the keyboard, not by their letter: the editor shows the letter of your keyboard (Z on AZERTY, where QWERTY has W). The gamepad's right stick turns the camera.

Some systems add their own when you activate them: Block (block, right-click, LB) with Basic combat, Drink a potion (heal, R, ↑) with Healing. See the systems reference.

items.title: Changing a key
items.text:
1. Click the key button, to the right of the label: it shows "Press a key…".
  2. Press the key, mouse button or wheel notch you want. Escape cancels.

The list next to it chooses the gamepad button (None for no button): A, B, X, Y, LB, RB, LT, RT, Start, Back, L3, R3 and the four arrows.

Changing a control of a system or of the engine keeps it in this game, with the new key. Ctrl+Z goes back.

items.title: Adding a control
items.text:
Add a control opens a small form:

  • Name for scripts: a word without spaces (open_map);
  • Label for the player: "Open the map";
  • Key: click, then press the key.

Add creates it ("This name is already taken." if a control already has this name). A script then reads it with game.pressed("open_map"): see the scripts reference.

The Remove this control cross deletes a control that belongs to the game. Engine and system controls cannot be removed: if you changed their key, removing it gives them back their starting key.

items.title: In the game
items.text:
• The mouse turns the camera. When the game shows a cursor (an inventory, a menu), it is used to click.
  • Esc is the Pause control: if no script uses it, it frees the mouse, to click outside the window or close it. A click in the window takes the mouse back.
  • When a game ends (won or lost), the screen shows "R: play again Esc: quit".
  • A connected gamepad is picked up at once; the game then shows the gamepad's buttons in its prompts.
  • The game's windows (menus, dialogues, inventory, shop, quest log) work with a gamepad and a keyboard: the d-pad, the left stick or the arrow keys move from one button to another, A or Enter clicks, B or Escape closes. While a window is used that way, these buttons do not fire their control (A does not jump). See Gamepad and keyboard.
  • A script can let the player change their keys during the game (game.bind).

items.title: Quality
items.text:
Quality sets how detailed the picture is: shadows, lights, water, the glow around strong lights, and how far the terrain and plants keep their detail. It has three levels.

Level What changes For whom Low Blurrier shadows up close (3 maps of 1,024 pixels), 256 lights at once, simpler water (no refraction), smaller glow, detailed terrain up to 512 m, plants up to 60% of their distance, fewer particles at once (in the game). An integrated graphics chip (most laptops). Medium Shadows almost as sharp as High (3 maps of 2,048 pixels instead of 4), 512 lights at once and fewer light shadows, water like High, a glow as wide but computed smaller, detailed terrain up to 768 m, plants up to 80% of their distance. The editor's views, by default; a player whose graphics card struggles. High The finest everywhere: 4 shadow maps of 2,048 pixels, 1,024 lights, water with refraction and scenery reflections, detailed terrain up to 1,024 m, plants at their full distance. A graphics card: the game's picture as you want it.

items.title: Where to set it
items.text:
• For the editor's views: Preferences, Display section, View quality (Medium at first). It only applies to you, in the editor. A scene's Shadow quality (Sky and light) never goes above it there.
  • For the game: it chooses at startup, from the player's computer (Low on an integrated chip, High on a graphics card). The game started with Play does the same: it does not take the editor's view quality.
  • For the player: with the Menu system, Options, Graphics, Quality (see below).

items.title: The editor's views only work when the picture changes
items.text: Whatever the quality, the editor only redraws a view when its picture would change: the camera moves, an object changes, a view setting changes, or something moves on its own (visible water, particles, terrain that is still arriving). Otherwise the view keeps its previous picture. While you type a message to the agent, or while the agent works, the views cost almost nothing. With four views, the ones that are neither under the mouse nor being edited follow an object you move a little less often (20 times per second), and water 10 times per second; the view under the mouse follows everything at every frame (water, 30 times per second).

items.title: Upscaling
items.text:
Upscaling draws the scene in an image smaller than the window, then enlarges it to the window's size. So as not to lose detail, it shifts the camera very slightly at every frame (by a fraction of a pixel) and blends the frames that follow one another: within a few frames, it knows more than a single frame shows. Object edges no longer look jagged ("staircase" edges), and the graphics card has fewer pixels to compute.

What enlarges the picture is the upscaling method:

  • None (default): WorldMint's own computation, on every graphics card;
  • FSR (all cards): AMD FSR 2, sharper, especially when the picture is much reduced; it works on every card and is already in WorldMint (see AMD FSR);
  • DLSS (NVIDIA): on NVIDIA GeForce RTX cards, if you provided it (see NVIDIA DLSS).

Where the chosen method doesn't work, WorldMint's replaces it, without telling the player.

items.title: Where to set it
items.text:
• For the game: nothing selected, Game window section, Upscaling (the level) and Upscaling method. The setting goes with the exported game. The agent can change it too (except choosing DLSS).
  • For the editor's views: Preferences, Display section, View upscaling and View upscaling method. It only applies to you, in the editor. A camera preview shows the game's setting.

items.title: The levels
items.text:
Level The scene is drawn at What you get Off (default) full size The image as before: sharp, but edges look jagged. Anti-aliasing only (100%) full size Smooth edges, the best image. Costs a little more than Off. Quality (67%) 67% of the width Almost as sharp, a little faster on a modest card. Balanced (58%) 58% In between. Performance (50%) 50% (a quarter of the pixels) Faster, a little softer when the camera moves. Ultra performance (33%) 33% The fastest; blurry when the camera moves. For a very weak card or a very large screen.

What we measured, at 1920 x 1080, on the integrated graphics of an AMD processor: on a continent with its sea, 5.4 ms per frame without upscaling, 4.3 ms with Performance and 3.7 ms with Ultra performance; on a small village the gain is smaller (the scene costs little), and Quality is a little slower than Off there. On a powerful graphics card the difference doesn't show: the image is already very fast.

items.title: Good to know
items.text:
• When the camera stops, the image gets sharper for about a second: that is upscaling blending the frames. In the editor, the view keeps drawing during that time, then rests.
  • A screenshot taken by the agent is always taken at full size, without upscaling. A game capture (--capture) keeps its upscaling, with its method, and its anti-aliasing: the picture is redrawn there until its whole jitter is blended.

items.title: The player chooses too
items.text: With the Menu system, the game's Options button has a Graphics section: the player chooses the quality there (Low, Medium or High: see quality), the upscaling (the same levels as above), the anti-aliasing when upscaling is off (see anti-aliasing), the shadows (As quality at first, then High, Medium, Low or Off, for the sun and every light: see light and shadows) and the upscaling method (None, FSR, and DLSS if you provided it; the line only shows when FSR or DLSS works on their card). At first, they find what you set here (and the quality chosen for their machine); each click moves to the next choice, at once. Their choice is kept from one game to the next; your game settings do not change.

items.title: Anti-aliasing
items.text:
When upscaling is off, anti-aliasing smooths the objects' edges, which otherwise look like stairs. (Upscaling, even "Anti-aliasing only", already does it: the choice then no longer matters.)

  • For the game: nothing selected, Game window section, Anti-aliasing. The agent can change it too, and the player chooses it in the game's menu (Display tab).
  • For the editor's views: Preferences, Display, View anti-aliasing (None at first). A camera preview shows the game's.
Choice What it does Automatic (as quality) The game's starting setting: TAA in High and Medium quality, FXAA in Low (TAA would cost 4 ms there on an integrated chip). A project created before 11 November 2026 keeps SMAA in High and Medium: its picture does not change. TAA (sharp in motion) Blends the frames that follow one another, like "Anti-aliasing only": the finest, but each picture is rebuilt from the previous ones. SMAA (sharp, no trails) Recognizes the shape of each edge in the finished picture and smooths it: sharp, nothing trails behind what moves. In High, it finds edges by color; otherwise by brightness. FXAA (lightest) A single pass over the finished picture: the cheapest, a little softer. None The edges as they are.

What we measured, at 1920 x 1080, on a scene of 225 cubes (graphics card time on top of None):

RTX 5090 AMD Radeon integrated chip FXAA + 0.01 ms + 0.85 ms SMAA + 0.03 ms + 1.5 ms TAA + 0.04 ms + 4.0 ms

Why TAA at first: on dense foliage, it shimmers a third less than SMAA (measured, see ADR-032). Its drawbacks: a slight trail behind what moves fast, a slightly softer picture. To get SMAA back, choose it in Anti-aliasing.

SMAA comes from its authors (Jorge Jimenez et al., MIT license); FXAA is written by WorldMint after the FXAA 3.11 algorithm.

items.title: AMD FSR
items.text:
AMD FSR 2 (FidelityFX Super Resolution 2.2, MIT license) rebuilds the full-size picture from the reduced one, its depth and the motion of each point. It is sharper than WorldMint's method when the picture is much reduced (Performance, Ultra performance), and it works on every graphics card: NVIDIA, AMD or Intel. It is already in WorldMint: nothing to download or provide, and nothing to show in your game.

  • Choosing it: Upscaling method: FSR (all cards). Upscaling switches to Quality if it was off. With Anti-aliasing only (100%), it smooths edges without shrinking the picture.
  • Good to know: when the camera turns fast, in Performance, the grain of soft shadows may show for a moment (WorldMint's method smooths it more, by being blurrier).

What we measured, at 1920 x 1080, on a scene of grass, trees and banners (the graphics card's time for the view, on 11 November 2026):

RTX 5090 AMD Radeon integrated chip (2 cores) Off (full size, no anti-aliasing) 0.64 ms 7.4 ms WorldMint, Anti-aliasing only (100%) 0.40 ms 11.7 ms WorldMint, Quality 0.26 ms 9.0 ms FSR, Anti-aliasing only (100%) 0.53 ms 23.4 ms FSR, Quality 0.36 ms 16.4 ms FSR, Balanced 0.32 ms 14.9 ms FSR, Performance 0.29 ms 14.2 ms

On the RTX 5090, FSR costs 0.1 ms more than WorldMint's method at the same level. (Off costs more than the others there: without upscaling, ray-traced shadows cast several rays per point.) On the small integrated chip of a desktop processor, it costs 5 to 12 ms more: WorldMint's method stays the fastest there; Performance saves 9 ms over Anti-aliasing only.

items.title: NVIDIA DLSS
items.text:
On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX card, upscaling can go through NVIDIA DLSS, sharper than WorldMint's when the image is much smaller. On every other card, the game keeps WorldMint's, without telling the player anything.

WorldMint doesn't provide DLSS. It is NVIDIA software: you download it yourself from NVIDIA, and you are the one who distributes it with your game, under NVIDIA's license. For every game that uses it, even a free one, it asks:

  • NVIDIA's logo when the game starts and in its credits;
  • every use of this logo submitted to NVIDIA, which must approve it in writing, two weeks ahead;
  • to tell NVIDIA before a commercial release of the game.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
1. Download Streamline from NVIDIA (Streamline releases) and unzip it. Its files are in bin\x64.
  2. Nothing selected, Game window section: Upscaling method, DLSS (NVIDIA). A window says what the license asks; read it (Read NVIDIA's license), then check I have read it: I will take the steps with NVIDIA myself.
  3. Choose the folder: Streamline's bin\x64 folder. WorldMint checks that sl.interposer.dll, sl.common.dll, sl.dlss.dll and nvngx_dlss.dll are there and carry NVIDIA's digital signature. A missing, changed or otherwise-signed file is refused, with a message.
  4. Turn DLSS on. Upscaling switches to Quality if it was off: the chosen level applies to DLSS too.

For the editor's view: Preferences, Display, View upscaling method, DLSS (NVIDIA), from the next start of the editor.

items.title: In the exported game
items.text:
The export copies NVIDIA's files into the game (nvidia folder, next to the program) only if DLSS is on, and reminds you of the logo and the steps. If they are missing, the game is exported anyway, with WorldMint's upscaling. The agent knows this setting but never turns it on: the agreement with NVIDIA is yours.

What we measured on an RTX 5090, at 1920 x 1080: about 0.4 ms more per frame than WorldMint's upscaling; the game takes about 3 seconds longer to start, while DLSS gets ready.

items.title: Ray tracing
items.text: Usually, a shadow is made by redrawing the scene as seen from the sun, several times per frame (the "shadow maps"): up close it is sharp, but it softens and loses detail further away. Ray tracing works differently: it casts real rays of light through a copy of the scene arranged to be searched quickly. Each point of the picture asks the sun whether it can see it; if an object is in the way, the point is in shadow. The shadow is accurate at every distance, and it can be soft like that of a real sun. The same rays make reflections: water, metal, glass and smooth floors reflect the scenery, even what is off screen.

items.title: Which cards have it
items.text: NVIDIA RTX cards (20 series and later), AMD Radeon RX 6000 and later, and Intel Arc. Some graphics chips built into the processor have it too, but they are too slow to use it in a game (see the measurements below). On every other card, nothing changes: the game is drawn with shadow maps, as before.

items.title: What each quality does
items.text:
Quality With ray tracing Low Never in Automatic: shadow maps, as before. The player can force it (On): it then takes Medium's settings, with a warning. Medium The sun's shadow by a ray, up to 1 km around the camera. Placed lights keep their shadow maps. Ray-traced reflections on what is nearly smooth (roughness up to 0.3: water, polished metal, glass), up to 500 m. High The sun's shadow up to 1.5 km, and the shadow of every placed light that casts one, by one ray each (with no limit on their number). Reflections up to a roughness of 0.5 (blurrier and blurrier), up to 1 km. Indirect lighting (which can be turned off on its own).

Shadow softness (in "Sky and light" for the sun, each light's own softness) applies to rays too: it is the size of what gives the light. With temporal anti-aliasing (the one of upscaling), one ray per point aims at a slightly different spot of the sun at every frame, and the frames are blended; without it, a few rays per point (4 in Medium, 8 in High). The rays' sun is never smaller than the real one (0.5°): a ray-traced shadow never has a perfectly sharp edge. At a softness of 0°, the edge also keeps the blur of the shadow maps: turning ray tracing on does not change the look of shadows, it makes them more accurate (at the foot of objects, far away). Shadows turned Off (the Shadows line of the player's menu, or the scene's shadow quality) turn the rays off too.

items.title: What keeps its shadow maps
items.text:
Rays see a copy of the scene arranged in advance. What is missing from it keeps its shadow through shadow maps, next to the rays:

  • animated characters (their pose changes at every frame; a later step will put them in the copy);
  • objects whose creator shader cuts holes in their surface or moves their vertices (a ray would see the model whole and still).

Particles and water receive the rays' shadows, but do not cast any. A piece of terrain or a tile that has just arrived is arranged within a few frames: meanwhile, it casts no shadow (far away, it does not show).

items.title: Reflections
items.text:
A ray leaves each point of water, metal, glass or a smooth floor, in the direction of the reflection. What it hits is lit as it would be on screen, more simply: its colour, the sun and its shadow, the sky. What reflects this way depends on the material's roughness (see materials): up to 0.3 in Medium, up to 0.5 in High. The rougher a surface, the blurrier its reflection; with temporal anti-aliasing, the ray aims in a slightly different direction at every frame, and the frames are blended. Beyond that roughness, or when the ray hits nothing, the reflection stays as before: the sky.

  • Realistic water keeps the screen's reflections first (they also show characters and all the light); the ray fills in what the screen cannot see, like the shore behind the camera.
  • Stylised water reflects the scenery in each facet, like so many small flat mirrors, slightly blurred and mixed with the sky: it keeps its flat colours.
  • Not reflected by the rays: animated characters, objects whose creator shader cuts holes in or moves their surface, particles, and the light of placed lights on what is reflected (at night, a reflection only shows what glows by itself).

Ambient occlusion (the soft shadow in corners) also uses rays, in Medium and High. Indirect lighting uses rays in High quality: the light bounced by surfaces (a sunlit floor lights the walls, a room is lit through its window), ray traced with a light cache. It costs about 1 to 2 ms per frame; on at first, it can be turned off on its own (see below). Off, or below High, shade gets the sky's ambient light, as before.

items.title: Automatic, On, Off
items.text:
• Automatic (at first): ray tracing only on a dedicated graphics card that has it, in Medium or High quality. Never on an integrated chip, never in Low.
  • On: always, on a card that has it, even where it is heavy (an integrated chip, Low quality). The player's menu then warns them: "Heavy on this card: the picture may slow down". There, only shadows use rays: reflections would cost too much (on an integrated chip, water went from 53 to 97 ms per frame).
  • Off: never; shadow maps, as before.

items.title: Where to set it
items.text:
• For the game: nothing selected, Game window section, Allow ray tracing (ticked by default). Unticked, the game is always drawn without it, on every machine, and the player has no choice. The agent only changes it if you ask.
  • For the player: with the Menu system, Options, Graphics, Ray tracing. The line only appears if their card has it and the game allows it; each click moves from Automatic to On then to Off. Their choice is kept from one play to the next.
  • For the editor's views: Preferences, Display section, View ray tracing (Automatic at first). It only applies to you; the views only use it if the game allows it. A camera's preview shows the game's, in Automatic.
  • Indirect lighting: for the player, the Indirect lighting line under Ray tracing in the menu (On at first, a click moves to Off, kept from one play to the next; a short line says what it does); for the editor's views, Preferences, View indirect lighting (on at first). It only works in High quality, with ray tracing on. A script reads and changes it with game.graphics and game.set_graphics (indirect_light).

items.title: When the graphics card's memory is full
items.text:
Ray tracing keeps a copy of the scene in the graphics card's memory. The game gives itself a share of that memory (most of it on a dedicated card, half on an integrated chip, which shares the PC's memory), and ray tracing never takes more than a quarter of it, nor the room of models and images. When it is full, ray tracing stops arranging anything new, gives back what is used least, then reaches less far; as a last resort it turns itself off: shadows come back from shadow maps at the next frame, without a stutter. The player's menu says so under the Ray tracing line ("Off: the graphics card's memory is full (classic shadows)"), and so do the editor's Preferences. It tries again as soon as the choice or the quality changes.

Large model images that have not been shown for a few seconds may also drop to a small resolution meanwhile: they stay visible, a little blurry, and become sharp again by themselves when they are seen again and there is room again.

items.title: What we measured
items.text:
On the city of the large-worlds bench (4 × 4 km with its countryside), at 1920 × 1080, High quality, on 10 November 2026:

  • on an NVIDIA RTX 5090, the card's time to draw a view stays the same: 0.17 ms in the street (shadow maps or rays), 0.15 against 0.18 ms flying over (where rays give the whole city its shadow, shadow maps only the first 150 metres); in the full city (100 % step), 0.39 ms with rays against 0.50 ms with shadow maps, and the whole frame goes from 4.4 to 3.2 ms. The scene arranged for rays takes 200 to 240 MB of the card (compacting gives back 440); everything is arranged in a little over 2 seconds at start-up, with no hitch over 3 ms;
  • on the integrated graphics chip of an AMD processor (forced On), the same view costs 9 to 10 ms more per frame (21 to 23 ms instead of 11 to 14), and the scene takes 260 to 600 MB of the PC's memory: too heavy for a smooth game. That is why Automatic never turns it on there;
  • reflections (on 10 November, on an island by the sea with polished metal, a mirror and a pane of glass) cost 0.05 to 0.1 ms per frame on the RTX 5090; in a city with nothing smooth, nothing. On the integrated chip they almost doubled the frame time (53 → 95 ms): where ray tracing is forced and heavy, they stay off;
  • when objects move (doors, physics), the scene arranged for rays is updated instead of rebuilt: in the full city, its preparation goes from 6 ms to 0.14 ms per frame.
  • what arrives (a tile, a model) is arranged for the rays in 2 ms at most per frame (1.5 in Medium), at the card's measured pace: on the integrated chip forced On, crossing the city went from 376 to 53 frames over 16.7 ms.

items.title: Particles and decals
items.text:
Particles bring the world to life: a campfire, a torch, smoke, sparks, magic, rain or snow, and what goes with an action (wood chips when chopping a tree, dust when the player lands, a flash when a hit lands). Decals lay an image on the ground or a wall: a footprint, an impact, a scorch mark, a stain, a puddle, a sign.

Everything is set without code. The effects are generic: they depend on no model, and chips take the colour of what is hit, measured on the model itself.

items.title: An effect on an object
items.text:
The Particle effect system goes on the object the effect comes from: a campfire, a torch, a cauldron. For an effect on its own (a fire in the middle of a camp, snow over a valley), Create > Particle effect places an invisible box that carries it: its settings come first in its properties, before its place and size. The effect already runs in the editor's view while you set it.

Its settings, in the object's properties:

  • Effect: fire (dancing flames, a brighter core, a warm glow, embers flying up and a little smoke), smoke, sparks, magic, rain, snow, dust, chips, explosion, hit impact.
  • Size: 1 for a campfire, 0.4 for a torch, 3 for a big blaze. For rain and snow, the width of the area where they fall.
  • Colour: the effect's own, or a chosen colour (a blue fire, green magic).
  • Amount: the number of particles, multiplied.
  • Looping: ticked, the effect runs as long as the object is there; unticked, it plays once when the game starts.
  • Duration and Height above the object's base (the flame at the tip of a torch).
  • Effect light and Light strength (fire, explosion, magic, sparks, hit): the light the effect gives around it, with its shadows, without them, or none (see the light of fires and effects).

Placed on a visible object, the effect stops while the object is hidden and comes back when it is shown. Place rain or snow on the player: it follows them everywhere.

items.title: Playing an effect with the Trigger
items.text:
The Trigger has two actions:

  • Play an effect: on the target, the one it carries (its Particle effect system, lit again: a brazier lit by a lever), or a ready-made effect played once (an explosion, chips, magic), with its size.
  • Stop an effect: puts out the effect the target carries.

For example, a barrel that explodes when broken: When: It dies, Then: Play an effect, Explosion, size 2; then a rule that destroys it.

items.title: What the game already does
items.text:
• The player raises a little dust when landing after a jump or a fall (Player tab, Dust on landing, to turn it off).
  • An object that bursts or collapses makes chips in its colour and dust; an object that falls raises dust where it hits the ground.
  • Gathering sends chips flying at each hit, from the spot hit and in its colour (wood for a tree's trunk, stone for a rock): setting Chips at each hit.
  • Simple combat makes a flash, sparks and a little dust when a hit lands: setting A flash and sparks when a hit lands.

items.title: A decal
items.text:
Create > Decal places a flat invisible box that carries the Decal system. Its image covers the box's width and depth, and lies on what is around its base: the ground, a floor, a rock. The box's scale sets the image's size; turning it around its height turns the image. Its settings come first in its properties.

  • Image: a stain, an impact, a scorch mark, a puddle, footprints, a skid mark (drawn by the engine), or an image of the project (PNG or JPEG, its transparency kept).
  • Opacity: from 0 (invisible) to 1.
  • Tint: white leaves the image as it is; dark red makes a blood stain, green a puddle of poison.

For a sign on a wall, tip the box so that its height points out of the wall, and place its base against it. The image lies on everything inside the box, characters included: keep it thin where people walk.

items.title: With a script
items.text:
The agent can also write a script:

  • game.effect("explosion", position, {size = 2}) plays an effect at a place; game.effect("eclats", rock) on an object (its chips take its colour). With loop = true, the effect runs until game.stop_effect.
  • game.object_effect(fire, false) puts out the effect an object carries, true lights it again.
  • game.decal("impact", position, {size = 1.5}) places a decal; life = 10 fades it out after ten seconds.

The details are in the script reference.

items.title: Light on effects
items.text: Smoke, dust, chips, rain, snow and decals are lit like the rest of the scene: by the sun, darker in the shadow of a roof or a tree, and by the placed lights close by (smoke passing in front of a lantern takes its colour). Fire, sparks, magic, explosions and hit impacts make their own light: they stay just as bright at night, and light up what is around them, with shadows for fire, explosions and magic: a cube next to a campfire casts its shadow. Nothing to place next to them; the details are in the light of fires and effects.

items.title: The agent's test
items.text: Particles are simulated by the game itself: the same game gives exactly the same particles. When the agent tests the game, its report counts the effects played by name, the particles born and the most alive at once, and the decals placed; its captures show them.

items.title: In the editor's view
items.text: An effect that can be seen in a view animates on its own, even when you touch nothing (30 frames per second in the view you are working in, 10 in the others): you see the fire dance while you adjust it. When no effect can be seen any more (out of view, or put out), the editor goes back to rest, and so does the graphics card.

items.title: Effect quality levels
items.text:
Effects follow the graphics quality, on three levels:

High Medium Low Particles at once, at most 6,000 3,000 1,500 Particles given off all three quarters, a little larger half, a little larger Light on smoke and dust the sun and its shadows, placed lights and their shadows without the placed lights' shadows the sun and the sky, no shadow Largest size of a particle on screen 90% of the image height 70% 50% Decals placed by the game, at once 128 96 48

An effect never breaks the game: beyond their number, new particles are not born, it only looks lighter. The same goes for decals placed during the game: beyond their limit, the oldest fades out to make room for the new one. The game started with --low-power takes Low; --particles low, medium or high chooses the effects' level on its own.

A particle brushing past the camera fades out instead of covering the whole screen, and none goes beyond its largest size on screen: walking through smoke does not slow the game down.

items.title: Exporting a game
items.text: Exporting turns your game into a standalone folder, with its .exe program, that anyone can run on Windows, without WorldMint. Like WorldMint, the game needs a graphics card that supports Vulkan 1.3, with an up-to-date driver: otherwise, it tells the player as soon as it opens.

items.title: Exporting
items.text:
1. Check that the game has a player (Set as player on a character): without a player, Export game... is greyed out.
  2. Give the game a title: in the game's settings (nothing selected), Game window section, Title field ("Jeu" at first). The folder and the program take this name; without a title, the project's.
  3. File > Export game..., then choose the folder to put it in.

The status bar shows "Exporting the game...", then "Game exported: ... (15 MB)", and the folder opens in File Explorer. The editor stays usable during the export.

The agent can also export the game for you.

items.title: What the folder contains
items.text:
My game/
  My game.exe       the game
  locales/          its texts, in French and English
  data/             its scenes, and only the models, animations, sounds and images it really uses

All the project's scenes go with the game, as they are saved (the open scene, as it is on screen). The exported game starts on the project's start scene, whichever one you were looking at.

items.title: The checks
items.text:
• Before replacing anything, the editor runs the exported game, without a window, to check that it starts. If it does not start, the export is refused ("The exported game does not start: ...") and the previous export stays intact.
  • An export replaces the previous one in the same folder. A folder with the same name that is not an export is never overwritten ("This folder exists and is not an export"). If the exported game is still open, close it first.
  • Warnings (a file named by a script but missing, a path specific to your computer...) show in the console, starting with "Export warning".

Players' saved games (game.save in a script) are kept between two plays of the exported game.

items.title: The editor
items.text:
I made a mistake. How do I go back? Ctrl+Z, as many times as needed; Ctrl+Y redoes. This also applies to what the agent did. Under each answer of the agent, Undo these changes undoes its whole turn at once.

The editor closed before I saved. Have I lost everything? No. An automatic backup keeps a copy of your work every 60 seconds. On the next launch, the editor offers Recover your work?: click Recover, then save (Ctrl+S).

Where are my files? In the project folder: File > Open project folder. The first project is in Documents\WorldMint\Mon premier jeu. See Projects and scenes.

An object disappeared from the view. It may be hidden by the eye of the scene list: View > Show everything again. Or it is elsewhere: select it in the list, then F to frame the view on it.

My model does not appear in the library. The editor reads .glb, .gltf, .fbx and .obj files. COLLADA files (.dae) are counted as "Not read (COLLADA)". Also check that its folder was added (Add a folder).

My model is tiny or gigantic. Change its Scale in the properties. The sizes that trigger a warning are set in the game's settings, Technical settings section.

How do I switch the editor to French? Help > Language > Français, or the Preferences.

The text is too small. Preferences > Interface size.

items.title: The game
items.text:
The Play button does nothing. The game needs a player: the console says "No player: select an object, then choose "Set as player"." Select a character and click Set as player.

The player falls through the ground. The ground needs a Collision (Appearance section of its properties), or must be a terrain.

The player appears anywhere when arriving in a scene. The scene has no arrival point, or the passage does not name one: see Linking scenes.

How do I get the mouse out of the game window? Esc frees it (unless the game uses Esc for its own pause).

The game crashed. The editor and your scene are safe: the console says "The game crashed (code ...)". Start again with F5.

How do I change the game's keys? Game tab, Controls section: see Game controls.

How do I give my game to someone? File > Export game...: see Exporting a game. Send the whole exported folder.

items.title: The agent
items.text:
Do I have to pay to use the agent? The agent works with your own account: a Claude subscription (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise), a usage-billed account (Anthropic Console, API key), or for Codex a ChatGPT account or an OpenAI API key. That account counts the agent's usage, under its own terms; under each answer, the editor shows the cost when the account is billed by usage.

Can the agent touch my files or my computer? No. It only has the editor's tools, which act on the open project: see What the agent does. An agent that arrives with other tools is stopped before it does anything.

The agent no longer answers. The panel says so after a while without news. It may still be working; the square button stops it. You can then write to it again: the conversation goes on.

Can it see what I see? It can look at the scene as an image by itself. You can also attach A capture of the 3D view, an image or a PDF (paperclip of the input area).

Can it use my models? Yes, all those in the library. If a folder is not there yet, write its path in your message: it is added.

How do I change the way it works? Agent settings > Agent rules > Customize for this project creates an AGENT.md file in the project, which you can edit. Or simply tell it: your request comes before its rules.

Which model should I choose? Default is fine. A higher reasoning effort gives more thought-out answers, but slower ones.

items.title: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields
items.text: Everything your game shows on top of the scene (a pause menu, a shop, a dialogue box, an inventory, a chat window, a screen to enter your name) is the game interface. A fixed interface is drawn with the mouse; what changes shape while playing is built by the game's scripts, which the agent writes for you: describe to it what you want to see. Its look, on the other hand, is set without code, with the Interface system.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: What the interface can show
items.text:
Element What it is Text A text, which wraps by itself within the given width. It can have words in bold and words in color. Button A clickable button, with a text or an image. Text field A box where the player types text: their name, a message, a code. Image An image from the library: an icon, a portrait. Bar A gauge that fills up: health, stamina, progress. Panel A background that arranges what it contains: in a column, in a row or in a grid. Panels nest: a menu in a panel, inventory slots in a grid. Scrolling list A panel with a fixed height: when its content is longer, the mouse wheel over it scrolls it, with a thin scroll bar.

The game places the elements of a panel itself, one after the other: there are no positions to work out.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The mouse
items.text: In the game, the cursor is hidden and the mouse turns the camera. When the game opens an interface you click in (an inventory, a menu), it shows the cursor: the camera no longer turns with the mouse, and the Basic combat system no longer strikes. The agent takes care of it when it writes the menu.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Text fields
items.text:
A text field behaves the same way in every game made with WorldMint:

  • A click on the field selects it and puts the cursor there: what the player types is written where the cursor is. Backspace erases the character before the cursor, Delete the one after.
  • The arrows, Home and End move the cursor; with Ctrl, the arrows jump a whole word (and Backspace erases it).
  • Shift with the arrows, or dragging the mouse with the button held, selects text; Ctrl+A selects everything. A letter typed replaces the selection.
  • Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V copy, cut and paste, with the Windows clipboard: a name copied elsewhere can be pasted.
  • On a gamepad, once the field is selected: the d-pad moves the cursor, A validates, B leaves the field. Writing needs a keyboard.
  • While a field is selected, the player does not move and no game control fires: typing "w" writes a w, without moving the character.
  • Enter validates the field and leaves it. The game receives the text, and the player can move again.
  • Escape, or a click elsewhere, leaves the field without validating it.

Keeping the field active after Enter

For a chat window, you often want to send several messages in a row, without clicking in the field again. That is not the standard behavior: it takes a script that selects the field again after each message. Ask the agent for it, for example: "In the chat window, after Enter, send the message, empty the field and keep it active."
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Gamepad and keyboard
items.text:
Every window of the game can also be used without a mouse, with nothing to write: the game finds its buttons by itself.

Gamepad Keyboard What it does D-pad or left stick Arrow keys Moves to the next button in that direction, by its place on screen. Held, it keeps moving: you go down a long list without pressing for each line. Tab Moves to the next button, and back to the first after the last. A Enter Clicks the chosen button. B Escape Closes the window, or goes back (from the options to the pause).
  • The chosen button shows from afar: lighter, with a thick frame in the accent color of the Interface system.
  • With a gamepad, a window that opens chooses its first button at once. With a keyboard, the first arrow shows the chosen button, the next one moves it.
  • A list that scrolls follows the chosen button.
  • While choosing in a window, the character does not move, and the buttons used by the window do not fire their control: A does not jump, the d-pad does not drink a potion.
  • The mouse works as before: as soon as it moves, the frame disappears, and the hovered button becomes the chosen one.

The engine does this for every window: the systems' windows as well as those the agent writes. The button that B and Escape click is the one the window marks as its "Close" or "Back" button; a window without one (a dialogue in progress) lets Escape open the pause, as usual.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Drawing a screen with the mouse
items.text:
A fixed interface (a score, a health or ammo bar, a timer, a help panel, a workshop menu) is drawn, without code, and seen without starting the game.

  1. Game tab, Interface screens section: New screen. The game screen opens above the 3D view, at the size of the game window; the list at the top right also shows it in 16/9, 4/3, 21/9 or as a phone held upright.
  2. The palette places a Text, a Button, a Bar, an Image, a Panel or a Text field: a click places it in the centre, or drag it where you want it. A chosen panel receives what you place: it arranges it itself, in a column, a row or a grid.
  3. With the mouse: a click chooses an element, drag it to move it, pull its handles to resize it. Delete removes it, the arrow keys nudge it. Each gesture is undone with Ctrl+Z.
  4. The properties, on the right: the text, the size, the colors (chosen, or from the theme of the Interface system), the layout of a panel.

The anchor. Each element holds on to a corner, an edge or the centre of the screen, chosen in the nine-point grid of Position and size. A score anchored top right stays in that corner on a wide screen as on a narrow one; a help bar anchored at the bottom stays centred at the bottom. Changing the anchor does not move the element.

What it shows in the game, Value shown in the game section, without code:

Read from For example An announcement of the game The player's health, in one click: the sante.change announcement of the Health system, its vie field out of its max field. A bar fills up, a text writes "Health: 75 / 100" with the format Health: {valeur} / {max}. A value of the game A score a script gives with game.set_value("score", 12), shown by "Score: {valeur}". An object's system A value of a system placed on the player or on a named object.

In the editor, a bound value shows an example (75 out of 100), to see the room it will take.

Buttons, On click section: a button sends its announcement (for example atelier.fabriquer), which a Trigger rule (when: an event) or a script answers; Then, it can close its screen, open another one on top, replace it with another, or open and close a screen.

When to show it, in the screen's properties (nothing chosen): from the start of the game, on announcements (atelier.ouvrir, which a Trigger sends when the player enters the workshop), or with a game control that opens and closes it (I for an inventory). A screen with buttons shows the cursor; a menu can pause the game.

In the game, the screen is placed by the same calculation as in the editor: what you draw is what the player sees. A script can still touch it: game.screen_show("atelier"), game.screen_hide("atelier"), and game.hud_set("jeu/score", {text = "10"}) for an element, named "screen/element". The agent also draws screens for you, and prefers a drawn screen to a script for a fixed interface: you can then touch it up with the mouse.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Ready-made windows: Menu, Dialogue, Inventory, Shop, Quest log, Map
items.text: Six systems give the game its most common windows, without a script. They are activated in the Game tab, Systems section, and take the look of the Interface system. While they are open, the world can stop: the player, enemies, rolling objects and game time wait, and only clicks on the window count. All of them also work with a gamepad and a keyboard (see Gamepad and keyboard), and a saved game keeps them as they were (see What a saved game keeps).
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Menu: the title screen and the pause
items.text:
• The title screen: at start, the game's title and the Play, Options and Quit buttons, over the stopped, darkened game. The title is the one from the game settings (Window section), or the one written in the Title shown setting.
  • The pause: Escape (or Start on a gamepad) stops the game and opens Resume, Options and Quit. Escape closes it.
  • The options, arranged in sections, one per tab: Sound (the master volume and each group of the sound mixer, in steps of 10%), Display (the language of a translated game, the graphics) and Controls (the key of each control: click it, then press the new one; Escape cancels). A section too long for the screen (many sound groups, many controls) scrolls with the mouse wheel or the gamepad: the window never overflows.
  • The menu's texts are in French or English, after the player's language.

Its settings and events are in the Menu system reference.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Dialogue: a character who talks
items.text:
Place the Dialogue system on a character: they talk when the player uses them (E). Their lines show one by one in a window at the bottom of the screen, under their name, with the player's answers as buttons.

A dialogue reads like a flowchart. It is a list of rows, in order, of four kinds:

  • The character says: a line. Without answers, it has a Next button (or End when nothing follows).
  • The player answers: an answer, placed under the line it answers. There can be as many as needed. An answer can be offered only under a condition: if the player carries an item (10 "Gold" to pay a toll), if a mark is set, if they already talked to the character.
  • Test: a question the dialogue asks the game, to choose what comes next. Either yes or no: does the player carry a Key?, is the mark "met_the_king" set?, with a next step for yes and one for no. Or by a number: how many talks already finished?, how much Gold do they carry?.
  • Test exit: under a "by a number" test, where to go from a given number on. 0, 1, 2, 3, then 4: the last one counts for "4 and more".

The dialogue starts at the first row. Each row says where to go next: another row's label (a word naming it, such as friend), fin, or nothing for the next row. A row that has a label starts another branch: the talk stops before it instead of going into it.

A row can also set a mark, a word the whole game remembers (the king blesses, the guard recognises it later), and send an event such as door.open. A Trigger rule "When the event door.open" on the door then makes it disappear, without writing code.

A guard who loses patience at every visit, then lets in who has the key:

Row Kind Content Then 1 Test Do they carry a Key? yes: in; no: the next row 2 Test By the talks already finished its exits 3 to 7 Test exits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and more key, again, nothing, enough, dungeon 8 The character says key: "You need a key." 9 The character says again: "You again?" … 12 The character says dungeon: "To the dungeon!" (sends dungeon) 13 The character says in: "Ah, you have the key. Come in."

The Show the map button, in the character's properties, shows it as a flowchart, from top to bottom: Start, one box per line, one diamond per test, a named arrow for each answer or exit ("Yes", "No", "4 and more"), and an End at the end of each branch. Branches spread side by side; drag to move the map, and zoom with Ctrl + wheel. Show all fits it whole in the window, Actual size puts it back to its size.

The dialogue can also be changed in the map, and Ctrl+Z undoes it:

  • drag the circle at the start of an arrow onto a box to make it lead there (or to an End); dropped in the void, it offers to create the step it will lead to;
  • right-click the background: add a line, a yes or no test, or a test by a number;
  • right-click a box: add an answer (or an exit), or delete the step;
  • right-click an arrow's name: make it lead to the end, or delete the answer or exit.

The texts themselves are changed in the properties: a click on a box brings you there. In the map, a label that leads nowhere shows in red. In the properties list, rows are ordered with the Move up and Move down arrows.

Its settings are in the Dialogue system reference.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Inventory: the window
items.text: The Inventory system now has its window: the I key (or Back on a gamepad) opens and closes it. It shows one slot per kind of item carried, with its quantity, in a grid; beyond four rows, it scrolls with the mouse wheel. A click on a slot tells the game (inventaire.choisi): eating an apple or equipping a sword is something to ask the agent. See the Inventory system reference.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Shop: a merchant who sells
items.text:
Place the Shop system on a merchant: when the player uses them (E), a window opens with their items, their prices, the player's money, and a Buy button per item. The world stops while shopping (setting Stop the game while shopping).

The money is a kind of inventory item, such as "Gold" or "Coin": the player picks it up, receives it as a quest reward, like any item. The Money setting says which one this merchant accepts.

What they sell is a list, in the merchant's properties, one item per row:

Setting of an item What it says Item The kind of item sold, as the inventory stores it, such as "Sword". They sell it Unticked, the merchant only buys it back: no Buy button. How many per purchase 10 for a quiver of 10 arrows. Price What one purchase costs, in the merchant's money. Stock at the start How many purchases before they run out: 1 for a unique sword, 0 for no limit. Buy-back What the merchant pays if the player sells them one: a Sell button appears. 0: they buy none.

Buying takes the price from the inventory, then gives the item; selling does the reverse, one item at a time. The window says it clearly when money is missing ("You need 5 more Gold."), when the inventory has no room left (the player then keeps their money), or when an item is sold out.

Each purchase and each sale tells the game (boutique.achat, boutique.vente): a sound, a quest step ("Buy a sword"), a Trigger rule.

A merchant who also has a Dialogue talks first. The player uses them: the conversation opens, alone. On its last line, next to End, a Show me your goods button closes the conversation and opens the shop. Nothing to untick, nothing to write. To put the way into the shop elsewhere in the conversation (an answer "Show me your weapons" in the middle), give that answer the event boutique.ouvrir with the next step fin: the Dialogue then does not add its own button. Unticking Opens when the player uses it also removes that button: the shop then only opens through boutique.ouvrir.

Its settings are in the Shop system reference.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Quest log: quests that move on by themselves
items.text:
The Quest log system is for the whole game. Its quests are written in its setting The quests and their steps, Game tab, Systems section: a Quest row, then its Step rows, in order.

A quest has a title, a description, and a start:

  • when the game starts;
  • when an event happens: a Dialogue answer ("I accept" sends wolves.accepted), a Trigger rule;
  • when a mark is set by a Dialogue;
  • when another quest ends: a chain of quests.

A step says what to do ("Defeat 3 wolves") and what ends it:

  • an event, as many times as needed, and only for the object named if one is given: sante.mort for "Wolf", 3 times, counts three wolves defeated (and not the bear); dialogue.fin for "Miller", a talk with him finished; zone.entree for a zone, a place reached;
  • a mark set by a Dialogue;
  • items carried: 3 "Wolf pelt" in the inventory;
  • items handed over: on an event (dialogue.fin for "Miller"), if the player carries 3 "Wolf pelt", the inventory takes them back and the step is done. Otherwise, an announcement says how many are missing ("Not enough: Wolf pelt 2/3").

Steps are done one after the other (the log does not reveal what comes next), or all at the same time if Steps one after the other is unticked. When all are done, the quest ends and gives its reward (items, such as 50 "Gold"). A finished quest or step can also set a mark (the miller thanks the player, his Dialogue sees it) and send an event (a Trigger rule makes the bridge appear).

A quest can also fail (setting Fails): when an event happens (sante.mort for "Merchant": the merchant to escort is dead), when a mark is set, or when time runs out (Time to finish it, in seconds of play: the tracker and the log show what is left). The player can abandon it from the log (Abandon button, a second press confirms), unless The player can abandon it is unticked. A failed or abandoned quest gives no reward; it can set its own mark and send its own event (the miller complains), and, if Can be taken up again is ticked, what gives it gives it again from the start.

What the player sees:

  • an announcement at the top of the screen for each new quest, each step done and each quest finished (with its reward), failed or abandoned;
  • the current step, on the right of the screen, with the progress ("Defeat 3 wolves (2/3)");
  • the log, with the J key (or → on a gamepad): the quests in progress with their steps, then the finished ones, then the failed or abandoned ones. It scrolls with the mouse wheel, and the same key closes it.

A miller who asks to hunt the wolves:

Row Kind Content Starts or ends 1 Quest "The mill's wolves", reward 50 Gold when the event wolves.accepted happens (the miller's "I accept" answer) 2 Step "Defeat 3 wolves", sets the mark wolves_hunted the event sante.mort for "Wolf", 3 times 3 Step "Go back to the miller" the event wolves.returned (the answer "Here they are", offered if the mark wolves_hunted is set)

Its settings and events are in the Quest log system reference.

No map yet

Unlike the Dialogue, quests do not have a map view yet: they are written in the settings list, and the agent can write them for you.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: What a saved game keeps
items.text:
When the game saves (a key, a checkpoint: ask the agent, which has a recipe for it), every system stores its own state in the save, and takes it back when loading:

System What it keeps Inventory What the player carries, kind by kind. Quest log The quests started, finished, failed or abandoned, the steps done, what is already counted ("2 wolves out of 3"), the time left to a timed quest. Shop What each merchant has left of the items with a limited stock. Dialogue The marks set, and the conversations already had with each one.

The player therefore goes on where they were: in the middle of a quest, after a purchase. Items given back when loading do not make the pickup sound.

The game also keeps the world: what the game changed in every scene visited (an object hidden, moved, destroyed or copied, a light, a door opened, the camera...) comes back as it was when loading. Nothing to do for it: see Saved games.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Map: the minimap, the big map and its markers
items.text:
The Map system is for the whole game, and is also placed on the objects to mark. Once activated:

  • the minimap, in a corner of the screen (bottom right by default), shows the world around the player, seen from above. The player is the white arrow in the middle; a small N marks north. It can be round or square, bigger or smaller, show nearer or farther, and turn with the player instead of keeping north at the top;
  • the big map opens with the M key (or ↓ on a gamepad) and closes the same way: the whole scene, with the player and the markers, their name written under them. The wheel zooms around the mouse, holding the mouse drags the map, and so do the gamepad's left stick and the walking keys. On a gamepad, the right trigger (RT) zooms in and the left trigger (LT) zooms out while held; on a keyboard, Page Up and Page Down. They are two controls of the game, Zoom the big map in and Zoom the big map out, whose keys can be changed in the Game tab. The world stops meanwhile (setting Stop the game while the big map is open).

The picture of the map is taken by the game itself: when the game starts, it photographs the scene from above (the terrain, its waters, its plants, the buildings), without the player or the characters, who move. It can be replaced by a drawn map (setting Drawn map): by default, it covers the same square of the world as the game's picture; otherwise, you give its west edge, its north edge and its side, in meters.

A marker, without code: place the Map system on an object (a town, a cave, a chest). In its properties:

Setting What it says Name on the map Written under the marker on the big map. Empty: the object's name, without number. Shape of the marker Circle, diamond, triangle, square, star, or an image (a sword icon for the forge). Color of the marker, Size of the marker Its color (it tints an image), and its size: 2 for a town. When it shows on the map Always; once discovered up close, when the player comes within the discovery distance (a message announces it; a saved game keeps the places discovered); or hidden, except as a quest objective. Objective of the quest The title of a quest: while it is in progress (or only during the step given), this marker is its objective.

Placed on a folder, the system gives a single marker for everything it holds, in place of the folder.

What marks itself: merchants (Shop system, a golden diamond) and characters who talk (Dialogue system, a light blue circle), named after their shop or their character. Placing Map on one of them chooses its look.

Quest objectives: during a step of the Quest log (above) that aims at named objects ("Defeat 3 wolves", for Wolf), their markers are ringed with the color of the objectives, even when usually hidden; on the minimap, a far objective stays at its edge, in its direction. The Quest log is not changed: the map only listens to what it announces.

The game can react when the big map opens or closes (carte.ouverte) and when a marker is discovered (carte.decouvert); a Trigger rule or a Dialogue answer can reveal a place (carte.reveler), like a villager who points to the cave. Its settings and events are in the Map system reference.

No fog of war yet

The parts of the world where the player has not been yet are not hidden in black yet: only markers wait to be discovered.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: The Interface system: the look of everything shown
items.text:
The Interface system gives its style to the whole game interface, from one place. It applies to the whole game and is not placed on objects.

  1. Game tab, Systems section: Activate under Interface (see The Game tab).
  2. Open its card: its settings apply at once to everything the game shows. A color is chosen by clicking its swatch, which opens a color picker.
Setting What it changes Panel background color Menus, windows, lists. Button and field background color Buttons and text fields. Accent color: hovered button, selected field, scroll bar What is under the mouse or chosen. Text color All texts. Text size (share of the screen height) The text keeps the same relative size whatever the window. Corner rounding (share of the screen height, 0: square corners) The shape of panels, buttons and fields. Background opacity (0: transparent, 1: solid) Lets the game show through the backgrounds, or not.

The exact values and their limits are in the Interface system reference.

A script can give an element its own color or size: it wins over the theme. To keep control of the style from one place, ask the agent to use the theme rather than colors written in the scripts. Without the Interface system, the interface keeps its original look.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Asking the agent
items.text:
A few requests:

  • "Add a title screen and a pause." The agent then activates the Menu system.
  • "The blacksmith offers to repair the sword; if the player accepts, the workshop door opens." The agent places a Dialogue on the blacksmith and a Trigger rule on the door.
  • "The blacksmith sells a sword for 30 gold coins and potions, and buys back wolf pelts." The agent places a Shop on the blacksmith.
  • "The miller asks to hunt three wolves, for 50 gold coins." The agent writes the quest in the Quest log, and the answer that gives it in the miller's Dialogue.
  • "At the start of the game, ask the player for their name, then show "Welcome, [name]!"."
  • "A chat window at the bottom left, with a scrolling history."
  • "Give the interface a dark and gold style." The agent then changes the settings of the Interface system, not every script.

To check a menu, the agent runs the game without a window: it sees where each element was placed, what overflows a list, how the texts wrap, then looks at the game's image. You can also try it yourself with Play (F5).

To go further, all the interface functions (game.hud_panel, game.hud_input...) are in the scripts reference.
path: The game interface: menus, lists, text fields

items.title: Getting started
items.text: This page takes you from creating a project to a running game. Each step links to the page that details it.

items.title: 1. Create a project
items.text:
File > New project...: choose where to put it and its name ("My game" is suggested). A project is a folder that holds your whole game: its scenes, the models it uses, its settings. See Projects and scenes.

Right after, the Creation assistant offers two choices:

  • With the assistant: it asks you a few questions about your game (the story, the mood, days and nights going by, the places, the character, what one does, people to talk to, merchants, quests, a title screen...), one step at a time. Each choice tells the agent which system brings it: ticking "Buy and sell at merchants" asks it for the Shop. Next moves on, Skip skips a question, Back returns. At the end, it prepares Your request to the agent: read it, change it if you like, then Launch sends it to the agent, which first presents its plan and waits for your go-ahead before building. Save and close keeps your answers for later.
  • Start from scratch: you build yourself, or by talking directly to the agent.

The assistant reopens at any time with Game > Creation assistant...; your answers are kept in the project.

items.title: 2. The window
items.text:
• At the top: the menus (File, Edit, Select, Object, View, Game, Agent, Help), a few buttons in the middle (gizmo axes, snapping, four views, undo, redo), and on the right the Preferences (gear) and the Play button.
  • On the left: three tabs. Scene lists what is in the scene, Game holds the game's controls and systems, Scripts its scripts.
  • In the middle: the 3D view, with its tool column on the left.
  • At the bottom: the Library, your models and sounds.
  • On the right: the Properties of what is selected, and the Agent panel. Each folds with its chevron; a handle between them shares the height.
  • At the very bottom, the status bar: Library opens or closes the library, the editor's last message (a click opens the Console), and on the right the agent's state, the time of the last automatic backup, the number of selected objects and the number of objects in the scene.

Each part has its page: see The editor.

items.title: 3. Add models
items.text:
1. Add a folder of models to the library: Add a folder, then Browse or paste its path. You can also drag a folder from File Explorer onto the window.
  2. In the library, double-click a model to add it to the scene, or drag it into the 3D view, where you want it.
  3. For a simple shape: Object > Create (Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Capsule, Plane), or right-click in the list of the Scene tab.
