Double-clicked, the model arrives at the center of the view; dragged, it arrives where you drop it. The Place on ground when adding preference, on by default, then sets it on the ground. The model's file is copied into the project: your library never changes.

items.title: 4. Place objects
items.text:
• Select: click the object, in the view or in the list. Ctrl + click adds to the selection; dragging in the view draws a rectangle.
  • Move, rotate, scale: keys W, E, R, or the tool column on the left of the view, then pull the handles (the gizmo). Or type the values in the Properties, Position and size section.
  • Place on ground: End key, or the Place on ground button in the properties.
  • Look around: hold the right mouse button to orbit, the middle button to pan, the wheel to zoom, F to frame the selection.

See The 3D view.

items.title: 5. Choose the player
items.text: The game needs a character to play. Select a model (an animated character, preferably), then click Set as player in its Properties. Its properties then show its Movement, its Animations and the Player camera: see The properties.

items.title: 6. Play
items.text:
F5, or the Play button at the top right. The game opens in its own window; the editor stays open beside it. While the game runs, the player settings you change in the properties apply live. F5 or Stop closes the game.

In the game, the player moves with the game controls: by default W A S D on a QWERTY keyboard (Z Q S D on AZERTY), Left Shift to run, Space to jump, the mouse to turn the camera. Esc frees the mouse.

items.title: 7. Undo
items.text: Everything can be undone, your changes and the agent's: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Y redoes. The same commands are in the Edit menu and as arrows in the middle of the top bar. Under each answer of the agent, Undo these changes undoes everything it did during that turn.

items.title: 8. Save
items.text: Ctrl+S saves the scene. Every 60 seconds, an automatic backup keeps a separate copy, without touching your file. If the editor closes before you saved, it offers to Recover your work on the next launch.

items.title: 9. Ask the agent
items.text: In the Agent panel, describe what you want to build and press Enter. The agent works in the scene before your eyes. See The agent.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
• Windows. WorldMint only runs on Windows for now.
  • A graphics card that supports Vulkan 1.3, with an up-to-date driver. Vulkan is what lets WorldMint draw in 3D. Recent NVIDIA, AMD and Intel graphics cards support it, as long as their driver (the card's software) is up to date. If yours is too old, WorldMint says so as soon as it opens: update the driver, from the NVIDIA, AMD or Intel website or through Windows Update, then start it again. Once the editor is open, the status bar, at the bottom of the window, shows the card in use.
  • 3D models, if you want to build with your own: .glb, .gltf, .fbx or .obj files. The editor ships none; you add their folders to the library.
  • For the agent: a Claude account (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise subscription, or usage-based billing) or a ChatGPT account for Codex. The editor installs the program that makes the link for you: see The agent.

items.title: Installing WorldMint
items.text:
WorldMint is installed with an installer, like most Windows programs. The installer will be available with the beta.

  1. Download the WorldMint installer.
  2. Run it (double-click) and follow its steps.
  3. Open WorldMint.

items.title: The first launch
items.text:
On the first launch, WorldMint creates an empty project, Mon premier jeu, in Documents\WorldMint\, and opens it. On later launches, it reopens the last scene you had open. A project is an ordinary folder, which you find in File Explorer (File > Open project folder): see Projects and scenes.

The editor uses the language of Windows, French or English. To change it: Help > Language, or the Preferences.

Then:

  1. Add your models: in the Library, at the bottom, click Add a folder, or drag a folder from File Explorer onto the editor window.
  2. Connect the agent: in the Agent panel, on the right, choose Claude or Codex, then how you want to sign in.
  3. Follow Getting started.

items.title: Where your settings are
items.text: The editor's preferences (language, theme, library folders, recent scenes) are kept in %APPDATA%\WorldMint\Editeur\preferences.json. They apply to all your projects. An API key you give the editor is kept encrypted for your Windows session.

items.title: Launch options
items.text:
For command-line users, WorldMint.exe accepts a project file (.worldmint) or scene file (.wmscene) to open, and these options:

Option Effect --project <folder or file> Opens this project, on its start scene. --scene <file> Opens this scene. --assets <folder> Adds this folder to the library for this session (the option can be repeated; your preferences keep nothing of it). --language fr or --language en Chooses the interface language. --low-power Prefers the most power-saving graphics card (a laptop with two cards). --no-preferences Starts with default preferences, without reading or writing yours.

items.title: Light and shadows
items.text: A scene's light comes from the sun, the sky and the ground, and from the lights you place. It is set in the game settings: deselect everything (or click the game's line, at the very top of the Scene tab), Sky and light section.

items.title: The sun, the sky and the ground
items.text:
Setting Effect Sun color, Sun intensity The color and strength of its light. A white surface facing the sun takes exactly its color. Sun direction Where it shines from (X, Y, Z): positive Y, it is up. Shadows go the opposite way. Sky The color of the sky's light: it lights everything, even in the shade, and is reflected by what is smooth or metal. Light from the ground The light bounced by the ground, which lights the underside of objects. Exposure How much light reaches the image, as on a camera. With automatic exposure, it adds to what the eye chose. Automatic exposure Like an eye getting used to it: when you walk into a dark place (a house lit by a small window, a cave), the image brightens over a second or two, and comes back when you walk out, without dazzling. In sunlight, the image does not change. On by default, also for scenes made before it. Brighten up to How many times brighter the image can get in the dark: 1 never, 4 by default (a dark room becomes readable without turning into daylight). Darken up to How many times darker it can get under a very strong light: 1 never (default: a sunny scene stays as you set it), 2 to 4 for a glare when walking out of a cave. Adaptation time The time the eye takes to get used to the dark: 1.5 s by default; it gets used to light three times faster. 0: at once.

In the editor, the views show the image once the eye is used to it; you see it brighten little by little in the game. A passage to another scene or a teleport arrives already used to it, without a flash. Night stays night: with the day and night cycle (or a script that lowers the sun), the eye only brightens what is darker than the current daylight; a dark house at noon is brightened, nightfall is not. Scripts set it with game.set_environment (auto_exposure, auto_exposure_brighten, auto_exposure_darken, auto_exposure_seconds).

items.title: Sun shadows
items.text:
Objects, characters, terrain and plants cast their shadow in the sun: on the ground, on the water and on each other, and also on the smoke, dust, rain or snow passing below them, and on decals. So does the object a character holds. Shadows are soft at their edges and don't flicker when the camera moves.

Setting Effect Sun shadows Unticked: no sun shadows, lighter rendering. Shadow quality For the sun and the lights (fires included). Depends on the computer: low on an integrated graphics chip (most laptops), high on a graphics card. High: sharp all the way. Medium: one shadow slice less in the distance, fewer lights with shadows. Low: blurrier up close, lighter to draw. Off: no shadows at all, from the sun or the lights, the lightest. In the editor, it never goes above the View quality (Preferences); the game follows it. The player can also choose their own in the game menu (Shadows row). Shadow distance How far around the camera they are drawn (150 m by default). Beyond that, they fade out gently. The further it is, the less sharp they are up close: for a game seen up close (a dungeon), 50 to 100 m is enough. Shadow softness Softens their edge as under a real sun: the shadow stays sharp at the foot of an object and gets softer further from it (a pole's shadow, sharp at its base, blurred at its end). It is the size of the sun in the sky, in degrees: 0 sharp (default), 0.5 the real sun, 2 to 4 a hazy sky, up to 10 very soft.

Shadows also show in the editor's view, except in wireframe only.

If the game is slow on a laptop

Lower the Shadow distance, or set Shadow quality to Low, or Off as a last resort. On an integrated chip, Depends on the computer already picks Low. Shadow softness costs a little more in High and Medium (the penumbra is searched at each point); in Low, it is only a fixed blur, almost free.

items.title: Fog and glow
items.text:
In the distance, the scene always fades gently into the Background color instead of being cut off: that is the horizon fog, with no setting. For more, in Sky and light:

Setting Effect Fog distance A fog over the whole scene: at this distance, it hides almost everything in its color. 0: none. A light mist: 300 to 800 m; a thick fog: 40 to 100 m. It also hides what is too far to be drawn. Fog color The color of what is in the fog, and of the sky behind it. Fog altitude, Thins out with height A fog that stays low (a valley, a swamp, the mist over the sea): at its altitude it has the set thickness, below it gets thicker, above it halves every so many meters (5 to 30). 0: the same everywhere. Glow of bright lights A soft glow around what shines very brightly: a material giving off light, the sun shining on water or metal, a lamp close by. 1 by default, discreet; 0: none. Sand or snow in full sun don't get it.

items.title: Volumetric fog: rays of light
items.text:
Turn on Volumetric fog (in Sky and light) so that sunlight shows in the air, with the shadow of whatever hides it: rays between trees and through windows, a darker mist under the leaves, a brighter one when looking toward the sun. The fog keeps its Distance and Color (it hides as much as before); it also works without fog, thanks to the air.

Setting Effect Rays in the air A slightly hazy air that shows the rays even without fog. 0: none; 0.2 by default, mostly when looking toward the sun; 1: very strong, from the side too. In a room, a little fog (dust) shows the rays from the windows. Scattering toward the sun How much brighter the mist shines when looking toward the sun. 0: the same everywhere; 0.3 by default; 0.6 to 0.9: a strong glow around the sun, bright rays against the light.

Rays need a sun low enough to pass between things (a Sun direction whose height, the second value, is small), and something that casts shadows: trees, walls. With ray tracing, the shadow in the mist comes from rays, through the gaps in the leaves; without it, from shadow maps: the same look.

Depending on the computer

In Low quality (an integrated chip), the fog stays the usual one, without its rays. In Medium (the editor's views) and High, it is light: a few hundredths of a millisecond per frame on a recent graphics card, the same whatever the image size.

items.title: Fog in one area only: the fog volume
items.text:
The fog of Sky and light covers the whole map. For a mist that stays in its place (a valley floor, an undergrowth, a marsh, the smoke of a cave), choose Create > Fog volume: an invisible box that the fog fills, and that fades out towards its edges. Move it and scale it like an object; several volumes can overlap. Its settings are those of the Fog volume system: its Visibility (at this distance you can hardly see anything), its Color, its Soft edges, and Thicker at the bottom for a mist that stays on the ground.

With volumetric fog on, the volume catches the sun's rays and shadows: a volume in a forest, with no fog in Sky and light (Distance at 0), shows rays there only. In Low quality, and far from the camera (beyond the shadow distance), it is drawn without its shadows, but always in its place.

items.title: Sun rays without mist: the glowing air
items.text:
For sun rays in a forest or a room, like dust lit by the sun, without a veil over the rest, choose Create > Glowing air (or, in a fog volume's properties, Kind: Glowing air (rays only)). It is an almost invisible air: it only shows where the sun crosses it, mostly when looking toward the sun, and the air in the shade stays clear. Its Air visibility sets how strong the rays are (200 m by default; 100 m for strong rays, 400 m for a light trace); it has no colour (it takes the sun's). It needs volumetric fog on, in High or Medium quality, and a sun low enough to pass between foliage or walls; in Low quality it does not show.

You want Choose Sun rays in the forest, through a window Glowing air The mist of a valley, a marsh, smoke Fog volume

items.title: Placed lights
items.text:
A lamp, a torch, a street lamp, a lit window, a spotlight on a stage: Create > Light (in the scene list). It appears a little above where you look; move it like an object.

  • A Bulb lights all around it; a Spotlight lights in a cone, toward the bottom of the object: turn it to aim.
  • Its Color is the object's. Its Intensity is its strength at 1 m: it falls off with distance, and fades out gently at its Range.
  • There can be many: each point of the image only computes the lights that reach it. Keep ranges short (a room: 5 to 10 m), that is what costs.
  • Light's shadows: what it lights casts its shadow. Only a few lights at a time get them, the closest to the camera (six spotlights, or one bulb, in low quality; twice as many in high). Keep them for the ones that matter.
  • Shadow softness (with its shadows): the size of what gives the light, in meters. 0 sharp, 0.05 a bare bulb, 0.3 a lantern or a globe. As in the sun, the shadow stays sharp at the foot of an object and gets softer further from it.
  • For them to show, it takes a bit of night: lower the Sun intensity and darken the Sky and the Light from the ground.
  • They light everything around them: objects and terrain, but also water (a lamp at the edge of a lake is reflected in it), smoke, dust, rain and snow passing near them, and decals. Fire, sparks and magic make their own light: lights don't change them.

items.title: The light of fires and effects
items.text:
A fire, an explosion, magic, sparks or the flash of a hit light up what is around them: each carries its own light, with nothing to place next to it. It follows the effect, takes its colour (a blue fire lights in blue), grows with its Size, comes on with it and goes out after its last flames. A fire's light flickers and moves a little with the flames; an explosion's is a flash that dies out in less than a second; magic's sways slowly.

Fire, explosions and magic cast shadows: a cube next to a campfire casts its shadow on the ground and on the wall behind it, as soft as the width of the flames. Sparks and hits, too brief, have none. The object carrying the effect (the logs of a campfire, the head of a torch) casts no shadow from its own light.

In the effect's properties (Particle effect system):

  • Effect light: With its shadows (default), Without shadows (the light alone, lighter), or None (the effect is only drawn).
  • Light strength: multiplied; 0.5 for a discreet glow, 2 for a blaze that lights the whole camp.

These lights count with the placed lights: the closest to the camera first, within the same limit (and the same shadow limit). They follow the Shadow quality, show in the editor's view while you set the effect, and change nothing in the game: only the image.

In the game, the Trigger switches them on, off (Switch a light on, Switch a light off, in turn) or changes their color: a lever lighting a lamp, an alarm turning red. Scripts do it with game.light and game.set_light (see the scripts reference). Hiding a light switches it off too.

When the game saves, the lights go into the save: a lamp switched on or off, recoloured or made brighter or dimmer during the game comes back as it was when loading, with nothing to write (see Saved games).

items.title: Rendering quality
items.text:
At startup, WorldMint picks a rendering quality for the computer: Low on an integrated graphics chip, High on a graphics card. Settings set to Depends on the computer follow it. To try the other one, start the game with --qualite basse or --qualite haute.

It also sets the terrain: in Low, the relief is simplified a little sooner in the distance, a large map's detail loads up to 500 m instead of 1 km, and plants stop at 60 % of their distance (see The terrain).

items.title: Materials
items.text:
A material says what a surface is made of: stone, wood, metal, grass, sand, snow... Its color, whether it is smooth or matte, whether it is metal, its relief and the light it gives off. It is a file of the project, kept in the materials/ folder: you create it once, put it on as many objects as you like, and changing it changes them all.

WorldMint ships a small starter library made of real royalty-free textures (ambientCG, CC0): Snow, Rock, Grass, Forest floor, Sand, Mud, Dirt, Cobblestones, Wooden planks, Brushed metal. Choosing one copies it into your project, with its images.

items.title: The material of an object
items.text:
Select an object (a model or a base shape): its properties have a Material section.

Setting Effect Material The model's own keeps its own colors. Otherwise, a material of the project, or one from the Library (copied into the project). New material Creates a material, with your name, put on the selected objects.

A material shows a preview on a sphere, under the light of the scene, and its settings:

Setting Effect Name The name you see in the lists. Color Tints the color image (white: as is). Roughness 0: smooth and shiny, like a mirror. 1: matte, like stone. Metal 0: stone, wood, plastic. 1: metal, which reflects its color. Pattern size The size of one repeat of the image, in meters. Placement On the model: the image follows the model's texture coordinates. Without stretching: it is laid by the world, at the same size on every face, even on an enlarged shape. The right choice for walls, floors and rocks. Image relief The strength of the relief map: 0 removes it, 2 doubles it. Emitted light Its color and strength: 0 nothing, higher the surface glows by itself (screens, lamps, lava). Shader A surface that moves or glows by itself: a hologram, a dissolve, lava, wind in the leaves. Choose a recipe, tune its sliders: see Shaders. Images Color, relief (normal map), roughness, metal, shadow of hollows, height, emitted light: the path of an image of the project, or drag one from the explorer.

Each setting is undone with Ctrl+Z. The material file is written when you save (and before the game starts).

items.title: Ground materials
items.text:
A terrain first shows the colors of its regions. Select the Terrain object: the Ground materials section offers Cover with materials. Each region then gets a real material (grass for plains and forests, rock, snow, sand for deserts and beaches, mud for swamps), and three automatic rules are added:

Rule Where it lays its material Slope On ground steeper than an angle (rock on cliffs). Altitude Above a height (snow on peaks). Water's edge Within a distance of water (sand on beaches).

Each rule has its material, its threshold and its Transition (the width of the fade, which waves so as not to draw a line). They apply in order: the last one wins. A switch turns each off.

  • Add: one more material to paint (16 at most). The cross removes it; its painting is erased.
  • Ground material, in the properties of a region: the material that covers it.
  • Variation: slightly lighter or darker areas, and the pattern blended with a larger copy of itself; the repetition of the images no longer shows.
  • Back to the region colors: the ground takes back its colors (Ctrl+Z to return).

On cliffs, the images are laid on the three axes: rock does not stretch. Where two materials blend, the one with the higher relief wins: pebbles stand out of the sand instead of a plain fade.

items.title: The Materials brush
items.text:
In the tool column of the view, Materials paints a material on the ground, over the one of the regions and the rules: hand painting always wins.

Setting Effect Size The radius of the brush, in meters. Strength How fast it covers. Softness 0: a sharp edge. 1: a fade from the center to the edge. The small circle shows where it covers fully. Material The one you paint, among those of the ground. Eraser Erases the painting: the ground takes back the material of its region and of the rules.

Each brush stroke is undone with Ctrl+Z. The painting is stored in tiles of 64 m: a stroke only touches the tiles it covers.

Regions still decide the vegetation, the footsteps and the systems: materials only change the look of the ground.

items.title: With the agent
items.text: The agent can make the same gestures: list, create and put materials, cover the ground, set the rules, paint an area (a square, a field), along a line (a path) or in dabs, erase, then check what covers the ground at a point and look at the result in an image. Each gesture is undone with Ctrl+Z.

items.title: Creating a move
items.text:
A model doesn't always have the move you need: a wolf without a walk, a guard who doesn't wave, a missing attack. Create it in the tool: keyframes bone by bone in the timeline, played in a loop, saved as a move of the model. Systems, timelines and scripts then play it like the moves of the files.

Nothing is specific to a model pack: the skeleton is read from the model, and angles are given around the character's axes, as when adjusting a pose.

items.title: Creating a move
items.text:
1. Select the character in the scene (the player, a guard, an animal: any model with a skeleton).
  2. In its Properties, open Skeleton pose and click Create a move.
  3. Give it a name ("Walk", "Wave"), a length, say whether it is Looping, and choose what it starts from:
    • The rest pose: an empty move, to build;
    • An existing move: read as keyframes, ten per second, to correct it without touching the original file;
    • The adjustment layer: its pose becomes the first keyframe.
  4. The timeline opens at the bottom, on this move: one row per animated bone, grouped by body part (head, back and hips, arms, legs, other bones), each keyframe a diamond.

items.title: Setting keyframes
items.text:
1. Place the playhead: click or drag on the ruler of seconds, or click on a row.
  2. Click a bone, in the view, in the list of bones or on its row in the timeline.
  3. Turn it with the gizmo (E), or move its point (W): the hips move, a hand or a foot bends the arm or the leg, the head or the back lean. Or type its angles under Bone rotation (and, for the hips, Bone offset). With Auto keyframe (on at first), a keyframe is set at the playhead.
  4. Do it again at another moment. Space (the mouse over the timeline) plays the move in a loop.

Every gesture is undone with Ctrl+Z, even on several keyframes at once (with the mouse over the timeline, Delete, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V and Ctrl+A go to the keyframes, not to the objects of the scene).

Gesture What it does Click a diamond Chooses this keyframe. On the row of a body part or on "All keyframes", all its bones at that moment. Ctrl+click, Shift+click, rectangle As in File Explorer: Ctrl+click adds or removes a keyframe from the choice, Shift+click chooses everything since the last click on this row, a rectangle dragged in empty space chooses what it covers (with Ctrl or Shift, in addition). Ctrl+A chooses them all, Escape none. Drag a diamond Moves all the chosen keyframes in time, together, by the same amount. Right-click a row Keyframe here, Remove keyframes, Copy keyframes, Paste keyframes here, Interpolation, Copy the pose, Paste the pose. Delete Removes the chosen keyframes. Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V Copies the chosen keyframes, then pastes them at the playhead with their spacing (into another move too). Interpolation For the chosen keyframes: linear (steady), smooth (slow at start and end), stepped (it jumps from one pose to the next). Ctrl+wheel, Shift+wheel, Show all Zooms around the mouse, scrolls (or drag the bar under the tracks), then goes back to the whole length. Keyframe Sets a keyframe of the chosen bone at the playhead, or of every animated bone if none is chosen. Copy the pose, Paste the pose Copies the angles of every bone to another moment (the end of a step takes back its start). Copy the left onto the right (or the reverse) The right side takes the left side's pose at that moment, seen in a mirror. Mirror The bone on the other side follows each gesture, as in a mirror. Close the loop Copies the first pose to the end. When looping, a bone with a keyframe at the start already goes back to it at the end. Onion skin Shows the skeleton a little before and a little after, in pale lines. Feet on the ground Turning the hips or the back leaves the feet where they are: the legs bend by themselves (to crouch, to lean). Bone gizmo Turn (E) rotates the bone; Move (W) takes its point where you drag it (the Move and Rotate buttons of the toolbar do the same). A hand or a foot bends the two bones above it. Bend direction For a moved hand or foot: the elbow or knee bends as in the model's rest pose, otherwise the elbow backward and the knee forward; Forward or Backward force it. Move length, Looping, Move name Can be changed at any time. The same name as a move of the file replaces it everywhere.

Angles are given around the character's axes at rest (as for a pose adjustment): for a model facing forward, X raises a leg or an arm forward (negative angle) or backward, Y turns the bone on itself, Z tilts it sideways.

items.title: Example: a walk for a wolf
items.text:
A walk cycle needs only a few keyframes. For a four-legged animal, at a trot, the legs go in diagonal pairs:

  1. Create "Wolf walk", 1 second, in a loop, from the rest pose.
  2. At 0 s: the front left and back right legs forward (negative X), the other two backward.
  3. At 0.5 s: the reverse (copy the pose of 0 s, paste it, then copy left onto right).
  4. At 0.25 s and 0.75 s: bend the lower part of the leg coming back forward, so it leaves the ground.
  5. Play it in a loop, tune it, then give "Wolf walk" to a system's animation setting (an enemy on patrol), or play it from a script: game.play(id, "Wolf walk").

items.title: Where the move goes
items.text:
It is a file of the project, animations/<name>.wmanim, saved with it. It belongs to the model: every character using this model has it, like the moves of its file (the player in its animation graph, characters through their systems, timelines, scripts). An exported game takes it along. On another model, add it to the player's animation files: it is borrowed like a file, through the bone map.

Pose layers are added on top of this move too, in the game.

items.title: If the model moves
items.text:
The move and the pose adjustments follow the path of their model, and an adjustment follows the name of the move it targets:

  • Rename or move the model in the library (right-click the project model: Rename, F2, or Move to; or drag it onto a folder): whatever uses it follows, the objects of every scene, its moves, its pose adjustments. Ctrl+Z puts the file back. A .gltf, .obj or .fbx, which keep files next to them, can only be renamed in place.
  • Rename the move (Move name): the pose adjustments that targeted it follow, in the same Ctrl+Z.
  • A link broken outside the editor (the model deleted or moved in File Explorer, a changed animation file): Skeleton pose says so in red, and offers Attach to this model, or Attach to a move for an adjustment.

items.title: With the agent
items.text: Just ask: "make a walk for the wolf". The agent reads the bones (pose_layers_get), creates the move (skeleton_animation_set), reads it back (skeleton_animation_get), looks at it frame by frame (view_capture with animation), in a single step that Ctrl+Z undoes. It never touches the model file.

items.title: Playing with several players
items.text: Your game can be played by several players: one player hosts the game on their PC, their friends join it by its address, and each has their own character. Players see each other move, what moves in the world is the same for everyone, everyone hears the game's sounds, and the group follows the host from one scene to the next.

items.title: Three things to remember
items.text:
1. The game is played on the host's computer. The others see and hear what it sends them.
  2. Each player has their own character, interface and controls. A copy of the player's character, with its animations, that walks, runs, jumps, swims, drives and aims like it, with their own health, bag and menus.
  3. A single-player game doesn't change. As long as the setting is off, nothing is different.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
With nothing selected, in the game properties, open Multiplayer and tick Several players. Three settings appear:

Setting What it does Default Players at most How many players in a game, the host included (2 to 8). 4 works anywhere; beyond that, the host needs a good connection 4 Network port The "door" number through which the others arrive. Change it only if it is already taken 48600 Updates per second How many times per second the host sends each player what moves 20

You can also ask the agent: "my game is played by four".

items.title: Trying it in the editor
items.text: In Game ▸ Play with several players (or the button of the same name, in the game settings, Multiplayer section), the editor starts the game twice on this PC: one window hosts the game, the other joins it as a friend. You try both sides this way, without exporting or typing an address. Stop closes both.

items.title: Playing with friends
items.text:
In the game, the Menu (the catalog's system) has two more buttons, on the title screen and in the pause:

  • Host a game: the game becomes an online game. The pause then says how many friends are there, and lets you stop it.
  • Join a game: type the address of the hosting PC (for example 192.168.1.20), then Join. If it fails (game full, another version of the game, nobody answers), the menu says so.

It also works from a command prompt: MyGame.exe --heberger, and MyGame.exe --rejoindre 192.168.1.20 --nom Lea.

Each friend has a key of their own, and the first time they come, the host hands them a secret token, kept on both PCs. When the host resumes a saved game, the friend who comes back with their token finds their bag, health, quests and place again. Someone who took their key without their token arrives as a new player: they get nothing back.

On the host's first start, Windows may ask to allow the game on the network: that is normal. To play over the Internet without changing anything on one's router, the matchmaking service planned later will be needed; until then, the local network works right away.

items.title: What each player sees
items.text:
• Their own character moves right away, without waiting for the host's answer: if the host saw something else (a wall, another player blocking the way), the character is gently put back in place.
  • The other players are shown a tenth of a second in the past, so they glide smoothly even if a message is lost. A pose adjustment that a script switches on or off on a player (game.pose_layer) shows for everyone, on that player.
  • Objects that the rules or physics move, show, hide or destroy change for everyone, like what a player builds, and an object that bursts bursts for everyone.
  • Their own interface: their health, bag, needs and menus. Online, a menu does not stop the game: it only holds the one who opens it.

items.title: Changing scenes, ending the game, sounds
items.text:
• The group follows the host: when the host goes to another scene (a door, a passage), the friends arrive there with them, around them, with their bag and health. If the host starts over, they start over too.
  • The end of the game (won or lost) shows for everyone. The host is the one who plays again.
  • Sounds: what happens in the world (footsteps, hits, the music) is heard by everyone, each from where they stand; the sounds of a player's interface (a click in their menu) are only heard by them.

items.title: Rules and scripts
items.text:
The game's rules only run on the host. A script there sees every player with game.players(), and receives "joueur.arrivee" when a friend arrives and "joueur.depart" when they leave.

A rule that says "the player" must say which one: the one who touched, the nearest, or all. The catalog's systems already do: what a player owns or feels (their health, bag, hunger, quests) is theirs; what is in the world (the time of day, trees, buildings, enemies) is everyone's. A script written for each player carries the line -- multijoueur: par_joueur: it then runs once per player.

items.title: What doesn't work yet
items.text:
• Videos and particles started by the rules are only seen on the host.
  • Players join by the host PC's address: no code to share yet, and no game found by itself on the local network.

items.title: Security
items.text: A game that receives messages from other PCs protects itself: each message is checked (its size, its numbers, the player's name) and refused at the slightest mismatch; a message never carries a script or a file. The host refuses a friend with another version of the game or a game already full, and closes the connection of a friend who sends damaged messages or far too many messages. Exchanges are encrypted. The editor itself never receives anything from the network.

items.title: Physics, zones and character walking
items.text: Two game systems bring objects to life without a script: Physics, for what falls, rolls and gets pushed, and Zone, to know who enters a place. The engine runs them itself; they are set in the Properties, and the agent can place them for you.

items.title: Physics: objects that move
items.text:
Objects that carry the Physics system fall, roll, slide, bounce, and the player pushes them by walking into them, as characters do: crates, barrels, a ball, rocks, a cart.

  1. Activate the system: Game tab, Systems section, Activate under Physics (see The Game tab).
  2. Place it on each object that must move: drag Physics from the library's Systems folder, or + System in the object's Properties. Placed on a folder, it applies to everything the folder contains: each object in the folder moves.
  3. Set the objects on the ground or on each other (Place on ground, End key). An object left in the air falls when the game starts.

An object carrying the system needs no other setting to collide with the others: its shape surrounds its model.

items.title: The settings of each object
items.text:
In the object's Properties, Systems section, under Physics:

Setting What it does Shape Box: a crate, furniture, Ball: a ball, a round rock or Cylinder: a barrel, a column. A barrel lying on its side rolls if it is a cylinder. Mass (kg): the heavier, the harder to push As a guide: a crate 10 to 30, a barrel 40, a rock 200. Friction: 0 slides as on ice 0.6 at first. Bounce: 0 does not bounce, 1 bounces without losing anything 0.1 at first. In water Floats (half sunk), In between (stays where it is let go), Sinks, or By its density: less than water (1,000 kg per m³), it floats, the higher the lighter it is (cork 200, wood 500); more, it sinks (stone 2,500). Drag in water (1 ordinary) How much the water slows it down and carries it: 0 glides without being held, 3 sticks to the water like a dead leaf.

items.title: The setting for the whole game
items.text: In the Game tab, Physics card: Force with which the player and characters push (N), 300 at first. At 0, nobody pushes anything.

items.title: Good to know
items.text:
• An object that falls out of the world disappears.
  • In the water of a lake or the sea, it floats or sinks by its In water setting, rocks with the waves and drifts with the water; broken, its pieces too. See What floats.
  • The number of objects physics can follow is a game setting: Max physics bodies, in the technical settings.
  • To throw an object without a script, the Trigger has the action Push a moving object (Physics system).
  • All the settings: the Physics system reference.

items.title: Zones
items.text: A zone announces who enters it and who leaves it: a pressure plate, a trap, a finish line, a goal. It is a box, invisible in the game, that carries the Zone system. The game then decides what happens, most often with the Trigger.

items.title: Creating a zone
items.text:
Object > Create > Zone, or, in the Scene tab, a right-click in the empty space under the list (or Create inside on an object). The zone is a box 2 metres wide, created where you are looking, and set on the ground if the Place on ground when adding preference is on (it is at first). If the Zone system was not activated yet, it is activated at the same time: a single Ctrl+Z removes the zone and the system.

Place it, then give it its size with its Scale: a plate at 2 × 0.2 × 2, a finish line at 10 × 4 × 1. The editor always shows it; in the game, it cannot be seen, and stops nobody.

The Zone system can also go on an ordinary object, a visible slab for example: the zone is then the box of its model, at its place, with its rotation and size.

items.title: Who triggers it
items.text:
In the zone's Properties, Systems section, under Zone, the Who triggers it setting:

Choice Who counts The player The player only (at first). The player and characters The player, and the game's characters (enemies, for example). Moving objects (Physics system) Objects carrying the Physics system: a ball in a goal, a crate on a plate. Everything that moves All of these at once.

What is already in the zone when the game starts enters it at the first moment.

items.title: Making the game react
items.text:
Place the Trigger on the zone, with a When rule: Someone enters this zone (Zone system) (or leaves). A few ideas:

  • A plate that opens a door: Then: Hide an object, the door. The full example is in The Trigger.
  • A trap: a zone at the bottom of a ravine, Then: Teleport the player to an object, a marker on the edge.
  • A finish line: Then: End the game, Victory.
  • A goal: a ball carrying Physics (Shape: Ball: a ball, a round rock), a zone in the net, set to Moving objects (Physics system), and Then: Show a message, "Goal!".

A zone is switched off and back on with the Trigger's Make passable (or switch a zone off) and Make solid (or switch a zone back on) actions: a plate that only works once, a trap disarmed by a lever.

For a richer reaction, the agent can write a script that listens to the zone.entree and zone.sortie events: see the events and the Zone system reference.

items.title: Where characters walk
items.text: Enemies and the other characters that move on their own (the Enemies system, or a script that makes them walk with game.walk_to) follow the walkable areas: the ground a character can reach. They follow the terrain's relief and the top of objects, go around walls, under bridges and up gentle slopes.

items.title: Seeing them
items.text:
View menu, Walkable areas: the scene gets colored over the ground.

Color What it is Blue Where a character can go, starting from the player's place. Orange An isolated spot, where one can stand but that can't be reached from the player: a roof, a room without a door, an island. No color Nobody walks there: a slope too steep, a passage too narrow, water too deep, the inside of an obstacle.

It updates by itself, in the background, when the scene changes: the editor stays usable meanwhile. The world is cut into plots of 32 m, and only those that changed are computed again: moving a house only redoes the plots around it. The console says how many plots were redone, and how long it took.

items.title: What blocks, what doesn't
items.text:
• Blocks: objects with a Collision, the trunks of the terrain's plants (the Trunk setting of their kind of plant), slopes too steep and water deeper than half a character's height.
  • Doesn't block: objects without collision, those with the Physics system (they get pushed), and anything lower than the highest step (a stair, a curb).
  • An object placed high, like a bridge, doesn't block those who walk under it if it leaves enough room.
  • In the game, an obstacle that moves, disappears or becomes passable (a door that opens) redoes the plots it touches: characters get through at once.

items.title: The typical character
items.text: The areas are computed for a typical character, set in the game settings (nothing selected, Character walking section, folded at first): its Radius (half its width; 0.4 m at first), its Height (1.8 m), the Steepest slope it climbs (50°) and the Highest step it steps over (0.35 m). A passage must be wider than twice the radius: a 1 m door lets a 0.4 m-radius character through.

items.title: Several character sizes
items.text:
A rat and a giant don't go through the same doors. In the same section, Add a character size creates another size, with its Name (Small, Large...), its Radius, its Height and its Step: each size has its own walkable areas. Each character takes the smallest size it fits in, from the radius and height its script gives it: a big monster doesn't go into a small one's corridor, and says "blocked" if it has no other way. The slope is the same for all of them. Each size is computed separately: add one only for characters really smaller or larger than the typical one.

View menu, Walkable areas of the size: chooses the size whose areas are shown.

items.title: Characters avoid each other
items.text:
Characters that walk on their own see each other, the player and the other characters coming, and step aside in time: two guards crossing in a corridor walk past each other instead of getting stuck face to face. It is set in the same section:

Setting What it does Characters avoid each other On at first. Off, they bump into and push each other. Avoidance quality How many directions each one tries before choosing. Medium at first; Low for crowds of several hundred. Anticipation How far ahead in time a character sees an encounter coming (2.5 s at first). Longer: it steps aside earlier and more calmly.

items.title: Good to know
items.text:
• A character that finds no path stops ("blocked" for scripts) and tries again every second: a door opened in the meantime lets it through.
  • After a windowless test run of the game, the agent knows which character didn't find its way, and why: placed off the walkable areas, an unreachable target, or no way between them. Its scene check also reports a character placed off the walkable areas, or on an isolated spot the player can't reach.
  • The areas are computed in the editor, not when the game starts. Once the scene is saved, the editor computes the areas of each size in the background, even when they aren't shown, and stores them in the project's work folder (.worldmint), in 256 m pieces: the game reads them back when it starts instead of computing them again. After a change, only the changed plots are redone. The exported game takes these areas along. It only computes what is missing (a scene never saved, a project just copied): about one second for a 512 m map on an eight-core computer, several seconds for a map of several kilometres.

items.title: Asking the agent
items.text:
• "Make these crates and barrels pushable."
  • "Put a ball in the middle of the field, and a goal: when the ball goes into the goal, show "Goal!"."
  • "Add a plate in front of the door: when the player steps on it, the door opens."

After running the game without a window, the agent can tell how far each moving object travelled, and whether it fell out of the world.

items.title: Adjusting a character's pose
items.text:
A move is often almost right: on the motorbike, the hands don't quite land on the handlebar; an arm goes through the body; a guard stands too straight. Rather than looking for another animation file, adjust the pose: turn a few bones, and the adjustment is added to the move, wherever it plays in the game.

Nothing is specific to a model pack: the skeleton is read from the model, its bones are recognised by their name and by its shape, and angles are given around the character's axes, not each bone's own.

items.title: Adjusting a pose
items.text:
1. Select the character in the scene (the player, a guard, an animal: any model with a skeleton).
  2. In its Properties, open Skeleton pose and click Adjust the pose. Its skeleton appears in the view: one point per bone, and the list of bones below.
  3. Choose the preview: the rest pose, one of its moves (playing, or stopped at a moment with the slider), or Seated on a motorbike / Seated in a car for the pose the game gives the driver.
  4. Click a bone, in the view or in the list (its plain name is in brackets: Left hand, Back…).
  5. Turn it with the gizmo (E, or Turn under Bone gizmo), or type its three angles under Bone rotation. The character changes before your eyes.
  6. Or move its point (W, or Move): drag it where it should be. The hips really move (to crouch, to lean); a hand or a foot bends the two bones above it without stretching them, the elbow backward and the knee forward (Bend direction for the other way); a foot keeps its orientation, flat; an elbow, a knee, the head or the back turn the bones that carry them. The layer still stores angles (and the hips' offset).

Every gesture is undone with Ctrl+Z.

Setting What it does Adjustment layer A layer groups turned bones. The first adjustment creates one, for the move shown. A model can have several. Adjusted move One move, Every move, or Seated on a vehicle (the driver's pose). Adjustment strength From 0 to 100% of the angle. Layer on Off, it no longer plays: handy to compare before and after. Mirror The bone on the other side follows, as in a mirror. Copy the left onto the right (or the reverse) The right side takes the left side's adjustments, mirrored. Reset the bone, Reset everything Removes the adjustment of one bone, or of the whole layer. Copy the pose, Paste the pose Copies the angles into another layer or onto another character; bones it does not have are ignored.

Angles are given around the standing character's axes: X tilts the bone forward or back, Y turns it around, Z tilts it sideways. Small angles (5 to 30°) are usually enough.

items.title: Example: hands on the handlebar
items.text:
A motorbike rider takes a pose the game builds from the skeleton (Vehicles). To correct it:

  1. Select the player's character, Adjust the pose, preview Seated on a motorbike.
  2. Click the left upper arm, switch Mirror on, and turn it forward: both hands move towards the handlebar.
  3. Click the back and lean it slightly forward.

In the game, every time they get on a vehicle, they take this pose.

items.title: Correcting the skeleton
items.text:
Many models have a badly placed skeleton, above all when it was rigged automatically (a model made by an AI, a skeleton added in one click): a knee behind the leg, an elbow inside the arm. The limb then bends beside the place where it should bend. Rather than adjusting each move, correct the skeleton itself:

  1. In Skeleton pose, click Adjust the pose, then switch on Correct the skeleton. The character shows at rest, its skeleton on top.
  2. Click the misplaced joint, in the view or in the bone list.
  3. Move (W): drag the joint where the limb should bend. Turn (E): turn it on itself, if the limb bends sideways. The model does not move: only the joint's place inside it changes. Ctrl+Z undoes the gesture.
  4. Switch Correct the skeleton off and pick a move in the preview: the limb now bends around the new joint, in every move of the model (those of its file, those you made, those borrowed from another character, and the adjustments).

By default, the joints below the one you move follow it (moving the shoulder takes the arm along). Switch on Move the joint alone to leave them where they are. The Joint offset and Joint rotation fields give the same settings as numbers.

  • Remove this joint: the skin it moved follows its parent, and the joints it carried are attached to the parent, at the same place. Its animations are ignored. The root of the skeleton cannot be removed. Restore the joint brings it back.
  • Add a joint here: a new joint, child of the chosen one, that you name and then place with the gizmo. Without skin it is an attach point: a weapon, a held object (Held by the character), particles. With Take the skin around, it takes from its parent the part of the model beyond it, with a smooth transition: it then bends that part, like the tip of a tail. It can then be animated like the other joints (adjustments, moves, timeline).
  • Reset this joint and Back to the original skeleton undo one correction or all of them.

The correction is saved with the project, for this model: the model file is never changed. It applies wherever the model plays: in the editor, in the game, in an exported game and for the other players in multiplayer. It follows the model when you rename or move it in the library. If the model was moved outside the editor, Skeleton pose shows it in red: Attach to this model gives it back to the chosen model.

items.title: Where adjustments go
items.text:
They belong to the model and are saved with the project: every character using this model has them (the player, script characters, other players in multiplayer). The model file is never modified.

A script can switch a layer on, off or partly for a single character: game.pose_layer(id, "Hunched guard", 0.5) (see the scripts reference). In multiplayer, what it changes on a player shows for everyone.

Renaming or moving the model in the library, or renaming the adjusted move, makes the adjustments follow; a link broken outside the editor is attached again in Skeleton pose (see Creating a move).

items.title: With the agent
items.text:
Just ask: "on the motorbike, move his hands a bit forward onto the handlebar and lean his back". The agent reads the skeleton and the layers (pose_layers_get), then changes them (pose_layers_set), in a single step that Ctrl+Z undoes. It never touches the model file.

For a badly placed skeleton: "the wolf's left knee is too far back, bring it to the middle of the leg". The agent reads the skeleton at rest (skeleton_fix_get), then corrects it (skeleton_fix_set: move, turn, remove or add a joint), also in a single Ctrl+Z.

items.title: A project
items.text:
A project is a folder that holds your whole game. It can be moved, copied, sent or backed up like any folder, without repairing anything:

My game/
  My game.worldmint    the project file: the whole game and its start scene
  scenes/              the scenes (.wmscene)
  assets/              the models, sounds and images the game uses, copied from your library
  AGENT.md             optional: the agent's rules for this project
  .worldmint/          working files: the conversation with the agent, automatic backups, deleted scenes
  • Create: File > New project.... The creation assistant then offers its help.
  • Open: File > Open project..., then the .worldmint file.
  • Find it in File Explorer: File > Open project folder.
  • A scene outside a project (an old file): File > Create a project from this scene... makes it a project, copying its models into it. The original scene is not touched.

When you use a model from the library, its file (and those it names, like its textures) is copied into assets/. A file already in the project is never overwritten: changing the library does not change the project.

A project made by a newer version of the editor does not open: update the editor.

items.title: The whole game and each scene
items.text:
A game can have several places: the outdoors, the inside of a house, a cave, levels that follow each other. Each place is a scene. Some things apply to the whole game, others to each scene:

The whole game Each scene The played character: its model, animations, settings Its objects, terrain, vegetation, water Activated systems and their settings for the whole game The systems placed on its objects, with their values The game's scripts Its light and sky Controls, window, simulation Its placed cameras, and the one that opens it Reusable objects Its arrival points The start scene

Scripts keep running when the player changes scene, and keep their variables.

items.title: Managing scenes
items.text:
In the Scene tab, the Game scenes section (see The Scene tab):

  • + creates a new scene;
  • a click opens a scene (the editor first offers to save the open one);
  • right-click: Open, Rename, Duplicate, Delete, Start the game here.

The word Start marks the scene where the game starts. F5 always plays from the scene you are looking at, to try it; the exported game starts on the start scene.

A scene name cannot contain < > : " / \ | ? *, nor start or end with a dot or a space, and has 80 characters at most.

items.title: Linking scenes
items.text:
To have a door lead inside a house:

  1. In the house's scene, create an arrival point (Object > Create > Arrival point, or right-click in the list): this is where the player will appear, facing the arrow. Name it (for example "Entrance").
  2. In the start scene, activate the Passage system (Game tab), and place it on the door.
  3. In the door's properties, Systems section, choose the Scene it leads to, then the Arrival: an arrival point of that scene.

The scene list then shows next to the door → House · Entrance, in red if the scene or the arrival does not exist. An arrival point's properties list the passages that lead to it. The player takes the passage with the interaction key (E by default), or by walking into it if Taken by walking into it, without a key is checked: see the Passage system. Think of the way back: a passage in the house, leading to an arrival point in front of the door. The player keeps everything when changing scene (inventory, health...).

A script can also change scene with game.go_to: see the scripts reference.

Before playing, if the scene you start has neither the player's character nor an arrival point, the editor warns you ("An arrival point is missing"): the player would appear anywhere. Create an arrival point places one where you are looking; Play anyway starts the game.

items.title: Saving and recovering
items.text:
• Ctrl+S saves the open scene, and the whole game with it.
  • An automatic backup keeps a separate copy every 60 seconds (set in the Preferences), without touching your files. The status bar shows the time of the last one.
  • If the editor closed without saving, it offers Recover your work? on the next launch. After Recover, save to keep it.
  • A deleted scene is set aside in .worldmint/: nothing is lost.

items.title: Large worlds
items.text:
A map of several kilometers is heavy: saving all of it on every Ctrl+S would take time. The Large world setting (nothing selected, Technical settings section) stores the scene in pieces of 256 m, in files next to it:

scenes/
  Ville.wmscene       the scene: its settings, and the list of its pieces
  Ville.tuiles/       one file per 256 m piece: its objects, its relief, its retouched plants
  • Nothing changes in the editor: you work as before, and you never see the pieces.
  • Only the pieces that changed are rewritten: a moved object or a brush stroke on the relief only saves the piece it touched. Undoing a brush stroke also keeps only the pieces it touched.
  • Nothing is lost if the computer stops while saving: the scene reopens as it was before, or as it is after, never half-way. If a piece is missing or damaged (by an incomplete copy, for example), the scene refuses to open and says which one, without changing anything.
  • Switching to a large world keeps the previous file next to it (Ville.wmscene.avant-grand-monde.bak). Going back (unticking) writes the scene again as a single file and sets the pieces aside (Ville.tuiles.bak).
  • Copying or sending a scene: take the .wmscene file and its .tuiles folder. Renaming, duplicating or deleting a scene from the editor takes them together.
  • Export takes the pieces with the game, and the exported game reads them all.

A small scene does not need this setting: it stays a single file.

To work on one part of the map without seeing the rest, and to lock what is finished, cut it into sectors: see The Scene tab. Sectors are saved with the scene; working on one and saving still rewrites only the pieces that changed.

items.title: What sleeps far from the player
items.text:
In a large world, the game only brings to life what is around the player. Beyond the Activity radius (300 m by default, under Large world), in squares of 256 m, objects fall asleep: they are still there and can be seen, but characters stop walking, moving objects stop, animations and zones wait. When the player comes back, they wake up as the world kept them. The radius is the same on every computer: your game plays the same everywhere.

  • What must live far away (a messenger crossing the map, a boss on patrol): tick Always active in the object's Details, or Objects always active on a system's card, in the Game tab. Keep it for few objects: what stays awake far away costs at every moment of the game. The editor shows how many there are, under Activity radius and in the object's Details, in red beyond Always active, advised (100 by default); the agent is warned too.
  • Scripts only see what is awake when they look for objects; they can ask for the sleeping ones too, and learn who falls asleep and who wakes up (see the scripts reference, game.awake).
  • A small scene never sleeps: everything stays awake.

items.title: Saved games
items.text: A player who leaves your game can pick it up later, where they were: a key to save, a checkpoint that saves by itself, a game that continues as soon as it starts. Ask the agent ("the player saves with F5 and continues at start"): it has a recipe for this, and sets it up the way you want.

items.title: What a saved game keeps
items.text:
A save has three parts, and you don't have to deal with any of them:

  • the game itself: where the player is and what the game has noted (a lever pulled, a choice made in a dialogue). This is what the agent's recipe stores;
  • the systems: each keeps its own state (see What a saved game keeps): what the player carries in the Inventory, the progress of the Quest log, the Shop stocks, the Dialogue marks;
  • the world: everything the game changed in the scenes, compared to what you placed in the editor.

items.title: The world remembers
items.text:
The engine keeps by itself what changed during the game, and puts it back when loading:

What changed For example An object shown or hidden A secret door that appears, a chest hidden once opened An object solid or not A wall you can walk through after a spell A place, a rotation, a size An object teleported by the Trigger, a crate pushed, a rock that rolled (with its speed: it goes on as it was going) An object destroyed, a copy created A defeated enemy does not come back; arrows stuck in a wall and enemies spawned during the game are still there Tags An object marked "opened" or "visited" by a script Lights A lamp switched on or off, recoloured, made brighter or dimmer (see Light and shadows) The sun and the sky The time of the Day and night system, a storm a script brought (see Making a survival game) Looping effects and decals A fire lit on an object, smoke placed somewhere, a stain on the ground The camera The placed camera that was showing the scene Animations playing A platform going back and forth carries on where it was Trees and plants A tree cut down stays cut down Joints, ragdolls, vehicles A door open, a plank broken, a character on the ground, the car and who drives it The player's settings Slower, unable to run or jump

Only the differences with the placed scene go into the save: it stays small, even for a large world.

items.title: Several scenes
items.text: A game with several places (a cave, the inside of a house) keeps the state of every scene visited, not only the one the player is in. During the game, a scene you leave stays as you left it; after loading too: the cave where the player took a treasure stays empty when they go back, even if they saved outside.

items.title: What a saved game does not keep
items.text:
• The player's exact place is the one the recipe stores; a script of yours can keep more.
  • What only lasts an instant: a sound, a burst of sparks, the pieces of an object that shatters.
  • The exact pose of a character on the ground: they fall again where they were.

items.title: Where the saves are kept
items.text:
• When trying the game in the editor (Play), saves go to the project's work folder (.worldmint/saves), apart from the players'.
  • In the exported game, they go to the player's Windows data, under the game's name: they survive an update of the game.
  • The agent's test runs keep their saves in memory: they never touch a real file.

A save made with an older version of WorldMint can still be read: what it does not contain stays as at the start.

items.title: For scripts
items.text: game.save(slot, table) and game.load(slot) do all of this: the game's table, the systems, the world. {systems = false} as the last argument leaves the systems and the world out, to read a save without resuming it. The scripts reference details these functions.

items.title: Shaders
items.text:
A shader tells the graphics card what a surface looks like. A material sets values (color, roughness, metal, images, glow); a shader goes further: a scrolling hologram, an object that dissolves into embers, flowing lava, a glowing rim, a tree that sways in the wind, cartoon water.

A shader goes on a material: every object that uses this material shows it. It only changes the surface (color, relief, roughness, metal, emitted light, cut-out holes) and, if it wants, where the vertices are. Lighting, shadows, transparency and anti-aliasing stay with the engine: a shader cannot break them.

items.title: Using a recipe
items.text:
Select an object that uses a project material. In the Material section, under Emitted light, the Shader list offers the project's shaders and the Recipes shipped with WorldMint:

Recipe What it does Hologram Scrolling lines and a glowing rim, on an almost black surface. Dissolve The object vanishes in patches, edged with embers; its shadow follows. Wind in foliage The top of the model sways, its foot stays in place (trees, bushes, tall grass). Glowing rim The edge of the object shines, like a magic item or one to pick up. Stylized water Opaque water with bold colors, sparkles and small waves. Lava Dark rock crossed by burning veins that flow slowly. Blinking The surface lights up and goes off, like a warning light.

Choosing a recipe copies it into the project's shaders/ folder: it is now your shader. Its settings appear just below, as sliders (a color, a speed, a strength...). They only change this material: two materials can use the same shader with different colors. Reset the shader's settings gives each one back the value its code gives it.

items.title: Changing the code
items.text:
A shader's code is a small text file, shaders/<name>.wmshader. Two ways to change it:

  • Shader code, in the material panel: type, and the shader is checked and recompiled as soon as you stop. The view shows the result at once.
  • Open the file: it opens in your text editor. Each time you save, WorldMint reads it again and recompiles it.

A shader is written in framed GLSL:

// Hologram: the first line describes the shader.
param color glow = vec3(0.2, 0.8, 1.0);       // a setting: a color swatch
param float speed = 2.0 range(0, 10);         // a slider, from 0 to 10

void surface(inout Surface s, Inputs i) {
    float line = step(0.5, fract(i.position.y * 8.0 - i.time * speed));
    s.color = glow * 0.08;
    s.emission = glow * (fresnel(i.normal, i.toCamera, 3.0) + line * 0.25);
}

void vertex(inout vec3 position, VertexInputs v) {  // optional: moves the vertices
    position.y += 0.05 * sin(v.time * 3.0 + position.x);
}
What the shader changes (Surface s) What it reads (Inputs i) color: the base color, from 0 to 1 position: the point, in the world roughness: 0 smooth, 1 matte normal: the model's normal metallic: 0 or 1 uv: the texture coordinates emission: the emitted light time: game time, in seconds (pauses do not count) opacity: under 0.5, the point vanishes toCamera: the direction of the camera normal: the relief, in the world tint: the object's color

Vertices read local (the vertex in the model), normal, uv and time, and move position (in the world). The library: noise (a soft noise from 0 to 1), fresnel (the edge seen from the front), quality() (0 in Low quality, 1 Medium, 2 High: a costly shader gets simpler in Low). Eight settings at most: float, vec2, vec3, vec4, or color.

items.title: Connected blocks
items.text:
Without writing code, a shader can be built with connected blocks: each block does one simple thing (read the time, make noise, mix two colors, light up the rim), and you join them like pipes, up to the Output block, which receives what the shader changes: color, emitted light, roughness, metal, opacity, relief, and the vertex displacement. The file is shaders/<name>.wmgraph.

  • Start: in the material's Shader list, choose New shader in blocks, or a recipe in blocks (each of the seven recipes exists in code and in blocks, with the same settings and the same image). Open the blocks opens the Shader blocks window over the bottom of the view: the object stays visible above it, and the material's sphere in the properties.
  • Add a block: the Add a block button, or a right click on the background. Blocks are sorted by family (Inputs, Values and settings, Math, Patterns and effects, Vectors and colors), with a search; hover a block to read what it does.
  • Connect: drag from the dot on the right of a block (its Result) to the dot on the left of another one (one of its inputs). Dropping a link in empty space opens the menu: the block you choose is already connected. A free input takes the small value set next to it.
  • Move, delete: drag a block by its title; its place is saved in the file. Click a block or a link, then Delete. Right-drag to move the background. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo, with the mouse over the window.
  • Settings: a Setting block (a number, with its name, value, minimum and maximum) or Color setting becomes a slider of the material, like a param in code.
  • Preview: each change is checked and compiled 0.3 s later, and the view shows it at once.
  • Show the code shows the code the blocks give, read-only: you change it through the blocks.

A link that does not fit (a loop, two different sizes, a surface block connected to the vertex displacement) is refused: the faulty block turns red, with its message, and the object keeps the last version that worked.

items.title: When the code is refused
items.text:
A shader is checked in three steps before it shows: the text (nothing the engine keeps for itself: no #, no resource, no while, loops of 64 turns at most), a compilation in a "sandbox" that only knows the contract above, then the compilation in the engine's real shader. If one refuses:

  • the panel says why, and on which line ("line 4: writing error, on this line or at the end of the previous one"); so do the console and the status bar;
  • objects keep the last version that worked, or their base material if there is none yet: nothing disappears, nothing turns pink.

After the shader, the engine replaces any value that is not finite (a division by zero) with the material's, and bounds everything else: a wrong shader never makes a black stain or breaks the image.

items.title: With the agent
items.text: The agent knows the recipes and the contract. Ask it "make this chest glow", "have the trees sway in the wind" or "cartoon water for the pond": it puts a recipe on the material and tunes its sliders, or writes a shader, in code or in blocks (it reads and changes the graph you see in the blocks window). It gets the same messages as you, by line, and fixes them before saying it is done. It never changes a shader from a pack: it copies it into shaders/.

items.title: Safety, exported game, performance
items.text:
• A shader from a downloaded pack is recompiled from its text, in a separate process: a booby-trapped text cannot crash the editor.
  • The exported game compiles nothing: the editor stores the compiled versions in the project, and the export takes them along. If a shader is refused, the game draws the material without it.
  • Checking and compiling a shader takes 5 to 7 ms; the graphics card then prepares its pipeline (0.1 to 0.5 s the very first time, a few milliseconds afterwards), on the side: the editor does not freeze, the object keeps the previous version until the new one is ready.

items.title: Sound and the sound mixer
items.text:
A WorldMint game plays WAV, MP3, OGG or FLAC files from your library: footsteps, hits, a fire's crackle, a music. The Sounds system places them on what makes them, without code (see its reference); a script plays them with game.sound and game.music (see the scripts reference).

All these sounds go through the game's sound mixer: it sets the balance between the music, the noises, the ambience and the voices, for the whole game and all its scenes.

items.title: Sound groups
items.text:
Every sound belongs to a group. A new game has five, which always stay:

Group Name for scripts What goes in it Music music the background music, the fight music Effects effects noises: steps, hits, doors, gathering (by default, any sound without a group) Ambience ambience the loops of a place: a fire, a river, the wind Voice voice what characters say Interface ui small cues: a menu click, an item picked up

They are set in the Game tab, Sound mixer section:

  • the slider sets the group's volume, from 0 to 100%;
  • the speaker mutes it (it is no longer heard); a second click brings it back;
  • Add a group creates a new one: a radio, a boss's voice. Its name is enough; the name for scripts comes from it ("Radio de bord" gives radio_de_bord), and shows on hover. The cross removes an added group; the five default ones cannot be removed.

Lowering a group changes all its sounds at once: for an ambience that is too loud, lower Ambience rather than each fire.

items.title: Automatic ducking
items.text:
A ducking rule makes a group quieter while another one plays, then brings it back: the music goes under the voices, without a script. A new game has one: Voice lowers Music to 40%.

In the Automatic ducking section:

  • While this group plays: the group that triggers it (a sound too far away to be heard does not count, nor a muted group);
  • Lower this group: the one that gets quieter;
  • Down to: how much of its volume it keeps;
  • Fall time and Recovery time: in how many seconds it gets quieter, then comes back once silence returns.

Add a ducking rule creates another one; Remove this ducking rule deletes it.

items.title: Muffling the sound
items.text:
A muffled group loses its highs, as if heard under water, behind a wall or through a radio. From 0 (clear sound) to 1 (under water).

  • While playing, most often: a Trigger rule with the action Muffle the sound. For example on a zone placed over the water: "on entering", muffle All the game's sound to 1; "on leaving", to 0. The action Mute or unmute a group of sounds silences a group (the ambience during a story scene), then brings it back.
  • All the time: the folded Muffled groups section muffles a group for the whole game.

There is no echo or reverb yet.

items.title: The game window in the background
items.text:
When the player minimizes the game window, or switches to another window (a browser, a chat), the folded section Game window in the background decides what the sound does:

  • Mute the sound (the starting setting): the game goes silent, then comes back when the player returns;
  • Lower the sound: it goes on, quieter (Lowered to, 30% by default);
  • Keep the sound: nothing changes, for a game you listen to while doing something else.

The sound fades out and back in smoothly, without clicks. A game started in the background for a test (by the agent or the tests) always stays silent: you never hear a test you are not watching.

items.title: The player's Options menu
items.text: The Menu system offers the player, in Options, Sound section, the Master volume and one setting per group of the sound mixer, under its name in the player's language. Their choice adds to your mix: if they set the music to 50% and you set it to 80%, it plays at 40%.

items.title: In scripts
items.text:
• game.sound(file, {group = "ambience"}) puts a sound in a group, by its name for scripts or by its name ("Ambience"); without group, it goes to Effects. game.music goes to Music.
  • game.mute(group, true) mutes a group, game.mute(group, false) brings it back; "master" means all the sound.
  • game.muffle(group, 0.8, {fade = 0.5}) muffles it, over half a second.
  • game.volume(group, 0.5) sets the player's volume, for an options menu of your own.
  • game.sound_groups() gives the list of groups, with their name in the player's language.

A group that does not exist is an error, shown in the game's console.

items.title: With the agent
items.text: The agent puts the sounds it writes in the right group, sets the balance with the sound mixer rather than by changing each sound, and places the Trigger rules for the water or a cave. When it tries the game, its report says how many sounds played in each group, and what the scripts muted or muffled.

items.title: Making a survival game
items.text: A survival game is played with what one gathers: chop trees and break rocks, craft tools, build a shelter, eat and drink so as not to die, and nights go by. WorldMint already does each of these parts: ask the agent in your own words, and it assembles the systems and sets them for your game, without any programming.

items.title: The simplest way: the creation assistant
items.text:
In Game > Creation assistant, tick Survival (or Gathering and crafting) in the genre. A Survival step is added:

  • what the character needs to live: eating, drinking, sleeping;
  • crafting items, and which ones;
  • building a shelter, and how pieces are placed (on a grid, or freely).

Everything is ticked by default; untick what your game does not want. Days and nights, and how long a whole day lasts (10, 20 or 40 minutes), are asked with the mood (the The mood step), for every game: for a survival or gathering game, the answer is already Yes. At the end, the request sent to the agent names the systems to activate.

items.title: The five systems
items.text:
System What it does What the player sees Gathering Placed on what can be gathered (a tree, a rock, a bush, a whole plant kind): the number of hits, what it gives, the tool needed (the axe chops wood), and whether it grows back. What needs a tool is struck with the attack, the tool held in hand The prompt "Click: Chop 2/3", then "+3 Wood" Inventory What the player carries, and the bar of items in hand at the bottom of the screen: the axe held shows in the character's hand The bar, the chosen slot, the axe in the hand Crafting The recipes: a "Recipe" row (what it gives) followed by its ingredients. An ingredient can be a tool that is kept (a hammer). A recipe can need a workbench: an object of the world carrying this system, such as a campfire or a forge The crafting window (C); in front of a workbench (E), with its recipes too Building The pieces: a "Piece" row (its name and its model, a hidden object of the scene) followed by its cost. The piece stands on what is aimed at, measured on its model, whatever it is Building mode (B): a preview where the player aims, blinking where it cannot go. With a character, one aims with the view (the centre of the screen) and the camera keeps turning; from above, with the cursor Needs Hunger, thirst, tiredness, or whatever you want: each goes down over time (faster while running); at zero, the player loses health. Foods of the inventory raise them, as does a source in the world (a well, a bed) or a Trigger rule ("Raise a need"). Each need can be switched off without losing its settings (its "On" box) One bar per need that is on, under the health bar Day and night The sun rises, crosses the sky and sets; night is darker and bluish. Broad daylight is your scene's light as you set it The sky and the light changing; a clock if you want one

Each one keeps its state in a saved game: the hits already struck and the time before a tree grows back, the pieces built, each need, the day and the time.

items.title: Playing
items.text:
Key (gamepad) What it does 1 to 9, wheel (←, which goes round the slots) Choose what is held in hand, in the bar; the key of the chosen slot puts the item away Click (X) Strike: chop the tree or break the rock, the tool in hand (the axe, the pickaxe) E (Y) Pick bare-handed (berries), use a workbench, drink at a well, sleep in a bed C (left stick pressed) Open or close crafting I (Back) The inventory: a click on a food eats or drinks it B (RB) Enter or leave building mode Click (X) Place the piece, where one aims: the centre of the screen with a character, the cursor from above. Fighting does not strike during the mode Wheel (right stick pressed) Turn the piece Q (←), or 1 to 9 Change piece X (B) Tear down the piece aimed at, which gives back part of its cost

All these keys can be changed in the Game controls panel.

items.title: What you can ask the agent
items.text:
• "Trees give 3 wood in 4 axe blows, and grow back after 5 minutes."
  • "An axe is made from 3 wood and 2 stones; meat is cooked at the campfire."
  • "I build wooden walls and floors, on a grid; a wall costs 4 wood."
  • "I get hungry after 20 minutes and thirsty after 10; an apple raises hunger by 30."
  • "A day lasts 20 minutes; the lanterns light up at night; wolves come out at night."
  • "I sleep in the bed to skip the night."
  • "Tiredness also goes back up by drinking a coffee, or resting by the campfire."
  • "Remove tiredness for now": the agent unticks its "On" box, its settings stay.

The agent tells you the numbers it chose (how long each need lasts, what a wall costs, how many hits a tree takes) and checks them by playing: doing nothing does not win, and starving takes minutes, not seconds.

items.title: Good to know
items.text:
• The same names everywhere: an item is one inventory kind, written the same in gathering, recipes, costs and foods ("Wood", not "wood" here and "Wooden plank" there).
  • A piece that does something keeps its model's systems: a campfire carrying Crafting becomes a workbench wherever it is built; a bed carrying Needs lets the player sleep.
