  • Tiredness is a row of the Needs like hunger: energy comes back by sleeping in a bed (a source that makes the night go by), by eating or drinking something (a food row), or any other way through a Trigger rule with the action "Raise a need" (near a fire, on a bench, at an altar). Switched off (its "On" box unticked), it has no bar, no longer goes down and no longer hurts; the bed and the coffee say it is switched off.
  • Aiming while building: the Building system's setting "How the player aims" follows the game's camera (the centre of the screen in first or third person, the cursor from above or from a placed camera), or forces one of them.
  • Interiors keep their light: the Day and night system has a setting for scenes without the cycle (a cave, an inn).
  • Large worlds: resources and built pieces stay in the game, asleep when far away; a tree chopped at the other end of the map still grows back on time.
  • Every setting is detailed in the systems reference.

items.title: The terrain
items.text: Without a terrain, a scene's ground is made of your objects (a large plane, tiles). A terrain is a map with relief, regions (forest, beach, snow...), water and vegetation, which you generate, then touch up with brushes.

items.title: Generating a world
items.text:
Deselect everything (or click the game row, at the very top of the Scene tab): the properties show the Terrain section. Set it up, then click Generate a world.

Setting Effect Size The side of the square map: 256 m, 512 m, 1,024 m, 2 km or 4 km (see Large maps). Relief 0: almost flat. 1: hills and mountains. 2: very steep. Relief details How many bumps and hollows there are between the large shapes (0 to 1). Max. altitude The height of the highest peaks, with a relief of 1. Coast level Below this share of the altitude: beaches and swamps, which water will cover. Shape Land to the edge, One continent, Several continents or Archipelago: land up to the edge of the map, or surrounded by a sea that reaches the horizon. Sea A sea at coast level: it covers everything lower. Always there around continents or islands. Seamless edges The left edge continues the right one, the top continues the bottom: a map that can one day wrap around the world. (The game does not cross from one edge to the other yet.) Regions Snow, Rock, Forest, Grassland, Desert, Swamp, Beach. Uncheck the ones you don't want: their areas take the most fitting neighboring region. A map keeps at least one region. Variant A number: the same variant gives the same world. The Another variant arrow draws one at random.

The terrain becomes the scene's Terrain object, with its regions and water stored inside. Objects already placed are set again on the new relief.

With a terrain, this section is called Relief, regions and sea (on the Terrain object) and its button Generate again: it replaces the relief and regions, but region objects keep their name, color and systems. Remove the terrain deletes it. Ctrl+Z goes back in both cases.

items.title: Importing a relief
items.text:
Import a relief (in the same section) makes the map from a heightmap: a grayscale image where white is the highest, like relief tools (World Machine, Gaea) and real-data converters make.

  • Files: a PNG image, preferably 16-bit (65,536 heights instead of 256: no steps on gentle slopes), or a raw .raw or .r16 file (16-bit heights, no header, in PC byte order; .r8 for 8-bit). The image must be square.
  • The box that follows shows the image ("1025 × 1025 points, 16-bit") and asks how to lay it out:
Setting Effect Meters per point The distance between two points of the image: 1,025 points at 1 m make a 1,024 m map. A map is at most 4 km per side. Black altitude The altitude of the image's black points, in meters. White altitude The altitude of its white points.
  • Import lays out the relief. Regions and sea follow the Generate a world settings (the checked regions, the coast level, the sea, the variant), as for a generated world. Placed objects are set again on the new relief, and Ctrl+Z brings back the old terrain.
  • An image whose number of cells (its points minus one) is not a multiple of 64 is resampled: the map keeps its size in meters.

items.title: Large maps (2 and 4 km)
items.text:
Beyond 1,024 m, the map is a large map. It is set up, sculpted and painted like the others; only the way it is drawn changes:

  • The ground is drawn in detail around the camera: up to 1 km in High quality, 500 m in Low quality (the quality is chosen from the graphics card). Further away, a simplified relief (one height every 4 m, its colors to within 4 m) takes over. As the camera moves, the detail loads little by little, without stutter.
  • Generating a 4 km map takes a few seconds.
  • In game, the ground is touched in 256 m squares, as a single piece: the player and characters cross from one to the next without noticing.

On every map, the relief is simplified in the distance: each 64 m piece is drawn with 64, 32, 16, 8 or 4 tiles per side, depending on how much of the screen it covers. It only changes detail when the relief's difference stays under one point of the screen (one and a half in Low quality): the difference cannot be seen. Under the edges of each piece, a skirt (a vertical strip of ground, normally invisible) fills the cracks that would open between two levels of detail.

items.title: The Terrain object
items.text:
Select Terrain in the scene list (or click the ground, or Edit the terrain in the game's settings). Its properties:

  • Position and size: the terrain moves, but does not turn or change scale;
  • Relief, regions and sea: the generation settings above;
  • Regions: New region creates a region of your own, to paint wherever you like (name it, give it its color and systems). The new object is selected, and the Paint tool taken;
  • Blend between regions: the width of the blend from one region to the next (0: sharp borders);
  • Systems: a system placed on the Terrain applies to all its regions.

items.title: Sculpting and painting
items.text:
With a terrain in the scene, the tool column on the left of the view shows seven tools: Hill, Dig, Flatten, Smooth, Ramp, Paint, Fill. With a tool taken, the left click in the view sculpts instead of selecting. Each tool and its options bar (Size, Strength, Region) are detailed in The 3D view.

  • While sculpting, slopes too steep for the player show in red.
  • Ramp: drag from one point to another for a path with an even slope.
  • Fill: click at the bottom of a hollow; water fills it up to its rim and becomes a Lake ("Lake created: its surface is at 12 m"). Nothing fills if the water would run off: dig a hollow first.
  • Each brush stroke is undone with Ctrl+Z. Esc puts the tool down.
  • Materials: cover the ground with real materials (grass, rock, snow, sand...) and paint them with the brush. See Materials.

items.title: Regions
items.text:
Each region is an object stored in the Terrain, with a dot of its color in the list. In the view, a first click on the ground selects the Terrain, a second the region under the mouse. Its properties:

  • what it covers ("23% of the map");
  • Regions: Paint this region takes the Paint tool with it;
  • Vegetation: see below;
  • Appearance: its Color;
  • Systems: they apply to what stands in it. For example the Sounds system and its surface setting: footsteps that crunch on snow.

Deleting a region (Del key) asks which region will take its areas ("Its areas will take this region:"). Its object goes with its systems; Ctrl+Z brings everything back. The terrain keeps at least one region.

items.title: Water
items.text:
The Sea and each Lake are objects stored in the Terrain. They cover what is lower than their level.

  • Style: Realistic (fine waves, reflections, see-through water) or Stylized, for a low poly game (see below).
  • Kind of water: a ready-made water, Sea, Stormy sea, Lagoon, Lake, Pond, Low poly sea or Low poly lake: the swell, the colors, the clarity and the foam at once (the last two also switch to the Stylized style). Everything stays adjustable afterwards.
  • Level: the height of the surface. Higher, the water covers more land.
  • Waves: the height of the largest waves. 0: calm water, like a mirror.
  • Wave length: from one crest to the next. Short, a chop; long, an ocean swell. Shorter waves are always added on top.
  • Swell direction: where the waves go, in degrees.
  • Choppiness: the wind on the water, from 0 (round, regular waves) to 1 (sharp crossing crests, foam).
  • Deep water color and Color near the shores: the water goes from one to the other with its depth.
  • Clarity: how far one sees through the water. Near the shores the bottom shows; further out it fades into the water's color.
  • Foam: on the crests, along the shores and around whatever touches the water (a rock, a pier, a floating crate).
  • Wakes: the V opening behind a boat, the churned water in its wake, the rings around a swimmer or a floating crate. They are only drawn. 0: none.
  • Systems: they apply to whoever walks in it (splashing steps).

Water reflects the sky, the sun and the scene's lights (a lamp by a lake draws its reflection on it); in High quality it also reflects the scenery, shows the bottom slightly bent by the waves, and the sun draws moving light patterns on it (caustics). The waves move with game time: what you see is what physics makes float.

In deep enough water, the player swims, at its Swim speed (in its properties): they follow the surface, rise and fall with it, and moving water gently carries them along. Del removes a body of water.

items.title: Stylized water
items.text:
For a low poly game, choose the Stylized style: the surface is made of flat facets, triangles laid on a fixed grid of the world, lifted by gentler, more readable waves; each facet takes its shade from its slope facing the sun. The colors go from the Color near the shores to the Deep water color in crisp steps, the foam lines the shores and whatever touches the water with a crisp band, the highest crests turn white and wakes are drawn as foam lines. The water reflects the sky and the sun (as a crisp spot), not the scenery, and shows the bottom without bending it. Its extra settings:

  • Facet size: the side of the triangles, in meters. Large, very low poly water; small, more detail.
  • Facet strength: at 1, each facet has its own shade; toward 0, the surface smooths out, with the same waves.
  • Color steps: the number of shades from the shore to the open water (0 or 1: a smooth gradient).
  • Foam width: the width of the white band along the shores and around objects.

The style does not depend on the render quality: stylized water stays stylized on a powerful computer. The quality only sets its cost: in High, a second foam band comes and goes beyond the first, and placed lights draw their reflection on it; in Low, the sea has a coarser mesh. At equal quality, stylized water costs less than realistic water. Floating and swimming things follow the drawn facets.

items.title: What floats
items.text: Water carries what moves: the objects of the Physics system float, sink or stay in between, by their In water setting; the water slows them down, rocks them with the waves and carries them when it moves. The pieces of a broken object do the same, and a rag doll floats. A boat sails on it and runs aground on land. The fluid is not simulated: the water's surface carries things, which stays light for the computer.

items.title: Vegetation
items.text:
To grow trees, bushes, grass or rocks on a region:

  1. Select the region.
  2. Drag a model from the library onto the area of the Vegetation section ("Drop a model from the explorer here: it will grow on this region.").

The model becomes a plant kind, an object stored in the region, and grows over the whole region. Drag other models to grow several kinds. The region's Vegetation section lists its kinds and their number of plants; a click selects one.

A plant kind's properties ("It grows on its region. Its settings and systems apply to all its plants."):

Setting Effect Density The number of plants per 100 m². Changing the density resows: hand edits may no longer land on the same plants. Min. size, Max. size Each plant takes a random size between the two. Max. slope Nothing grows on steeper ground. Sink into the ground Each plant rests on the lowest ground under its base, then sinks this much: its base seems to come out of the ground. Visible up to Beyond this, it is not drawn: closer makes the game faster. In Low quality (an integrated chip), plants stop at 60 % of this distance. Reseed New places for all its plants. Hand edits are forgotten. Trunk (In game section) The diameter that stops the player in the game. 0: walked through (grass, flowers, bushes).
  • Select all its plants: to edit them or give them a system together.
  • Put all plants back: forgets the hand edits (if there are any).
  • Stop growing it: removes this plant kind.
  • A system placed on the plant kind applies to all its plants: for example Gathering, for trees to chop down.

items.title: Editing a plant
items.text:
A plant is selected with a click in the view, or in the scene list, under its plant kind (with the word "plant"). Ctrl + click and the rectangle take several. It is not a scene object, but it is edited like one and keeps its edit if the terrain changes:

  • Position, Rotation, Size, or the gizmo;
  • Place on ground (End);
  • Put back in place: as sown, with its original place, rotation and size;
  • Erase (Del): it will not grow back, even if the terrain changes;
  • Make it an object: it leaves its plant kind and becomes a scene object, in the same place. Not needed to give it a system;
  • Select its plant kind;
  • Systems: a plant can carry its own systems, and stays a plant.

items.title: Translating your game
items.text: You write your game in your language. To offer it in English, Spanish or German as well, add these languages and fill in their translations: yourself, cell by cell, or the agent, in one click. No code is needed.

items.title: Choosing the game's languages
items.text:
With nothing selected in the scene, the properties show the game settings. In the Game languages section:

  • Original language: the language you write the lines, the messages and the title in. Usually yours.
  • Add a language: each added language is offered to players. The cross next to a language removes it; its translations stay in the project, and adding it back finds them again.

The agent can do it too: "put my game in English and Spanish".

items.title: Which language the player sees
items.text:
When it starts, the game picks the player's language:

  1. the one they chose last time in the menu options;
  2. otherwise the Windows language, if the game offers it (a Canadian English Windows gives English);
  3. otherwise the original language.

With the Menu system, the Options button shows a Language row: each click moves to the next language, and everything on screen updates. The game remembers it for the next plays.

A text without a translation shows in the original language: a half-translated game stays playable.

items.title: The Translations window
items.text:
The Game > Translations menu (or the Translations... button of the game languages) opens the list of every text the player sees, found automatically:

  • the systems' texts: the lines and answers of the Dialogue, a character's displayed name, the messages and ending text of the Trigger, the title-screen title of the Menu, an Interaction prompt's text, the item kinds of the Inventory, the resources, tools and verbs of Harvesting, a Shop's name, money and items, the titles, descriptions, steps and rewards of the Quest log;
  • the systems' own texts: "Play" and "Options" of the Menu, "Buy" of the Shop, "Quest log", "Map"... The Where column says "system text". They already exist in French and English: their cell shows that text in grey, and the game shows it until you write another one. In the other languages, they wait for their translation like the others;
  • the game's title, and the names of the controls you named;
  • the scripts' texts written with game.t("...").

There is one column per offered language. A red cell is waiting for its translation: click it, type, then press Enter. At the top, each language says how many texts it still lacks; Only what is missing hides the ones already translated. The Where column says where each text appears. A changed translation is undone with Ctrl+Z (and comes back with Ctrl+Y), like any change in the editor.

items.title: Asking the agent
items.text:
The Ask the agent to translate button sends a request to the agent: it reads the missing texts, translates them keeping the game's tone, and fills in the tables. The cells fill in before your eyes; you can then correct any of them.

Formatting stays

A text like [b]Garde[/b] or Il faut : {outil} keeps its tags and marks in its translation: [b]Guard[/b], You need: {outil}. The agent knows it; if you translate yourself, copy them.

items.title: Where translations are stored
items.text:
Each offered language has its table in the project, in the translations folder: translations/en.json for English, translations/es.json for Spanish. One line per text: the text as written in the game, then its translation.

{
  "Bonjour, voyageur.": "Hello, traveller.",
  "Halte !": "Halt!"
}

The file can be read and corrected with any text editor, and compares well in Git. If you change an original text, its translation does not follow: it shows in red again in the Translations window.

The exported game takes these tables with it.

items.title: For scripts
items.text: A script passes every text it shows through game.t: game.hud_text("score", game.t("Coins: {1}", coins)). {1}, {2}... are replaced after the translation, so the word order can change from one language to another. The systems' texts are already translated. The scripts reference details game.language, game.languages and game.set_language.

items.title: The Trigger: "when… then…"
items.text:
The Trigger system makes the game react without writing code. You place rules on an object that read like a sentence: when the player steps on this plate, then the door opens. They are all set in the object's Properties, and the agent can place them for you.

Every field is detailed in the Trigger reference.

items.title: Placing a rule
items.text:
1. Activate the system: Game tab, Systems section, Activate under Trigger (see The Game tab).
  2. Place it on the object the rule is about (the plate, the lever, the boss): drag Trigger from the library's Systems folder onto the object, or, in its Properties, Systems section, click + System.
  3. In the object's Properties, under Trigger, click Add: Rule. A Rule 1 appears, in its own frame; the cross on its right removes it. An object can carry as many rules as needed.
  4. Choose When, then Then, then fill in the fields that appear: only those useful for the chosen action are shown.

Every change goes through the history: Ctrl+Z undoes it.

items.title: When
items.text:
When What the object needs Someone enters this zone (Zone system) The Zone system: see Physics and zones. Someone leaves this zone (Zone system) The Zone system. The player uses it (Interaction system) The Interaction system: the player walks up to it and presses its key (E at first). It dies (Health system) The Health system. When the game starts Nothing. After a time Nothing: you give the number of seconds of play. When an event happens Nothing: you give the event's name, one of a system (see The events) or a name chosen for this game. Its joint breaks (Joint system) The Joint system, with a breaking force or the Break action.

How many times: Only once, or Every time. With After a time and Every time, the action comes back every so many seconds.

Wait before acting (seconds): a delay between the moment the rule fires and the action. A door that closes three seconds after the player went through.

items.title: Then
items.text:
Then What it does Show an object, Hide an object A hidden object can no longer be seen and no longer stops anyone: a hidden door is an open door. Show or hide, in turn Each time, the opposite of the time before: a lever that opens, then closes. Switch a light on, Switch a light off, Switch a light on or off, in turn A placed light: a lever that lights a lamp. Change a light's color It takes the New color of the light: an alarm turning red. Destroy an object Removes it from the game (never the player). Make a copy appear Copies the chosen object, at the place chosen in Where it appears. The copied object is usually a hidden model, kept aside. Teleport the player to an object The player ends up where that object is. Make solid, Make passable A passable object stays visible but no longer stops anyone. On a zone: switches it back on, or off. Go to another scene The player goes to the chosen Scene, at its Arrival point. End the game Victory or Defeat, with a Text to show; the game offers to play again. Play a sound A sound from the library, played where the object is. Play a video A video from the library, full screen, with its sound; the world stops meanwhile. The player can skip it or not; Event sent at the end chains what comes next. See Videos. Play an effect (fire, chips, explosion…), Stop an effect Lights again the effect the target carries (its Particle effect system: a brazier lit by a lever), or plays a ready-made effect on it, once, at the chosen Size of the effect; Stop an effect puts it out. See Particles and decals. Muffle the sound (under water, behind a wall) Muffles a group of the sound mixer, or all the game's sound, from 0 (clear again) to 1 (under water), over a few seconds. Mute or unmute a group of sounds Silences a group of the sound mixer (the ambience during a story scene), or brings it back. Show a message A text on screen, for the Message duration. Push a moving object (Physics system) Throws an object that carries the Physics system, away from the player and upwards: a kick in a ball. Send an event Announces an event, which another rule (When an event happens) or a script can listen to. Open (a door, a drawbridge: Joint system), Close (Joint system) The joint's motor brings it to its open or closed stop: see Vehicles, joints and ragdolls. Break its joint: it falls The joint gives way, even an unbreakable one. Make it fall limp (ragdoll), Get it back up (ragdoll) An animated character falls like a rag doll, or gets back up.

On which object: a list of the scene's objects, with a search. Left at This object, the action targets the object carrying the rule.

items.title: A plate that opens a door
items.text:
1. Object > Create > Zone: a box invisible in the game, which carries the Zone system. Rename it "Plate" (F2), place it in front of the door and set its Scale, for example 2 × 0.2 × 2.
  2. Place the Trigger on the plate, then Add: Rule:
    • When: Someone enters this zone (Zone system);
    • Then: Hide an object;
    • On which object: the door.

For the door to close again when the player steps off, add a second rule: Someone leaves this zone, Every time, Show an object, the door. Set the first one to Every time as well.

items.title: A lever
items.text:
1. Place the Interaction system on the lever. In its settings, Prompt text can say "Lever": the player sees "E: Lever" when walking up to it.
  2. Place the Trigger on the lever, with one rule:
    • When: The player uses it (Interaction system);
    • How many times: Every time;
    • Then: Show or hide, in turn;
    • On which object: the door, or the gate.

items.title: A defeated boss wins the game
items.text:
The boss carries the Health system (like the enemies of the Enemies system). Place the Trigger on it:

  • When: It dies (Health system);
  • Then: End the game;
  • Result: Victory;
  • Text to show: "The dragon is defeated!".

For a sequel rather than an ending: Then: Show an object, a hidden chest near the boss; or Go to another scene.

items.title: Reusable actions
items.text:
When no ready-made action fits (a door that slides aside, a bridge that rises, a light that blinks), ask the agent for it. It writes it once, as a reusable action: it is then added to the Then list of every Trigger in the game, under Written for this game, next to the ready-made actions.

For example, in the Agent panel:

Make me a reusable action "Sliding door": the target slides aside, by a distance I can set.

Then:

  • In a rule, Then offers Sliding door; hovering it shows its description.
  • Its settings (here, the distance) appear under the rule, like those of the ready-made actions, and change rule by rule.
  • You reuse it on other objects, without asking the agent again.

The action is a game script, visible in the Scripts tab under the name action. followed by its identifier (action.porte_glissante). If that script is deleted, the rule that used it says so: "The action “porte_glissante” no longer exists in this game: nothing will happen."

As long as no action has been written for this game, the Then list reminds you: "For an action that does not exist yet, ask the agent for it: it will be added to this list."

items.title: Asking the agent
items.text:
The agent knows the Trigger and prefers it to a script for these reactions, so that you keep control of the rules. A few requests:

  • "When the player steps on the plate, open the dungeon door."
  • "The lever opens and closes the gate."
  • "When the boss dies, the game is won."
  • "Every 30 seconds, make an enemy appear near the tower."

The rules it places then show in the object's Properties: you can read them and change them.

items.title: Vehicles, joints and ragdolls
items.text:
Three game systems give objects real game mechanics, without writing code: Joint, for what turns on a hinge, slides on a rail or hangs from a rope; Vehicle, for a car, a motorbike or a boat you drive; Ragdoll, for a character that falls limp then gets back up. They are set in the Properties, and the agent can place them for you.

As with physics, nothing is tied to a model pack: the attachment point is taken on the model's box, the wheels are measured on their models, and the ragdoll on the character's skeleton.

items.title: Joints
items.text:
A joint links an object to another one, or to the world: a door on its hinges, a drawbridge, a wheel on a cart, a drawer, an elevator, a chandelier, a plank that gives way under a weight.

  1. Turn the system on: Game tab, Systems section, Turn on under Joint. The Physics system comes with it: the jointed object is an object that moves.
  2. Place it on the moving part (the door, not the wall): drag Joint from the Systems folder of the library, or + System in its Properties. Give it a Mass under Physics: 20 to 40 kg for a door.
  3. Set it under Joint. When the object is selected, the 3D view shows its attachment point (a dot) and its axis (a line): you see at once whether the door turns the right way.
Setting What it does Kind of joint Hinge (turns around an axis), Slider (slides along an axis), Ball (turns every way around a point), Fixed (holds in place until it breaks), Rope (never goes further than a length), Spring (comes back to its length). Attached to (empty: the world) The object that holds it, chosen in the scene: the cart of a wheel, the furniture of a drawer. Empty, it is held where it stands. Attachment point Where it is held, on its model's box: in the middle, on a side, at the bottom, at the top, at the front or at the back. Axis For a hinge or a slider: Vertical (a door, an elevator), Sideways (a drawbridge, a wheel), Front to back (a drawer). Stops How far it turns (in degrees) or slides (in meters) from where it starts. A hinge from −180 to 180 turns endlessly, like a wheel. For a ball, how far it swings. Springiness (0: rigid) Stops that cushion like a spring; for a spring, its stiffness. Motor None: it moves when pushed. To a position: it stays closed, and opens to its stop when asked. At a steady speed: it turns or slides without stopping (a mill, a conveyor). Motor strength 500 for a door, 20,000 for an elevator carrying the player. Open at the start With a motor to a position: it starts open. Breaking force (N, 0: unbreakable) Beyond it, the joint gives way and the object falls: 800 for a rotten plank the player breaks by jumping on it.

items.title: Open, close, break
items.text: The Trigger has the actions Open, Close and Break its joint, with On which object: a lever (Interaction system) that opens the door, a zone in front of the drawbridge that lowers it. And the rule Its joint breaks reacts when it gives way: a message, a sound, what happens next.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• A door you push: Hinge, attachment point on a side, vertical axis, stops 0 and 100. The player opens it by walking into it.
  • A door opened by a lever: the same, with the motor To a position and a strength of 800; on the lever, a rule The player uses it → Open, on the door.
  • A drawbridge: Hinge, attachment point at the bottom, sideways axis, stops −90 and 0, motor to a position, Open at the start; a Close rule lowers it.
  • A chandelier: Ball, attachment point at the top, stop 30 degrees.
  • A plank that gives way: Fixed, breaking force 800.

items.title: Vehicles
items.text:
The Vehicle system turns a model into a car: its wheels spin, steer and follow the suspension, and the player drives it.

  1. Turn the system on, then place it on the car itself, or on the folder that holds its body and wheels. Place it on the ground.
  2. The wheels: the objects inside the car whose name contains "roue", "wheel", "tire", "tyre" or "pneu" are found on their own. Otherwise, list them in Wheels. Their size and place come from their models.
  3. A one-piece model (the car and its wheels in a single file, without separate wheels): with Wheels of a one-piece model checked (the starting setting), the system looks for its wheels inside the model itself, the round pieces at its bottom seen from the side. When the car is selected, a circle marks each one. In the game, they come off the body and turn like real wheels.
  4. If none is found (wheels welded to the body), four invisible wheels carry it, at the corners of its underside, and the model's wheels do not turn.
  5. The front of the model: most face +Z. When the car is selected, an arrow shows its front, and a circle marks each wheel found. The front wheels steer.

Getting in and out: the player walks up and presses Use (E, or Y on a gamepad). At the wheel, Move forward and Move back accelerate or brake then reverse, Move left and Move right steer, Jump holds the hand brake. The camera follows the car and comes back behind it when you do not turn it. Use again, and they get out on the left side.

Setting What it does Mass (kg) A car 1,200, a kart 150, a truck 8,000. Engine power (N·m) It makes it accelerate: 600 for a car, 150 for a kart. Top speed (km/h) Beyond it, it no longer speeds up. Grip (1: dry road) 0.4 slides as on snow, 1.5 sticks to the road. Suspension travel (m), Suspension stiffness A soft or firm car, an off-roader that rides high. Front wheel steering (degrees) More, it turns tighter. Brake strength The hand brake locks the rear wheels. Driving assist (1: arcade) 1, as in an arcade game: at speed it steers less, the wheel turns smoothly even on the keyboard, and it follows the road without spinning out or sliding (the hand brake still makes it drift). 0: physics alone, like a simulation.

The driver stays visible: seated in the driver seat (on the left), hands on the wheel, you see them through the windows; on a motorbike, astride the saddle, hands on the handlebars, they lean with it. Their place is measured on the model. If they sink into the seat or float above it, set Seat: forwards, upwards and to the right (in meters). If the player's character has a driving animation (its name is about driving or sitting: drive, ride, sit, seat…), it is played; otherwise a seated pose is made from their own. Driving animation picks another one. Uncheck Visible driver to hide them, as behind tinted windows. With several players, everyone sees the others at the wheel.

A zone sees the driven car as the player: a finish line works for a race.

Copying a car during the game: a script that calls game.clone on a vehicle (a hidden model used as a template, or a placed car) gets another vehicle, with its wheels, that the player can drive. A car hidden then shown again is a vehicle again too.

items.title: The motorbike
items.text:
A vehicle of the Motorbike kind rolls on two wheels, one behind the other. Place the system on the bike (or the folder holding its frame and wheels), choose Kind of vehicle: Motorbike, and set Mass (200 for a motorbike, 110 for a scooter) and Engine power (150): the starting values are a car's.

  • Its wheels are found like a car's: by their name, in the Wheels list, or inside a one-piece model. The front one steers, the rear one drives. With no wheel found, two invisible wheels carry it.
  • It stands upright by itself, parked or ridden, as on its kickstand, and leans into turns, the more so the faster it goes.
  • It can fall over: hit from the side (a rock, a car) or knocked down in a crash, it falls on its side and its rider is thrown off (falling limp if they carry the Ragdoll system). To set it upright, just get back on with Use.
  • It is driven like a car, and the camera follows it the same way.
Setting (motorbike) What it does Lean in turns (degrees) How far it leans at most: 45 for a road bike, 55 for a racing bike, 25 for a scooter. Balance (1: ordinary) The strength that keeps it upright: 2 very steady, 0.5 wobbly. Handling (1: ordinary) How fast the handlebars turn: 2 quick, 0.5 heavy. Too quick, a sharp turn can knock it down. Hit that unbalances it (m/s) A sideways blow sharper than this makes it lose its balance for a moment: 4 ordinary, 8 sturdy, 0 never. Can fall over Unchecked: it never falls, as in an arcade game.

The Trigger and scripts know when it falls: the vehicule.tombe event.

items.title: The boat
items.text:
A vehicle of the Boat kind floats instead of rolling. Place the system on the boat (or the folder that holds its hull, mast, cabin), choose Kind of vehicle: Boat, and place it on the water of a lake or the sea.

  • Its hull is measured on its model: its length and width, slice by slice from the back to the front, and its bottom. A thin bow carries less than a wide stern. How deep it sits comes from its Mass: the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does. Its center of gravity is at its waterline: a mast does not make it capsize.
  • An engine at the back pushes it, a rudder turns it, the better the faster it moves. You drive it like a car: Move forward to speed up, Move back to slow down then go backwards, Move left and Move right to turn. The camera follows it.
  • It rocks with the waves and follows the water's surface; a current carries it along.
  • It runs aground on land: its engine only pushes in water. Sent at a beach, it climbs a little, then stays there.
Setting (boat) What it does Mass (kg) A motorboat 1,200, a rowing boat 150, a fishing boat 8,000. Heavier, it sits deeper. Engine thrust (N) It makes it speed up: 4,000 for a 1,200 kg motorboat, 800 for a rowing boat. Top speed (km/h) The water holds it back more and more: at full thrust, it levels off at this speed. Turn at full rudder (degrees per second) 40 for a motorboat, 15 for a big boat.

items.title: Ragdolls
items.text:
An animated character carrying the Ragdoll system falls limp: its body is built on its own from its skeleton (long enough bones become limbs, fingers and toes follow their hand or foot), then it can get back up, and its animation resumes smoothly.

Setting What it does Falls limp when it dies (Health system) When its health reaches zero, it collapses, and stays down. Falls under a hit harder than (m/s) An object that hits it hard enough knocks it down: a rolling rock, a thrown barrel. 0: never. Gets back up after a hit, Gets up after (s) Knocked down by a hit, it gets up once it has been still for that long. Mass (kg) The body's weight, shared among its limbs. Limb looseness (degrees) 45 is natural, 20 falls stiff, 90 is very floppy.

Fallen into water, the rag doll floats, the head and shoulders just above the water, and drifts with it; untick Floats in water to make it sink, like a knight in armor.

The Trigger has the actions Make it fall limp and Get it back up. The character must be animated: a model without a skeleton cannot fall as a ragdoll.

items.title: Asking the agent
items.text:
The agent places these systems and checks its work by running the game: the report tells it the angle each joint reached and whether it broke, the speed each vehicle reached, the distance travelled and whether it turned over (for a motorbike: how far it leaned and how many times it fell; for a boat: whether it floats or ran aground, and how deep its hull sits), and how many times each character fell and got back up. Ask it for example:

  • "A wooden door in the castle entrance, that you push to get in."
  • "A drawbridge that lowers when you pull the lever."
  • "A car parked in front of the house, that the player can drive."
  • "A rowing boat moored at the jetty, to cross the lake."
  • "A racing motorbike on the starting line, that leans well into turns."
  • "The guards fall like rag dolls when they die."

All the settings: the reference of the Joint, Vehicle and Ragdoll systems.

items.title: Videos
items.text: A game can show videos: a full-screen cutscene (an intro, an ending, a story moment), or a video in the interface (a screen in a menu, an animated portrait). The video's sound plays with it, in a group of the sound mixer: Voice for a cutscene (the game's music lowers meanwhile), Effects for a video in the interface; the "Video sound" setting or the group option picks another one.

items.title: The files
items.text:
WorldMint reads MP4 videos, the most common format: the one of phones, editing software and video sites. M4V and MOV files are read too when they hold the same thing (H.264 picture and AAC sound).

Windows decodes the videos: there is nothing to install, neither for you nor for your players. A video it cannot read (another format inside the file) shows a message; save it as MP4 from your editing software. On an "N" edition of Windows, without a media player, add the Media Feature Pack (Windows Settings, Optional features): without it, the game plays without its videos.

items.title: In the library
items.text: Add to the library a folder that contains your videos (see The library). Each video has its tile there, with a picture of its beginning; the tooltip gives its length and size. Double-click to watch it in the Windows player; the right-click menu also offers Open file location and Copy path. The bottom of the panel counts each folder's videos.

items.title: A cutscene, without code
items.text:
The Trigger has the Play a video action:

  1. Place the Trigger on an object, and add a rule. For an intro: When: When the game starts.
  2. Then: Play a video, then choose the Video in the list.
  3. The player can skip it: checked, Escape, Enter, Space, a click or A on the gamepad skip it; a small prompt says so at the bottom of the screen. Unchecked, it is watched to the end.
  4. Event sent at the end (optional): a name, for example "intro_done". It is sent when the video ends, or when the player skips it.

During the video, the world is paused: nobody moves, game time does not count.

To chain what comes next, add another rule: When: When an event happens, with the same name ("intro_done"), and Then: what follows, such as Go to another scene or Show a message. A missing or unreadable video does not stop the game: the event is sent anyway.

items.title: With a script
items.text:
The agent can also write a script:

  • game.video("videos/intro.mp4", {event = "intro_done"}) plays a cutscene; skip = false forbids skipping it, pause = false keeps the world running behind it.
  • game.hud_video("screen", "videos/loop.mp4", {x = 0.05, y = 0.6, w = 0.3}) puts a video in the interface, at its real proportions, looping; game.hud_remove("screen") removes it.
  • At the end of every video, the game announces the video.fin event (see Events).

The details are in the scripts reference.

items.title: The agent's test
items.text: When the agent tries the game without a window, it neither sees nor hears the videos, but they start and end at the same moments as on screen: its report says which ones played, for how long, and whether they went to the end, were skipped or stopped.

items.title: When exporting
items.text: The videos named by rules and scripts go with the exported game (see Exporting a game). The player has nothing to install.

items.title: Not possible yet
items.text: A video on an object of the world, such as a television screen, isn't possible yet: it will come before the public beta.

items.title: The editor window
items.text:
The window has five areas. Each has its page:

Area What you find there Menus and top bar The File, Edit, Select, Object, View, Game, Agent, Help menus; the gizmo and undo buttons, the Preferences and Play. All the keyboard shortcuts. Left column Three tabs: Scene (the game's scenes and the objects of the open one), Game (the game's controls and systems), Scripts. The 3D view The scene, with its tool column: move, rotate, scale, and the terrain tools. The library At the bottom: your folders of models and sounds, reusable objects and systems to place. Right column The Properties of what is selected (or the Preferences), and the Agent panel.

items.title: Arranging the window
items.text:
• Change a column's width: drag the edge of the left or right column. Drag the top of the library to change its height.
  • Hide an area: View menu > Left panel, Right panel, Library, Console. The library also opens and closes with Library, at the bottom left of the status bar.
  • Fold Properties or Agent: the arrow (chevron) to the right of their title. A click on the title reopens the panel. When both are open, a handle between them shares the height: drag it up to enlarge the Agent.
  • Fold a section: each group of settings (Position and size, Appearance, Systems...) folds with a click on its title. Rarely used settings (Details, Technical settings...) start folded.

items.title: The status bar
items.text:
At the very bottom of the window:

  • on the left, Library opens or closes the library;
  • in the middle, the editor's last message (Ready at first). A click opens the Console, which keeps all the messages (the Close the console cross closes it);
  • on the right: The agent is working or Agent allowed, the time of the last automatic backup if the scene has unsaved changes, the number of selected objects, and the number of objects in the scene.

items.title: Object colors
items.text: Each kind of object has its color and icon, the same in the scene list and on the card at the top of the properties: model, basic shape, folder, played character, camera, arrival point, terrain and its regions.

items.title: The Game tab
items.text: The second tab of the left column holds what applies to the whole game, in all its scenes, and belongs to no object: its Controls, its Sound mixer and its Systems.

items.title: Controls
items.text:
One control per key of the game: Move forward, Jump, Attack... Scripts read its name, the player sees its label. For each one, a button shows its key (click, then press the key you want) and a list its gamepad button. Add a control creates a new one.

Everything is detailed in Game controls.

items.title: Sound mixer
items.text:
Every sound of the game belongs to a group: Music, Effects, Ambience, Voice, Interface, and those you add with Add a group. For each one, a slider sets its volume and the speaker mutes it. Further down, Automatic ducking makes a group quieter while another plays (the music under the voices), and Muffled groups muffle a group all the time.

Everything is detailed in Sound and the sound mixer.

items.title: Systems
items.text:
Systems are ready-made game rules: health, a health bar, combat, enemies, an inventory, harvesting, sounds, physics, passages between scenes... The full list, with every setting, is in the systems reference.

A system is used in two steps: you activate it for the game, then you place it on the objects that should carry it.

items.title: Activating a system
items.text: Under Add a system, each system not yet activated shows its name and what it does. Some need another one: "Also activates: Health". Click Activate.

items.title: Activated systems
items.text:
At the top of the section, each activated system has its card, folded. A click on its name opens it:

  • what it does;
  • where it is placed: "Placed on 3 objects or groups", or "Placed on no object yet";
  • its settings for the whole game (those not set object by object), which apply at once;
  • "Its scripts were changed: they stay as they are" if a script of the system was changed by hand;
  • Deactivate: removes it from the game. If it is placed on objects, the editor asks for confirmation ("Deactivate this system?") and says from how many objects it will be removed, with their values; Keep gives up. Ctrl+Z brings everything back. A system another one needs cannot be deactivated: the button says so on hover ("The “Basic combat” system needs it").

items.title: Placing a system on objects
items.text:
Once activated, a system that goes on objects appears in the Systems folder of the library. To place it:

  • drag it from the library onto an object or a folder, in the scene list or in the 3D view; on the ground of a terrain, it goes on the Terrain;
  • or double-click it in the library: it goes on the selection;
  • or, in an object's Properties, Systems section, click + System.

Placed on a folder, a system applies to everything the folder contains: once for a whole troop of enemies. Its per-object settings are then changed in the properties: see An object's systems.

items.title: The library
items.text: At the bottom of the window, below the 3D view: your models and sounds, arranged as in File Explorer. It opens and closes with Library, at the bottom left of the status bar, or with View > Library. Drag its top edge to change its height.

items.title: Adding your folders
items.text:
The editor ships no models: you add the folders where yours are.

  • Add a folder, then Browse to choose it, or paste its path in the field ("A folder's path, or drop it here").
  • Or drag a folder (or a file) from File Explorer onto the editor window: its folder is added.
  • Or write a folder's path in a message to the agent: it is added to the library.

Added folders apply to all your projects. The cross at the end of a folder's row, in the tree, removes it from the library (nothing is deleted from the disk).

Formats read: models in .glb, .gltf, .fbx and .obj, with their skeletons and animations; sounds in WAV, MP3, OGG and FLAC. COLLADA files (.dae) are counted apart ("Not read (COLLADA)"): the editor does not read them yet. The same model shipped in several formats appears only once.

items.title: Browsing
items.text:
• On the left, the tree: Library, then your folders and their subfolders; Systems (the activated systems) and Reusable objects, when there are any. A click opens a folder.
  • At the top, the path: each name can be clicked. The Back and Parent folder arrows are on the left, as in File Explorer.
  • Search the library searches the open folder and its subfolders.
  • The slider next to the search sets the preview size (also Ctrl + mouse wheel over the grid).
  • The cross on the right closes the library.
  • At the bottom, the number of models and sounds in the folder.

On hover, a model shows its name and path.

items.title: Using a model
items.text:
• Double-click: adds the model at the center of the view.
  • Drag into the 3D view: places it where you drop it.
  • Drag onto the Vegetation area of a terrain region: it grows there. See The terrain.
  • Right-click: Place in the scene, Open file location, Copy path.

When a model is used in a project, its file is copied there: the project stays complete if you move it, and your library never changes.

items.title: Sounds
items.text:
• Double-click: plays the sound; a second double-click stops it.
  • Right-click: Listen (or Stop), Open file location, Copy path.

Sounds are used by systems (the Sounds system) and by scripts.

items.title: Folders
items.text: Right-click a folder in the grid: Open, Open in File Explorer. On hover, it says how many models and sounds it contains.

items.title: Systems
items.text: The Systems folder shows the activated systems that go on objects, with the number of objects carrying them. Drag one onto an object or a folder, in the scene list or in the view; a double-click places it on the selection. See The Game tab.

items.title: Reusable objects
items.text:
A reusable object is a set of objects (a house, a stall, a lamp post) that you place as many times as you like, and whose copies all change together.

  • Create it: right-click an object of the scene, Make a reusable object (or the Object menu). It appears in the Reusable objects folder.
  • Place it: double-click, drag into the view, or right-click > Place in the scene.
  • Delete it: right-click > Delete.

A copy is managed in its properties: apply its changes to all copies, discard them, or detach it.

items.title: Online
items.text:
The Online folder, at the bottom of the tree, offers free models to download into your project, with their licence.

Choosing where they come from. At first, no source is chosen and the editor contacts no site. The Sources button offers two kinds:

  • Poly Haven: free 3D models from polyhaven.com, in the public domain (CC0). The "Powered by Poly Haven" notice stays shown under their previews, as their site asks.
  • Library address: an index in the WorldMint format. To try it without Internet, python tools/bibliotheque_demo.py <folder> --licence CC0-1.0 serves a folder of your models on this computer and prints the address to paste here.

Nothing about you is sent: neither your files nor your searches. A source's catalogue is read whole, and the search runs on your computer.

Browsing and searching. The grid shows the models of the chosen sources, with their preview and their licence (CC0 or CC BY) at the top right. Search the library looks in their name, author and tags. On hover: the author, licence, source and size. At the bottom, the chosen model and its licence. Refresh reads the catalogues again.

Adding a model. Double-click it: it is downloaded into the project, then placed at the centre of the view (the percentage shows on its tile while it downloads). Right-click: Place in the scene, Add to project (without placing it), Open the asset's page. It arrives in assets/<source>/<model>/, with a LICENCE.txt file giving its author, source and licence. A model already downloaded is not downloaded twice.

What is checked. Every file from the Internet is treated as data that may be booby-trapped: its size is bounded while it downloads, its fingerprint must match, only model, image and text formats are accepted (never a program or a script), an archive is unpacked within strict limits, and the model is read by the editor before it enters the project. An asset without an accepted licence (CC0 or CC BY) is not offered. What is refused is refused with the reason, and leaves nothing in the project.

The game's credits. A CC BY licence requires crediting the author. The export writes CREDITS-ASSETS.txt next to the game, with each model from the online library, its author, source and licence; credit them in your game's credits too.

The agent can also search and add online models, in the sources you chose: it tells you which ones, by whom, and under which licence.

items.title: The top bar
items.text:
On the left, the menus. In the middle, five buttons:

Button Effect Globe: World axes / Object axes The gizmo follows the scene's axes, or those of the turned object. Magnet: Snapping: moves by grid steps Moves, rotations and sizes go by steps (set in the Preferences). Four squares: Four views (Q) Splits the 3D view in four. Arrows: Undo (Ctrl+Z), Redo (Ctrl+Y) Undoes or redoes the last change.

On the right: the gear opens the Preferences, and Play (F5) starts the game; during the game, the button becomes Stop.

items.title: File
items.text: Command Shortcut Effect New project... Creates a project in a new folder, then offers the creation assistant. Open project... Opens a .worldmint file. Open project folder Opens the project folder in File Explorer. Create a project from this scene... For a scene outside a project: makes it a project, copying its models into it. New scene... Ctrl+N Asks where to save it, then opens an empty scene. In a project, the + of Game scenes is simpler: see Projects and scenes. Open... Ctrl+O Opens a scene (.wmscene). Open recent scene The last scenes opened; on hover, their path. Save Ctrl+S Saves the scene. Save as... Ctrl+Shift+S Saves it to another file. Export game... Turns the game into a folder with its program: see Exporting a game. Only possible when the game has a player. Preferences Opens the Preferences in the right column. Quit Closes the editor (offering to save).

items.title: Edit
items.text: Command Shortcut Undo Ctrl+Z Redo Ctrl+Y Cut Ctrl+X Copy Ctrl+C Paste Ctrl+V Duplicate Ctrl+D Delete Del

items.title: Select
items.text: Command Shortcut Select all Ctrl+A Invert selection Ctrl+I Select nothing

items.title: Object
items.text: Command Shortcut Effect Create Folder, Camera, Arrival point, Zone, Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Capsule, Plane: see The Scene tab. Make a reusable object With a single object selected: see The library. Group Ctrl+G Puts the selection in a new folder. Ungroup Ctrl+Shift+G Takes the folder's contents out. Place on ground End Sets the selection on what is below it. Reset rotation to zero Reset scale to 1 Turn collision on The player and characters no longer pass through. Turn collision off

items.title: View
items.text: Command Shortcut Effect Perspective, Top, Bottom, Front, Back, Left, Right Numpad 5, 7, 1, 3 (with Ctrl: the opposite) The point of view of the active view. Normal, Polygons, Wireframe Z The rendering of the active view. Four views Q One view or four. Frame selection F Brings the views close to the selection; with nothing selected, shows the whole scene. Show the whole scene Home Brings the views back to the whole scene, seen from a little above. Show everything again Shows again the objects hidden with the eye of the list. Grid Shows or hides the grid. Walkable areas Shows where characters can walk: blue, what they reach from the player; orange, isolated spots. See character walking. Left panel, Right panel, Library, Console Shows or hides each area.

items.title: Game
items.text: Command Shortcut Effect Play F5 Starts the game in its window. Stop F5 Closes the game. Creation assistant... Reopens the assistant that prepares a request for the agent (in a project).

items.title: Agent
items.text: Command Effect Conversation Opens the Agent panel on the conversation. New conversation Starts again from an empty conversation. Agent settings Opens the settings: account, model, reasoning effort, rules. See The agent.

items.title: Help
items.text:
• Keyboard shortcuts: the list of shortcuts below.
  • Licenses: the licenses of the open-source software inside WorldMint and your games. The same file, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt, sits next to the editor, and the export puts it in every game: nothing to do on your side.
  • Language: Français or English. The interface changes at once.

items.title: All shortcuts
items.text:
Keys Effect W, E, R Move, rotate, scale End Place the selection on the ground F Frame selection Home Show the whole scene Arrows, Page Up, Page Down Nudge the selection by one step (Shift: × 10, Ctrl: ÷ 10) Q One view or four views Numpad 7, 1, 3 Top, front, right view Ctrl + numpad 7, 1, 3 Bottom, back, left view Numpad 5 Back to perspective Z Cycle Normal, Polygons, Wireframe Click, Ctrl + click Select, add to the selection Drag in the scene Rectangle selection Ctrl+A, Ctrl+I Select all, invert selection Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V Copy, cut, paste Ctrl+D, Del Duplicate, delete Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y Undo, redo Ctrl+S Save F5 Play, stop Right-click Orbit around the point under the mouse Ctrl + right-click Orbit around the selection Middle-click, wheel Pan the view, zoom F2 Rename the selected object Ctrl+G, Ctrl+Shift+G Group, ungroup Ctrl+N, Ctrl+O, Ctrl+Shift+S New scene, open, save as Esc Stop the terrain tool in use

Single-key shortcuts do nothing while you type in a field.

items.title: Dialog boxes
items.text:
• Save your changes?: before opening another scene, creating one or quitting, if the scene has changes. Save, Don't save, or Keep working (nothing happens).
  • Recover your work?: at launch, if the editor closed without saving and an automatic backup holds your work. Recover reopens it (then save to keep it); Don't recover discards it. "The scene file stays unchanged until you save."

items.title: Preferences
items.text: The gear at the top right (or File > Preferences) opens the preferences in place of the properties, in the right column. "These apply to the editor, across all your projects." Close preferences goes back to the properties.

items.title: Appearance
items.text: Setting Effect Language Français or English. Also in Help > Language. Dark theme Dark interface (default) or light. Accent color The color of the main buttons, of the selection, of markers. Interface size Enlarges or shrinks texts and buttons (× 1 by default).

items.title: Placement
items.text: Setting Effect Place on ground when adding An added model is set on the ground (on by default). Grid step The step of moves when snapping is on (1 m by default). Rotation step The step of rotations, in degrees (15° by default). Scale step The step of size changes (0.1 by default). Arrow keys step How far the arrow keys nudge the selection (0.1 m by default; Shift × 10, Ctrl ÷ 10).

items.title: Navigation
items.text: Setting Effect Orbit speed How fast the view turns with the right button. Pan speed How fast the view moves with the middle button; by default, what is under the mouse follows it. Zoom step The effect of one wheel notch. Gizmo size The size of the move, rotate and scale handles.

items.title: Display
items.text:
View quality: how detailed the work views are (shadows, lights, water, glow, distant terrain and plants), Low, Medium or High. Medium, the starting setting, keeps the editor smooth on a large scene with four views; High shows the picture as the game draws it on a graphics card, to judge the final look; Low helps a small computer. The game started with Play keeps its own quality, and a scene's Shadow quality never goes above the views' quality. See display settings.

View upscaling: the same thing as the game's setting, for the editor's work views (off by default). It doesn't change the game, which has its own in Game window. See display settings.

View anti-aliasing: when the view's upscaling is off, smooths the objects' edges (TAA, SMAA, FXAA, Automatic, or None, the starting setting). See anti-aliasing.

View ray tracing: the work views' shadows and reflections drawn with real rays of light, on a graphics card that has it. Automatic (at first): only on a dedicated card, in Medium or High quality; On: always, even where the view may slow down; Off: the usual shadows and reflections. The views only use it if the game allows it (Game window, Allow ray tracing). When the graphics card's memory is full, a line under this choice says so: "almost full" (rays reach less far) or "Off" (the usual shadows); changing this choice makes it try again. See ray tracing.

View indirect lighting: the light bounced by surfaces (a sunlit floor lights the walls, a room is lit through its window), ray traced with a light cache. High quality with ray tracing only; it costs about 1 to 2 ms. On at first; unticked, the views keep the sky's ambient light. Below High, a line under the switch says so. See ray tracing.

items.title: Saving
items.text: Automatic backup: every 60 seconds by default. "0 turns it off. It keeps a separate copy and doesn't touch the scene file." If the editor closes without saving, it offers to recover this work on the next launch.

items.title: Console
items.text: Lines kept: how many messages the console keeps.

items.title: The properties
items.text:
The Properties panel, at the top of the right column, shows the settings of what is selected. With nothing selected: the game's settings. The content changes with the kind of object: a played character shows its movement, a camera what it looks at, a terrain region its vegetation.

At the top, a card says what the object is: its icon, its name, and its kind (the model's file name, Basic shape, Folder, Played character, Camera, Arrival point, Terrain, Terrain region, Terrain water or Plant kind), with a sentence of explanation.

items.title: Changing a value
items.text: Number fields are set in two ways: "Click to type a value, or drag to adjust it (Alt: finer)." A drag, however long, is undone with a single Ctrl+Z. Three-value fields give X (red), Y (green, up) and Z (blue), in metres.

items.title: The buttons at the top
items.text:
• Place on ground (End key): sets the object on what is below it.
  • Set as player: makes this model the character you play. See The player.

items.title: Position and size
items.text: Field Effect Position Where the object is in the world, in metres. Rotation Its rotation, in degrees, around X, Y and Z. A horizontal half-turn shows as "0, 180, 0". (Absent for a camera that follows an object: it turns by itself.) Scale Its size, per axis: 1 is the original size.

items.title: Appearance
items.text: Field Effect Collision The player and characters cannot pass through it. For an object carrying the Physics system, the row says instead "Movable: it collides with everything (Physics system)". Color Tints the model or colors the shape. White changes nothing. Visible in game Unchecked, the object is not seen in the game (a model that scripts copy, for example). It stays visible in the editor.

items.title: Held by the character
items.text:
For an object placed inside an animated character (a sword in the hand, a bag on the back):

  • Attached to bone: choose a bone of the skeleton in the list (a search filters their names). In the game, the object follows this bone as the character animates. Choosing a bone places the object on it; then adjust it if needed, on the rest pose. None: it follows the character detaches it from the bone.
  • Place on the bone: places and orients it like the bone again.

items.title: An object's systems
items.text:
The Systems section lists the systems the object carries, with their per-object settings. Each system's settings are described in the systems reference.

  • + System places an activated system the object does not carry yet. (To activate a system, see The Game tab.)
  • The cross to the right of a system's name removes it from this object. A system that another system of the object needs cannot be removed alone: it is marked "Needed by ...".
  • Inheritance: a system placed on a folder applies to everything inside. An object in the folder shows "Inherited from the folder “Enemies”". If it changes a value, the value is marked Changed on this object, and the arrow beside it goes back to the folder's value; the other values stay the folder's ("Value of the folder “Enemies”").
  • Do not inherit: cuts inheritance for this object and what it contains. Restore inheritance brings it back.
  • "Nothing to set on the object: its settings apply to the whole game": this system is set in the Game tab.

items.title: A copy of a reusable object
items.text:
The Reusable object section says which object this is a copy of ("Copy of “House”"). If the copy was changed:

  • Apply to all copies: every copy takes these changes;
  • Discard my changes: the copy becomes like the reusable object again.

Detach from the reusable object makes it an ordinary object, which no longer follows the other copies.

items.title: Details
items.text:
Folded at first:

  • Dimensions: the object's real size, in metres;
  • Triangles: the number of triangles of its model;
  • Tags: words by which scripts find the object ("merchant", "coin"), separated by commas.

items.title: Several objects
items.text:
With several objects selected, the panel says "3 objects selected". "The gizmo and these fields act on the whole selection, around its center":

  • Center: moves the whole set;
  • Turn by: turns the set by these degrees, then the field goes back to zero;
  • Multiply size by: enlarges or shrinks the set, then goes back to 1;
  • Collision (or Collision (some) if only some have it): for all;
  • Place on ground, Duplicate, Delete;
  • Systems, + System: each selected object receives the system. To set it once for all, put them in a folder (Ctrl+G) and place it on the folder.

items.title: The player
items.text: When the played character is selected, its settings come first. "Press F5 to play and tune live": while the game runs, each change applies to it at once.

items.title: Movement
items.text:
Field Effect Walk speed In m/s. Run speed In m/s, while holding the run key. Jump strength The jump's starting speed, in m/s. Swim speed In m/s, in deep water. Acceleration In m/s²: how fast it reaches its speed. Turn speed In degrees per second: how fast it turns towards where it goes. Gravity In m/s². Fall limit In metres: if it falls below this height, it respawns. Face the camera It always faces where the camera looks, instead of turning towards where it goes: it walks sideways or backwards, as in a shooter. While holding the control (without the setting above) A game control, aiming for example: while it is held, it faces the camera. None: it always turns towards where it goes.

Reset to defaults puts these settings back to their starting values.

items.title: Animations
items.text:
• Animation files: the files the character's moves come from. Add an animation file picks one from the library; the Remove this file cross removes it. The number of moves available shows above.
  • One row per situation: Idle, Walk, Run, Jump, In the air, Landing, Swim, Fall... For each, choose the move it plays. The eye Show this move in the scene shows it on the character, in the view.
  • Advanced animation settings (folded), in two tabs:
    • Situations: each situation, with its name, its move, its Playback speed (× 1 = normal), Looping, and At start (the starting situation). Add a situation creates one; the cross deletes it. A looping situation (a walk, a run) has its moves By direction: Move backwards, to the left, to the right, and the diagonals Move forward-left, forward-right, back-left, back-right. When the character faces the camera, they are blended with the situation's move (forward) according to the direction taken, on 8 directions: between two neighbouring directions, shared by the angle. A diagonal with no move (Blend of its neighbours) is shared by its two neighbours: half one, half the other, as on 4 directions. Without any of them, the situation's move is used in every direction, as before; when a side one is missing, it stands in for it (played in reverse to walk backwards). Script characters have their own (game.character, walk_directions and run_directions, with strafe).
    • Sequences: when to go from one situation to another. Each sequence goes from a situation (or from Any situation) to another, with conditions (Speed, Share of run speed, Vertical speed, On the ground, Time in the air, Jump started, Movement input, Run key, Time in the situation, Move progress), a comparison sign, a value, and a Fade in seconds. Condition adds a condition. "The first possible sequence in the list wins": the Higher priority and Lower priority arrows change the order. Add a sequence creates one. Three values serve walking sideways: Forward speed (negative backwards), Sideways speed (positive to its right) and Facing the camera (1 when it faces the camera).
  • Feet on the ground: on a slope, a step or a terrain, each foot rests on the real ground (moving objects included: a platform, a boat, a vehicle), and the hips lower as needed, for the foot touching the ground only: the leg the animation lifts (the one swinging forward while walking) follows the body without going under the ground. Largest feet gap: the largest gap corrected under a foot, in metres. The engine looks for the legs in the skeleton (a foot, a knee, a hip); without them, it says so, and nothing changes.
  • Animation borrowing (on by default): a file made for a character with the same bones but other proportions (taller, stockier) is played with this character's proportions: its rotations only, and the hips' movement scaled to its legs. Limbs do not float. The file then shows (adapted). A file made for a skeleton whose bones have other names (Mixamo, Unreal, Blender, Unity…) is borrowed: bones are found on their own, by their name and then by the shape of the skeleton (spine, arms, legs, left and right), and the move is replayed on the character, even when its rest pose differs (arms in a T or an A). The file then shows (borrowed). Off, moves are read as they are, by bone names.
    • Bone matching (opens by itself when a bone is to check): for each body bone of the character, the bone of the file it follows, and where that choice comes from: by name, by shape, same name, by hand, or to check when the clue is weak. Choose another bone of the file in the list if it is wrong, (none) so that it keeps its rest pose, or Automatic choice to go back to the engine's choice. Show all bones adds fingers and helper bones. File shown picks the file when several are borrowed.
    • The preview shows both skeletons side by side, the file on the left and the character on the right, playing the Preview move: they should strike the same pose. Hover a bone in the list: it lights up on both sides.

items.title: Player camera
items.text:
The camera that follows the character in the game.

Field Effect Distance Its distance to the character, in metres. Target height The height of the point it looks at, above the feet. Field of view In degrees: wider shows more. Tilt Its downward angle, at the start. Mouse sensitivity In degrees per mouse pixel.

More camera settings (folded): Min tilt and Max tilt (how far it can go down or up), Return after obstacle (how fast it comes back after moving closer because of a wall), Obstacle margin, Minimum distance.

items.title: Character body
items.text: Folded at first. "The invisible shape that stops it at walls and lets it climb steps": Radius, Height, Step height (the highest step it climbs without jumping), Maximum slope (in degrees), Mass (in kilograms, 70 by default: the heavier it is, the less a thrown crate or a rock knocks it).

items.title: A camera
items.text:
A placed camera (Create > Camera) shows the game from where it stands; it is not seen in the game. When selected, it shows in a corner of the view What this camera shows.

Field Effect Field of view In degrees. Look at Straight ahead (it looks along its rotation), or an object of the scene it keeps in view. Opens the game The game starts on this camera, instead of the one following the player.
  • Move to current view: the camera takes the position and direction of the 3D view.
  • Look through this camera: the 3D view takes its place.

Scripts switch cameras during the game: see the scripts reference.

items.title: A light
items.text:
A placed light (Create > Light) lights around it; it is not seen in the game, only its light. In the view, an icon marks its place, and its range when selected. Its color is the object's Color. See Light and shadows.

Field Effect Kind of light Bulb (all around) or Spotlight (a cone toward the bottom of the object: turn it to aim). On Off, it stays in place; the Trigger or a script switches it back on. Light intensity Its strength at 1 m; it falls off with distance. Light range How far it lights, in meters. Spotlight opening The width of its cone, in degrees. Light's shadows What it lights casts its shadow (only a few lights at a time). Shadow softness With its shadows: the size of what gives the light, in meters (0 sharp, 0.3 a lantern).

items.title: An arrival point
items.text: "The player appears here, facing the arrow, when a passage or a script brings them into this scene." The Arrival point section lists the passages leading here, in every scene of the game. See Projects and scenes.

items.title: The terrain, its regions, its plants
items.text: The Terrain, its regions, its water and its plant kinds have their own settings: see The terrain.

items.title: Nothing selected: the game's settings
items.text: With nothing selected (or after a click on the game row, at the top of the Scene tab), the card carries the game's title and says "Nothing selected: the game's settings".

items.title: Terrain
items.text: Without a terrain, the Terrain section offers to generate one; with a terrain, Edit the terrain selects it. See The terrain.

items.title: Sky and light
items.text:
Field Effect Sky The color of the sky. Background The color behind everything else. Sun color The color of its light. Sun intensity Its strength. Sun direction Where its light comes from (X, Y, Z). Light from the ground The color of the light bounced by the ground, which lights the underside of objects. Exposure How much light reaches the image, as on a camera: 1 leaves it as it is. Automatic exposure The image brightens in a dark place and comes back outside, like an eye getting used to it; with Brighten up to, Darken up to and Adaptation time. Sun shadows Objects, terrain and plants cast their shadow. Shadow quality For the sun and the lights: Depends on the computer (low on an integrated chip, high on a graphics card), High, Medium, Low or Off (no shadows). Shadow distance How far around the camera they are drawn, in meters. Shadow softness The size of the sun, in degrees: 0 sharp, 0.5 the real sun, up to 10 very soft. Sharp at the foot of an object, softer further from it. Fog distance At this distance, the fog hides almost everything; 0: none (only the horizon fade remains). Fog color, Fog altitude, Thins out with height Its color; the altitude where it has its thickness, and every how many meters it halves above it (0: the same everywhere). Glow of bright lights The glow around what shines very brightly; 0: none.

In detail: Light and shadows.

items.title: Game window
items.text: Field Effect Title The title of the game window, and the name of the exported game. Width, Height The window size, in pixels. Fullscreen The game fills the whole screen. Synced with the screen Frames follow the screen's rhythm (no image tearing). Upscaling Draws the scene smaller, then enlarges it by blending the frames that follow one another: faster, and edges no longer look jagged. Off by default. See display settings. Anti-aliasing Without upscaling: TAA (sharp in motion), SMAA (sharp, no trails), FXAA (lightest) or None; Automatic (the default) follows the quality: TAA in High and Medium (SMAA in a project from before November 2026), FXAA in Low. See anti-aliasing. Allow ray tracing The player may draw shadows and reflections by ray tracing, on a card that has it (their choice: Automatic, On or Off, in the game's menu). Unticked: the game is always drawn without it. Ticked by default. See ray tracing.

items.title: Character walking
items.text:
Folded at first. The typical character for whom the walkable areas are computed (see character walking).

Field Effect Character radius Half its width, in metres: it keeps this distance from walls. Character height It walks under anything higher. Steepest slope In degrees: beyond it, the ground isn't a walkable area. Highest step In metres: what it steps over without a detour.

items.title: Technical settings
items.text:
Folded at first; you almost never touch them.

Field Effect View distance Beyond it, nothing is drawn. Nearest visible distance Closer than it, nothing is drawn. Rate The number of simulation steps per second. Max catch-up How many simulation steps the game catches up at most, per frame, after a slowdown. Max physics bodies The number of objects physics can follow. "The number of bodies applies the next time the game starts." Warning: tiny model, Warning: huge model In metres: a smaller or larger model is reported as having an unusual size.

items.title: The Scene tab
items.text: The first tab of the left column. You choose the place (the scene), then what it contains (its objects), like folders in File Explorer.

items.title: The game row
items.text: At the very top, with the globe icon, a row carries the game's title ("Jeu" at first; This game if the title is empty). On hover: "The game's settings: its sky, its window, its terrain". A click deselects everything, and the Properties then show the game's settings: its terrain, its sky and light, its window. See The properties.

items.title: Game scenes
items.text:
In a project, the Game scenes section lists the places of your game: one scene per place (the outdoors, the inside of a house, a cave, a level). "One place per scene: a click opens it."

  • Open a scene: click its name. If the open scene has changes, the editor first asks whether to save them.
  • Create a scene: the + to the right of the title ("New scene: another place of the game (a house, a cave, a level)").
  • Start: the word shown to the right of the scene where the game starts. The exported game opens on it.
  • On hover, a scene shows its passages (which scene they lead to) and its arrival points.
  • Right-click a scene:
Command Effect Open Opens this scene. Rename Changes its name in place. The passages leading to it are updated in every scene. Duplicate Creates a copy of the scene. Delete Asks for confirmation, and lists the passages and scripts that name it and will lead nowhere. The scene is set aside in the project's work folder (.worldmint, "scènes supprimées"): nothing is lost. These cannot be deleted: the start scene, the one that holds the player's character, and the game's last scene. Start the game here Makes it the start scene.

To link scenes together (a door that leads into a house), see Projects and scenes.

items.title: Sectors (large maps)
items.text:
In a large world, the Sectors section cuts the map into named parts: the harbour, the old town, the north forest. They help you find your way, work on one part at a time, and lock what is finished. “One click: work on it alone.”

  • Create a sector: the + on the right of the title, then click and drag on the ground, in a view (preferably the top view, 7 on the numeric keypad). Its size shows while you draw; Escape cancels. You name the sector right away, like a new folder.
  • Work on a sector: click its name, in the list or on its label in the view. The object list, the selection, Ctrl+A and framing then only see it; the other objects are hidden in the views (nothing is deleted), and seen from above the rest of the map darkens. The line “Sector “Harbour”: 1,462 objects hidden around it” reminds you above the list. Whole map shows everything again.
  • The number on the right of a sector counts its objects: a building made of twenty pieces counts once.
