Facet strength Stylized water, from 0 to 1: at 1, each facet has its own crisp shade, from its slope facing the sun; toward 0, the surface smooths out, with the same waves. Floating things follow the facets in any case. Foam The white foam, from 0 to 1: on wave crests, along the shores and around whatever touches the water. 0: none. Foam width Stylized water: the width, in meters, of the white foam band along the shores and around whatever touches the water. In High quality, a second thinner band comes and goes beyond the first. The foam is also set with Foam (0: none). Import Lays the heightmap as the terrain's relief, with the regions and sea set for “Generate a world”. Ctrl+Z to go back. Import a relief Makes the map from a heightmap: a grayscale image where white is the highest (preferably a 16-bit PNG, or a raw .raw or .r16 file), like World Machine, Gaea or real-data converters make. You then choose its scale and altitudes. Up to 4 km per side. Kind of water A ready-made kind of water: sea, stormy sea, lagoon, lake, pond, low poly sea or low poly lake. Choosing one sets the swell, the colors, the clarity and the foam at once; the two low poly kinds also switch the water to the Stylized style. Everything stays adjustable afterwards. Level The height of the water surface, in meters. Higher, the water covers more land: the sea rises, a lake overflows its hollow. Meters per point The distance between two points of the image, in meters: a 1,025-point image at 1 m makes a 1,024 m map. A map is at most 4 km per side. New region A region of your own, to paint wherever you want: name it and give it its color and systems. Paint this region Takes the Paint tool with this region: click and drag on the ground, in the view, to spread it. Regions The large areas of the ground: snow, rock, forest, grassland, desert, swamp, beach. Each one is an object with its color, plants and systems. When generating, untick those you do not want: their areas take the most fitting neighboring region. Remove the terrain Deletes the terrain from the scene, with everything stored in it: its regions, its water, its plants. Ctrl+Z brings it back. Sea A sea at the coast level: it covers everything lower. It is always there around continents or islands. Seamless edges The left edge continues the right edge, and the top continues the bottom: a map that can wrap around the world. The game does not cross from one edge to the other yet. Shape The shape of the land: up to the edge of the map, one continent, several continents or an archipelago. Except with land up to the edge, a sea surrounds it up to the horizon. Size For the map: its side (256 m, 512 m, 1,024 m, 2 km or 4 km), used at the next generation. Beyond 1,024 m, a large map: the ground is drawn in detail around the camera and simplified in the distance. For a plant: its size compared with its model (× 1: as is, × 2: twice as big). Style The look of the water, chosen for the game. Realistic: fine waves, reflections of the sky and the scenery, see-through water where the bottom shows. Stylized: for a low poly game, a surface of flat facets, gentle readable waves, bold color steps and crisp foam bands; it costs less. Floating and swimming things follow the drawn waves in both cases. The render quality (Low, Medium, High) only sets the cost: stylized water stays stylized on a powerful computer. Swell direction Where the waves go, in degrees, like a compass laid on the terrain. The smaller waves stray from it a little. Variant The number that sets how the world is drawn: the same number, with the same settings, gives the same map again. The button next to it picks another one at random. Vegetation The plant kinds growing on this region, with their count. Drag a model from the explorer into the frame (a tree, a bush, grass, a rock): it grows over the whole region. Wakes The wakes and ripples around whatever moves in the water, from 0 to 1: the V opening behind a boat, the churned water in its wake, the rings around a swimmer or a floating crate. They are only drawn: floating things do not feel them. 0: none. Wave length The distance from one crest to the next, for the biggest waves, in meters. Short: a chop; long: an ocean swell. Shorter waves are always added on top. Waves The height of the biggest waves, in meters. 0: calm water, like a mirror. White altitude The altitude, in meters, of the image's white points: the highest possible.

items.title: The timeline: animations and cutscenes
items.text:
Explained in detail: Animate and make cutscenes.

Control What it does Add here Adds a moment where you clicked: a camera, a character (the selected one), a sound, a subtitle or an event, to set in the row above. Animation Creates an animation of the selected objects (a door that opens, a platform that rises) and opens it in the timeline, with a first keyframe of each as it is. Animation timeline Shows or hides the timeline, at the bottom of the view: there you animate objects frame by frame and put cutscenes together. Can be skipped The player can skip the cutscene with Esc (or Start): everything is set as at its end, and its events are sent. Cutscene Creates a cutscene and opens it in the timeline: cameras, characters, sounds, subtitles and events, while the player watches. Delete the timeline Removes this animation or cutscene from the scene. Ctrl+Z brings it back. Fade to black A fade to black of this length, centred on the camera change. From the start of the game Plays the timeline as soon as the game starts: a platform that comes and goes, an intro cutscene. Otherwise a Trigger rule or a script starts it. Glide The camera glides from the previous one during this time, instead of cutting at once. Keyframe Sets a keyframe of the selected objects, as they show, at the playhead. An object that already has its row also gets one as soon as you move, turn or scale it. Keyframe here Sets a keyframe of the object, as it shows, where you clicked. Lecture de l'animation Once: it stops at its end. Loop: it starts again. There and back: it goes back in reverse, forever (a platform that comes and goes). Length The length of the timeline, in seconds. It cannot cut keyframes off: move them first. Looping The character's animation repeats forever, instead of playing once. Music A music: it loops, and replaces the one that was playing. Otherwise, a sound played once. Name The name you see in the lists. The id does not change: the rules and scripts that play it still find it. New animation A new animation, with the selected objects as they are as its first keyframe. New cutscene A new ten-second cutscene: add its moments by right-clicking its rows. Remove the keyframe Removes this keyframe: the object goes straight from the previous one to the next. Remove this object from the timeline Removes this object's row and all its keyframes: it stays where it is in the scene. Règle de la frise The seconds of the timeline. Click or drag to move the playhead: the view shows the objects at that moment. Vers l'image clé suivante How the object goes from this keyframe to the next: linear (at a steady pace), smooth (it starts and stops gently), in steps (it waits, then jumps). Visible Shows or hides the object from this moment on: a blinking light, a bridge that appears. World stopped During the cutscene, the rest of the world stops: enemies, physics, scripts. Only it goes on, with its characters. Otherwise the world lives around it. Événement envoyé The name of the event sent at this moment: a Trigger rule ("When an event happens") or a script can wait for it.

items.title: Vegetation
items.text:
Explained in detail: The terrain.

Control What it does Density The number of plants per 100 m². Changing the density redoes the sowing: hand edits may no longer land on the same plants. Erase Removes the selected plant (Delete key). It will not grow back, even if the terrain changes. In game How its plants behave during the game. Max. size The largest size of a plant, compared with its model (× 2: twice as big). Each plant takes a random size between the min. size and the max. size. Max. slope The steepest slope it grows on, in degrees: nothing grows on steeper ground. Lower it to keep cliffs bare. Min. size The smallest size of a plant, compared with its model (× 1: as is). Each plant takes a random size between the min. size and the max. size. Put all plants back Forgets all hand edits of this kind: each plant goes back to the place, rotation and size it was sown with, and erased ones grow back. Put back in place As sown: the plant goes back to its original place, rotation and size. Reseed New random places for all its plants. Hand edits are forgotten. Select all its plants Selects all the plants of this kind, to edit them or place a system on them together. A system placed on the plant kind already applies to all of them. Select its plant kind Selects the plant kind that sowed this plant: its sowing settings and systems apply to all its plants. Sink into the ground Each plant is set at the lowest point of the ground under its foot, then sunk by this much, in meters: the foot seems to come out of the earth. Sowing How this plant kind spreads over its region: how many, what size, on which slopes. Stop growing it Removes this plant kind from its region: all its plants disappear. Ctrl+Z brings it back. Trunk The diameter, in meters, that stops the player in the game. 0: you walk through (grass, flowers, bushes). Visible up to The distance, in meters, beyond which its plants are no longer drawn (60 % of this distance in Low quality, on an integrated chip). Closer, the game runs faster: grass can stop early, trees further away.

This page is generated automatically from the WorldMint code (help/*.json, locales/*.json): it always matches the editor.

items.title: Game scripts (Luau)
items.text:
Scripts give the game its own rules. They are written in Luau, in the editor's Scripts tab, and the agent writes them for you. Here is the full reference, exactly as the agent reads it (tool scripts_reference).

Game scripts are Luau, stored in the scene. They run on every simulation step, with the same result for the same inputs: there is no clock, no file or network access, and math.random is seeded.

A script may define on_start() and on_update(dt), and on_save() and on_load(state) to keep its state in a saved game (see Saving). Each script has its own global variables; the table shared is common to all scripts. An error stops that script and is listed by game_run.

Objects are designated by id (a string). Positions are vectors: vec(x, y, z), with .x .y .z, arithmetic, and vector.magnitude(v), vector.normalize(v). Y is up, metres. A rotation is a yaw in radians; 0 faces +Z.

items.title: Finding objects
items.text:
game.player() -> id                    game.find(name_or_id) -> id or nil
game.players() -> {ids}. The character of every player: the one playing on this computer first, then, in a game with several players (the game setting Multiplayer), each guest who joined. The engine sends "joueur.arrivee" {joueur, numero, nom} when a guest joins and "joueur.depart" {joueur, numero} when they leave.
Several players: game.player() is the player whose action is being handled. A script whose first lines hold the line "-- multijoueur: par_joueur" runs once per player (the host's copy, then one for each guest who joins, with its own variables, its own HUD and its own saved state): inside it, game.player() is always its player. A listener of an event that carries a field joueur handles that player; game.each_player(function(id) ... end) runs the function once per player, as that player. Elsewhere game.player() is the host's own player: in a game with several players, say which player. An event emitted while handling a player gets joueur = that player if it has none; the per-player copies of a script only receive the events of their player, and those that name no player.
game.player_name(id?) -> the player's name (what they typed to join; "Joueur 1" for the host), nil if id is not a player    game.player_number(id?) -> 1 for the host, then 2, 3...; 0 if id is not a player (game.player_number(id) > 0 asks "is it a player?").
The controls, the mouse and the body of a player take an optional last argument, the player: game.pressed("attack", id), game.action, game.released, game.player_forward(id), game.set_player_speed(scale, id), game.set_player_can_run(on, id), game.set_player_can_jump(on, id), game.player_running(id), game.player_jumped(id), game.player_landed(id), game.player_swimming(id), game.show_cursor(on, id), game.cursor_shown(id), game.drive(vehicle, id), game.leave_vehicle(id), game.driving(id), game.active_camera(id), game.camera_view(id), game.using_pad(id), game.pause(on, reason, {actions}, id), game.paused(id). game.use_camera and game.use_player_camera take {joueur = id}. Without it: the player whose action is being handled.
game.with_tag(tag, {asleep=false}?) -> {ids}     game.near(pos_or_id, radius, tag?, {asleep=false}?) -> {ids}, nearest first
game.exists(id) -> bool                game.name(id) -> string
game.awake(id) -> bool. In a large world, objects in 256 m tiles beyond the activity radius around the player (300 m by default) are asleep: they still exist and can be read, but do not move, walk, animate or detect, and game.with_tag, game.with_system and game.near leave them out unless {asleep = true}. The engine sends "monde.sommeil" {objets} and "monde.reveil" {objets} when they fall asleep and wake up; compare game.time() on waking to catch up the time they slept. The tag "toujours_actif" (or a system listed in the game setting alwaysActiveSystems) keeps an object awake everywhere. Without "Large world", everything is awake.
game.has_tag(id, tag)   game.add_tag(id, tag)   game.remove_tag(id, tag)
game.distance(a, b)                    game.line_of_sight(a, b) -> bool, blocked by colliders. a and b: id or vector.

items.title: Moving and changing objects
items.text:
game.position(id) -> vector            game.set_position(id, v). Moves its collider too; teleports a character.
game.rotation(id) -> yaw               game.set_rotation(id, yaw)      game.face(id, pos_or_id)
game.bounds(id) -> low, high or nil. The box it fills in the world, what it contains included, measured on its models (hidden ones too): low.y is its foot, high - low its size. nil if it has no model. Never guess a model's size: measure it.
game.scale(id) -> vector               game.set_scale(id, number_or_vector). What it contains follows, along its own axes, as in the editor: their place, size and collider; the player put inside it moves with it, at their own size.
game.go_to(scene, arrival?). Goes to another scene of the game (a building's inside, a cave, the next level), after a fade to black, at the object named arrival (an empty marker placed there), or where the player stands in that scene. Scripts keep running and keep their variables; the scene left stays as it was. Sends "scene.change" {depuis, vers} once there.
game.scene() -> name of the current scene    game.scenes() -> {names}. A scene's name is its file name, without folder or extension.
game.visible(id) -> bool               game.set_visible(id, bool)            game.set_solid(id, bool). false: it stops nobody any more, but stays visible (a tree falling).
game.effect(id, kind, {duration=1, away_from=pos_or_id, after="destroy" or "hide"}?). The engine animates it around its base, whatever the model: "fall" (tips over, away from away_from), "collapse" (breaks into pieces of its own model that fall in a heap), "shrink", "burst" (breaks into pieces that fly out, bounce and fade), "shake" (trembles, then comes back). after="destroy" removes it at the end; after="hide" hides it and puts it back as it was, so it reappears upright when shown again. What it contains (its children) follows it, as with game.set_scale, and comes back with it.
game.effect(preset, pos_or_id, {size=1, color=vec, amount=1, duration, loop=false, direction=vec, light=true, light_intensity=1, light_shadows=true}?) -> handle. "feu", "explosion", "magie", "etincelles" and "impact" also give their own light (it follows the effect, flickers with a fire, grows with size, casts shadows for "feu", "explosion" and "magie"): light=false removes it, light_intensity multiplies it, light_shadows=false keeps it without shadows. It changes nothing in the game. Particles, simulated by the game (the same game gives the same particles) and drawn by the renderer. preset: "eclats" (chips; on an object they take its colour), "eclats_bois", "eclats_pierre", "poussiere" (dust spreading on the ground), "feu" (flames with a little smoke and sparks: a campfire at size 1, a torch at 0.4), "fumee", "explosion", "etincelles", "impact" (a hit: a flash, sparks, dust), "pluie", "neige" (falling from a disc around the place: size widens it), "magie". On an object, a looping effect follows it. size scales the whole effect; amount the number of particles; duration in seconds (loop: 0 runs until game.stop_effect). direction: where chips or sparks fly (on an object, chips jump from the spot nearest the player, in its colour, toward the player). The report counts them under particles.
game.stop_effect(handle). It stops emitting; its particles end their life.
game.object_effect(id, on). Starts again (true) or stops (false) the effect an object carries with the "particules" system (a campfire lit or put out), and stops the looping effects scripts put on it.
game.decal(image, pos_or_id, {size=1, normal=vec(0,1,0), angle=0, opacity=1, color=vec(1,1,1), life=0}?) -> handle. Projects an image on the surfaces under it: a footprint, an impact, a stain, a puddle, a sign. image: "tache", "impact", "brulure", "flaque", "pas", "trace", or an image file of the project (PNG, JPEG). normal: the surface it lies on (up for the ground, a wall's outward direction). angle: radians around the normal. life: seconds before it fades, 0 to keep it. A game keeps a limited number of decals: the oldest disappears to make room. game.remove_decal(handle) removes one. The report counts them under decals.
game.parent(id) -> id or nil             game.children(id) -> {id}. Moving, turning, scaling, hiding, cloning or destroying a parent carries its children along.
game.clone(id, pos, {tags={...}}?) -> new id. Clones a template (usually hidden, with visible: false), which keeps tags, collider, animations and systems; the clone is visible. A vehicle (car, motorbike, boat) clones into another vehicle you can drive, with its wheels.
game.destroy(id). Removes it and its collider: a door or a wall can open that way. Not the player.
game.attach(id, holder, {bone=, offset=vec(0,0,0), rotation=vec(0,0,0), like=}?). Holds an object on a bone of an animated character (the player, another player, a character): an axe in the hand, a torch, a bag on the back. It follows the bone as the character walks, runs, strikes or chops, and no longer blocks anything. bone: a bone of the holder (read them with asset_info); without it, the bone that holds things, found by measuring the skeleton (game.hand_bone). The object is placed on the bone at rest, offset (metres) and rotation (degrees) counted along the bone's axes. like: an object already placed on a bone in the editor (a hidden axe set in the hand by hand): its exact place on its bone is reused. A copy held this way is not kept by game.save: put it back in the hand after game.load (the inventaire system does it for the item held).
game.detach(id). Lets go of it: it stays where it is, free.
game.hand_bone(id) -> bone name or nil. The bone of a character that holds things: a bone made for it under the right hand if the model has one (its name says slot, grip, weapon, prop...), else the right hand, found by its name (hand_r, RightHand, mixamorig:RightHand...) or by the shape of the skeleton. Nothing is assumed of a pack.
game.pool(template, count). Prepares count copies of a template without children, once, in on_start. game.clone then takes one, and game.destroy gives it back, which avoids rebuilding the world's list each time. Use it for what appears and disappears often: projectiles, coins, waves of enemies. A copy given back has gone for the game (game.exists is false), but its id can come back with a later game.clone: do not keep ids of destroyed objects. If the pool is empty, game.clone makes a new copy as usual.

items.title: Characters
items.text:
Objects that walk on the ground, stopped by colliders and by each other, with gravity

game.character(id, {radius=0.4, height=1.8, turn_speed=540, idle="Idle", walk="Walking_A", run="Running_A", run_above=3.5, feet=false, feet_height=0.5, mass=70})
  Makes it a character. With clip names, it plays them by itself according to its actual speed. feet=true sets its feet on the real ground (slopes, steps), its hips lowered as needed, if its skeleton has legs the engine recognises; feet_height is the largest gap corrected, in metres. mass, in kg (1 to 10000): how hard thrown or falling objects knock it, and how heavy what it pushes feels; the player's is in player_set (mass).
  strafe=true: it no longer turns towards its movement but keeps the facing game.face or game.set_rotation gives it (a guard circling the player while watching him), and walks sideways or backwards with walk_directions and run_directions = {back=, left=, right=, forward_left=, forward_right=, back_left=, back_right=} (clip names, all optional): blended by direction, on 8 directions when the diagonals are given, 4 otherwise; a missing back plays walk in reverse, a missing side plays walk.
game.walk(id, velocity). Call on each step it should move, in m/s. It turns towards its movement. Without a call, it stops.
game.walk_to(id, pos_or_id, speed?) -> "moving", "arrived", "blocked" or "asleep". Call on each step instead of game.walk: it follows the walkable areas (the terrain and the objects with a collider: around walls, up gentle slopes, under bridges) to reach the place, or follows an object. "arrived": right next to it. "blocked": no way there (the game_run report says why); it tries again every second. "asleep": far from the player in a large world, it waits until it wakes up (see game.awake). On the way, walkers avoid each other, the player and the other characters (game settings, navigation avoidance). It uses the walkable areas of the smallest character size it fits in (its radius and height, game settings navigation sizes): a giant does not squeeze through a small door. When an object with a collider is placed or removed (a tree cut down, game.set_solid), the walkable areas around it are redone in the background and used about 0.1 s later; an object that moves counts once it has stood still for 0.5 s (a shake or a falling copy changes nothing). Nothing to do in a script: never rebuild or wait for it.
game.path(a, b) -> {points} or nil. The way around obstacles from a to b, along the walkable areas, the last point being b (or the nearest walkable point to it). a and b: id or vector.
game.push(id, impulse). A knockback that fades quickly; works on the player too. On a moving object (Physics system), a blow that changes its speed by impulse, in m/s, whatever its mass: game.push(crate, vec(0, 6, 0)) throws it up.
game.velocity(id) -> vector, in m/s: the player, a character or a moving object. Zero for an object that does not move by itself.

Physics: objects carrying the "physique" system (modules_add, then systems_attach on objects or a group) fall, roll, slide and are pushed by the player and characters walking into them: crates, barrels, balls, rocks. Their shape wraps their model (forme: boite, boule or cylindre); masse, frottement and rebond are per-object settings. The engine moves them: read where they are with game.position, place one with game.set_position (it starts again at rest), throw one with game.push. One that falls out of the world disappears. Characters' paths ignore them, since they move.

Zones: objects carrying the "zone" system announce "zone.entree" {cible = the zone, qui = who entered} and "zone.sortie" {cible, qui} when something enters or leaves their box. Its detecte setting says who counts: joueur (default), personnages (the player and characters), objets (moving objects), tout. Usually an invisible box (visible: false): a zone works hidden. game.set_solid(zone, false) switches it off. A pressure plate, a trap, a finish line, a ball in a goal.

items.title: Joints, vehicles, ragdolls (systems "articulation", "vehicule", "chiffon"
items.text:
Set them with systems_set, the engine runs them):

game.joint_open(id), game.joint_close(id). A hinge or slider's motor drives it to its open or closed stop. game.joint_break(id) makes it give way.
game.joint(id) -> {kind, position, broken} or nil. position: degrees for a hinge, meters for a slider. "articulation.cassee" {cible, autre?} when one breaks.
game.drive(id) puts the player at the wheel of a vehicle (a fallen motorbike is set back on its wheels); game.leave_vehicle() gets them out; game.driving() -> the vehicle driven, or nil. The player also gets in and out with "interact".
game.vehicle(id) -> {speed (km/h), driven, flipped, boat, aground, motorbike, fallen, lean} or nil. aground: a boat resting on the bottom or the shore. fallen: a motorbike lying on its side; lean: how far it leans, in degrees (positive: to its right). "vehicule.monte" and "vehicule.descendu" {cible, qui}; "vehicule.tombe" {cible, qui?} when a motorbike falls over (qui: its rider, thrown off).
game.ragdoll(id, on, push?). An animated character falls limp (on) or gets back up (false), push a vec in m/s. game.ragdolled(id) -> true while down. "chiffon.tombe" and "chiffon.releve" {cible}.

items.title: Animation (skinned objects)
items.text:
game.clips(id) -> {names}              game.clip_length(id, clip) -> seconds or nil
game.play(id, clip, {loop=true, speed=1, fade=0.15}?). With loop=false, the clip plays once, then the character returns to its usual animation. On the player, this temporarily takes over from the animation graph: use it for attacks.
game.pose_layer(id, layer, weight). Pose layers are hand corrections of a model's animations (pose_layers_get/pose_layers_set): weight 0 switches one off, 1 on (true/false work too), in between a part of it; for this character only, until the game ends. A guard who stands straighter while alert, a wounded arm hanging lower.

items.title: Player and inputs
items.text:
game.action(name) -> held              game.pressed(name) -> pressed on this step       game.released(name) -> let go on this step
  Actions are the game's controls (controls_list, controls_set): one per key the game uses, never a key read directly. By default "attack" (left mouse button) and "interact" (E); modules add theirs (block, heal). Moving, running, jumping and pausing are controls too: move_forward (w), move_back (s), move_left (a), move_right (d), run (lshift), jump (space), pause (escape). Escape does not close the game: if no script reads "pause", it frees the cursor.
game.bindings() -> {action = key}      game.bind(action, key). Changes a key during the game, for a key configuration menu. A gamepad button (pad_a, pad_b, pad_x, pad_y, pad_lb, pad_rb, pad_lt, pad_rt, pad_start, pad_back, pad_ls, pad_rs, pad_up, pad_down, pad_left, pad_right) changes the gamepad binding and leaves the key.
game.pad_bindings() -> {action = button}. By default: jump pad_a, attack pad_x, interact pad_y, run pad_lt, pause pad_start. The left stick moves, the right stick turns the camera.
game.action_label(action) -> text to show in a prompt: the key ("E") on keyboard, the button ("Y") when the player plays with a gamepad.
game.action_name(action) -> what the action is called for the player, in their language ("Jump", "Block"): for a key configuration menu.
game.last_key() -> the key pressed on this step, or nil. Key names: letters, digits, space, lshift, mouse_left, mouse_right...
game.player_forward() -> vector        game.set_player_speed(scale). 0 stops the player, 1 is normal.
game.set_player_can_run(bool)          game.set_player_can_jump(bool). Takes running or jumping away without stopping the walk: tiredness, a heavy load.
game.player_running() -> bool          game.player_jumped() -> bool. On the last step: the player moved while running; the player left the ground by jumping.
game.player_landed() -> bool. On the last step: the player touched the ground again after a jump or a fall.
game.player_swimming() -> bool. In water deeper than about half its height, the player swims: it floats with its head out, moves at its swim speed, and cannot jump. The animation graph gets a "swimming" parameter (1 or 0) for a swim state.
game.footsteps() -> {ids}. Those whose foot touched the ground on the last step, read from their walk or run animation: the player and animated characters.
game.ground(id) -> id or nil. The object under its feet (one with a collider): a floor of stone, a wooden bridge. On a terrain: the biome object (Forest, Snow...), or the water object (Sea, Lake) when it stands in water.
game.water_depth(id) -> metres of water where it stands, 0 on dry ground. For wading, slowing down, drowning: the engine itself only draws water.
Moving, running, jumping and the camera are handled by the engine: see player_set.

items.title: Placed lights
items.text:
Objects created with a light field (a bulb, or a spot that points down from the object). Hiding one with set_visible switches it off too.

game.light(id) -> {on, color, intensity, range, angle, kind} or nil if it is not a light. color is a vector (r, g, b), from 0 to 1.
game.set_light(id, {on?, color?, intensity?, range?, angle?}). Only the given fields change: game.set_light(lamp, {on = false}) switches it off, {color = vec(1, 0.2, 0.1)} makes it red. Fails if the object is not a light. game.save keeps it: no need to save lights yourself.

items.title: The sun and the sky of the scene being played
items.text:
A day and night cycle, a storm. Colors are vectors (r, g, b), from 0 to 1.

game.environment(authored?) -> {sun_direction, sun_color, sun_intensity, sky_color, ground_color, background, exposure, fog_distance, fog_color, auto_exposure, auto_exposure_brighten, auto_exposure_darken, auto_exposure_seconds}. sun_direction points toward the sun (y up: high in the sky). authored=true gives the scene as the creator lit it, whatever the game changed since.
game.set_environment({...}). Only the given fields change, from the next frame: game.set_environment({sun_intensity = 0.1, sky_color = vec(0.05, 0.07, 0.15)}) makes it night. game.save keeps it. The "jour_nuit" system turns the sun and the sky for you: prefer it to a hand-written cycle. Automatic exposure (auto_exposure, on by default; auto_exposure_brighten 1 to 64, auto_exposure_darken 1 to 64, auto_exposure_seconds 0 to 30) brightens dark rooms like an eye getting used to them; it only brightens relative to the light still there, so a night made with set_environment stays dark.

items.title: Placed cameras
items.text:
Objects created with a camera field, which show the game from where they stand. While one is active, the mouse does not turn the view, and the player moves relative to what it shows.

game.use_camera(id, {blend=0, joueur=id}?). blend is a smooth move in seconds; 0 cuts at once. Fails if the object is not a camera. With several players, only that player (joueur, or the player whose action is being handled) sees through it.
game.use_player_camera({blend=0}?). Back to the camera that follows the player.
game.active_camera() -> id, or nil for the one that follows the player.
game.camera_view() -> the kind of view the player has: "fixed" (a placed camera is active), "top_down" (the camera that follows the player never rises below 45 degrees: its lowest tilt, in the player settings, is 45 or more), "first_person" (its distance is 1 m or less) or "third_person". To aim like the game is seen: the centre of the screen with a character, the cursor from above.
game.using_pad() -> true while the player plays with a gamepad (always false for a guest, for now).
Move or turn a placed camera like any object, with game.set_position and game.set_rotation. If it is destroyed, the game returns to the player's camera.

items.title: Animations made by hand and cutscenes (timelines of the scene, made in the editor or with timeline_set)
items.text:
The engine plays them: objects take their keyframes, a cutscene shows its cameras, moves its characters, plays its sounds and subtitles, takes control away from the player and gives it back at the end.

game.play_timeline(id, {speed=1, from=0, end_event=nil}?). Plays it from the start (or from seconds); playing it again restarts it. end_event: an event name sent when it ends. Fails if there is no such timeline, or if another cutscene is playing.
game.stop_timeline(id). Stops it where it is, objects left as they are.   game.timeline_playing(id) -> bool.
Sends "timeline.debut" {timeline, sorte} when one starts, and "timeline.fin" {timeline, sorte, passee, arretee} when it ends (passee: the player skipped the cutscene; arretee: stopped by game.stop_timeline). Its own events are sent with {timeline}.

items.title: On screen
items.text:
Coordinates and sizes are fractions of the screen, from the top left. The key identifies an element: calling again updates it, in place. Elements are drawn in the order they were first created: create a background before what goes on it.

With several players, each player has their own HUD: an element made by a per-player script, inside game.each_player, or given {joueur = id}, is seen by that player only; one made by a script for the whole game is seen by everyone, even while it answers one player's event (say {joueur = game.player()} to show it to that player). A guest's HUD is sent to their computer and laid out there, at their screen's size; their clicks come back as "hud.clic" {cible, joueur}. Videos stay on the host's screen.
game.hud_text(key, text, {x=0.5, y=0.5, size=0.035, color=vec(1,1,1), alpha=1, align="center", w=nil}?). align: left, center, right. With w, the text wraps at word boundaries to that width.
game.hud_bar(key, fraction, {x=0.02, y=0.02, w=0.2, h=0.02, color=vec(1,0.2,0.2), alpha=1, align="left"}?)
game.hud_image(key, file, {x=0, y=0, w=0.1, h=0, color=vec(1,1,1), alpha=1, align="left", uv={0,0,1,1}, rotation=0, shape=nil}?). h=0 keeps the image's proportions. Find image files with assets_search and kind "image".
  uv={u0, v0, u1, v1}: the part of the image shown, from 0 to 1; it may go past the image's edge, where nothing is drawn. rotation turns the picture inside its frame, clockwise, in radians. shape="circle" cuts it round.
The map: the file "@map" is a view of the whole scene from above, north (-Z) at the top, drawn by the engine when the scene starts. game.map_area() -> x, z, size: the square of the world it shows, in metres, from its north-west corner (smallest x and z); a point (px, pz) is at u = (px - x) / size, v = (pz - z) / size. game.map_refresh() draws it again (a bridge built, a wall knocked down). game.screen_aspect() -> width / height of the screen: w = h / game.screen_aspect() makes a square. The "carte" system is a ready-made minimap and map window: prefer it.
game.hud_button(key, text, {x=0.5, y=0.5, w=0.12, h=0.06, color=vec(0.15,0.16,0.2), alpha=0.85, align="center", text_color=vec(1,1,1), size=0.03, image=file, back=false}?)
  A button with its exact area: a menu entry, an inventory slot (with an image, and its text as a quantity in the corner). Lighter under the cursor.
  back=true: the button that closes or goes back (Close, Back, Resume). B on a gamepad and Escape click it; Escape then does not reach the game as "pause".
game.hud_at(x, y)? -> key or nil. The element under that point (by default the cursor), the one drawn on top. Texts alone are not clickable: use a button.
game.hud_rect(key) -> x, y, w, h or nil. Its area, top left corner first, where the engine placed it (inside a panel too).
game.hud_remove(key). Removing a panel removes what it contains.

items.title: Interface building blocks
items.text:
Menus, shops, dialogues, chat, name entry. Let panels place elements instead of writing positions by hand.

game.hud_panel(key, {x=0.5, y=0.5, w=nil, h=nil, align="center", color=, alpha=, layout="column", columns=2, gap=0.01, padding=0.015, scroll=false, parent=nil}?)
  A background that places its children, in the order they were created, inside its padding and with gap between them (gap and padding are fractions of the screen height, the same on both sides). Without w or h, it fits its content.
  layout "column": one under the other; a child without w takes the inner width (a text wraps to it). "row": side by side, centred in height. "grid": columns cells per row, all the same width.
parent=key, accepted by every hud_ function: the element goes in that panel, which must exist already; its x and y are ignored. Panels nest.
shape="circle", "diamond", "triangle", "square" or "star": the panel is drawn as that shape in its frame, a map marker; rotation turns it, clockwise in radians (a triangle points up at 0: an arrow).
scroll=true with a h: when the content is taller, the mouse wheel over the panel scrolls it (the wheel then does not reach the game), with a thin scroll bar; its children are cut at its frame, neither drawn nor clickable outside it. Calling hud_panel again on each step keeps the scroll.
game.hud_input(key, {x=0.5, y=0.5, w=0.25, h=nil, text="", placeholder="", max=0, size=, parent=nil}?). A text field. A click selects it and puts the cursor there, then what the player types goes in it, at the cursor: the arrows, Home and End move the cursor (Ctrl: by word), Shift or dragging the mouse selects, Ctrl+A selects all, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V copy, cut and paste (the system clipboard), Backspace and Delete erase, Enter validates, Escape or a click elsewhere leaves it. On a gamepad, once selected: the d-pad moves the cursor, A validates, B leaves. While a field is selected, the player does not move and no control fires. text only sets the value when the field is created: calling hud_input on each step keeps what was typed. max: most characters, 0 for no limit.
game.hud_value(key) -> text or nil. What a field holds (or an element's text).   game.hud_set_value(key, text)
game.hud_focus(key) selects a field; on a button, gives it the gamepad and keyboard focus (seen when the player uses them). game.hud_focus(nil) leaves both.
game.hud_focused() -> key or nil. The field being typed in, or the button with the visible gamepad or keyboard focus.
Events sent by the engine: "hud.clic" {cible = the button's key} when a button is clicked (pressed then released on it, or chosen with the gamepad or keyboard); "hud.valider" {cible = the field's key, texte} when a field is validated with Enter. React to them with game.on instead of comparing game.hud_at() yourself.
Gamepad and keyboard, with nothing to write: while the game shows the cursor, the engine finds the buttons of the window in front (the last created element without parent, a panel usually, that holds buttons). The d-pad, the left stick, the arrow keys and Tab move a visible focus from one button to the next by their place on screen (held, it repeats); A or Enter clicks it; B or Escape clicks the window's back button. A window that opens gives the focus to its first button when the player plays with a gamepad; with a keyboard, the first arrow shows it. A list that scrolls follows the focus. While a window has the focus the player does not move, and the controls bound to these buttons (jump on A, a potion on the d-pad) do not fire. The mouse hides the focus and keeps working as before.
game.hud_navigation(false) leaves the gamepad to your script (a key configuration menu waiting for a key); game.hud_navigation(true) gives it back.
Rich text, in hud_text and button texts: [b]bold[/b], [color=#ff8800]colored[/color]. Another tag is shown as it is.
The "interface" system (modules_add): its game settings are the look of every element: panel and button backgrounds, accent color (hover, selected field, scroll bar), text color and size, corner rounding, background opacity. Values a script gives win over it.
Example: game.hud_panel("menu", {y=0.2, w=0.3}) game.hud_text("titre", "[b]Pause[/b]", {parent="menu"}) game.hud_button("reprendre", "Resume", {parent="menu"})
In game_run, a segment's text is typed into the selected field on its first step: "\b" erases, "\n" validates.

items.title: Drawn screens
items.text:
Interface screens made in the editor or with screens_set (a score, an ammo bar, a help panel, a workshop menu). Prefer them to hud_ calls for a fixed interface: the user sees and changes them. They live by themselves: bound values, buttons that send their event, screens shown or hidden by an event or a control. Their elements are in the HUD under the key "screen/element".

game.screen_show(name)                  game.screen_hide(name)                  game.screen_shown(name) -> bool
game.set_value(name, value). A value of the game (number, text or boolean; nil removes it) that a screen element bound to "value" shows: game.set_value("score", score). game.value(name) -> it, or nil.
game.hud_set(key, {text=, value=, color=, text_color=, alpha=, disabled=}). Changes only what is given of an element on screen, a drawn screen's element included ("score/total"); disabled = true greys a button out and it no longer clicks (its "disabled" image if it has one); a bound value replaces its text at the end of the step.
A screen's button sends its event (if it has one) with {cible = "screen/element", ecran, element}, after "hud.clic": the Trigger system reacts to it with quand = evenement.

items.title: The mouse
items.text:
The cursor is hidden and the mouse turns the camera, until the game shows the cursor for an interface (an inventory, a menu, a building mode).

game.show_cursor(bool, player?)        game.cursor_shown(player?) -> bool. Each player has their own cursor. Shown, the camera no longer turns with the mouse, and combat.basique does not strike.
game.mouse() -> x, y or nil. Where the cursor is, in fractions of the screen like the HUD.
game.mouse_down(button?) -> held        game.mouse_pressed(button?)        game.mouse_released(button?). button: "left" (default), "right", "middle". For interfaces; gameplay uses controls.
game.wheel() -> notches on this step, up positive. A control can also use wheel_up or wheel_down as its key.
game.stick() -> x, y. The gamepad's left stick, from -1 to 1 (x to the right, y down), 0, 0 without a gamepad: to move a window's content, such as a map. Moving the player goes through controls.
Drag and drop: on mouse_pressed take what game.hud_at() gives, move it with game.mouse() while mouse_down, and on mouse_released drop it on the slot under the cursor (game.hud_rect).
game.pick({tag=, x=, y=}?) -> id or nil, point or nil. What is under the cursor (or that point): the nearest visible object (with that tag if given), and the point hit, on it or on the ground, the terrain and colliders. To place a building where the player points.
game.to_screen(pos_or_id) -> x, y or nil. Where a place of the world is on screen, nil behind the camera: a name above a head, a marker.
game.quit(). Closes the game: a "Quit" button of a menu.
game.host() -> true, or false and why. Hosts a game with the "Multiplayer" game setting: others join on this PC's address, at the port of the setting. game.join(address) -> true, or false and why. Joins the game hosted at "192.168.1.20" or "192.168.1.20:48600": this game then shows the host's game (its scripts stop here). game.leave_online() stops hosting or leaves. Only the player on this PC asks; the game on screen does it (in game_run nothing happens: game.network() says available=false). The Menu module has Host and Join buttons: use it rather than your own.
game.network() -> {available, mode, port, guests, address, error}. available: the game can be hosted or joined here. mode: "solo", "host", "joining" or "guest". guests: how many joined. error: why the last host or join failed (a refusal, no answer).
game.pause(on, reason="script", {actions}?, player?). In a game hosted online (several players), a menu does not stop the game: it only holds that player (their controls, except "pause" and the actions listed, and their movement), while the world goes on. Otherwise it pauses the world: the player, characters, physics, animations and game.time stop; the HUD still answers (hud.clic, hud.valider, scrolling). on_update keeps running with dt = 0, and the only controls that still reach scripts are "pause" (to resume) and the actions listed (the key that closes a window). Each reason holds the pause: a menu and a dialogue each pause with their own reason, and the game resumes when none holds it. game.paused() -> true while paused. The Menu and Dialogue systems use it: prefer them to a hand-written pause menu.
game.title() -> the game's title (game settings, Window), in the player's language.

Languages. The creator writes the game in their language (the original language, game settings, Languages). Each other language the

items.title: game offers has a translation table in the project, translations/<code>.json
items.text:
The text as written in the game, then its translation.

game.t(text, ...) -> text. The text in the player's language, from the game's table; without a translation, the text as written.
Write every text the player reads through it, as a literal: game.hud_text("score", game.t("Coins: {1}", gold)). {1}, {2}... are
replaced after translation by the values that follow, so the word order can change from one language to another. The Translations
window and translations_get find game.t("...") written with quotes; a text built with .. cannot be found nor translated.
The systems already translate what the user typed in their settings (lines and answers of a Dialogue, messages of the Trigger, the
title of the Menu, names): never wrap a system's text again.
game.language() -> the player's language ("fr", "en", "es"...): the system's language when the game offers it, else the original one,
or what the player chose in the Menu options.  game.languages() -> {codes}, the original first.  game.language_name(code?) -> "Français".
game.set_language(code) -> bool. Changes the player's language and remembers it for the next plays; refused if the game does not
offer it. The engine then sends "langue.change" {langue}: redraw the texts already on screen.

items.title: Graphics
items.text:
What the player chooses for the picture, on top of the game settings (Window): for an options menu (the menu module does it).

game.graphics() -> {quality = "low"|"medium"|"high", upscaling = "off"|"native"|"quality"|"balanced"|"performance"|"ultra_performance",
upscaler = "none"|"dlss"|"fsr", dlss = bool, dlss_available = bool, fsr_available = bool, antialiasing = "auto"|"taa"|"smaa"|"fxaa"|"none",
shadows = "auto"|"high"|"medium"|"low"|"off", ray_tracing = "auto"|"on"|"off",
ray_tracing_available = bool, ray_tracing_heavy = bool, ray_tracing_cut = bool, indirect_light = bool}, or nil when nothing is drawn (game_run without capture). quality also sets the
particles budget. upscaler: what rebuilds the full-size picture when upscaling is not "off": "none" is WorldMint's own, "fsr" is AMD FSR 2
(sharper, every card: fsr_available), "dlss" is NVIDIA DLSS (dlss_available is true only when the creator provided NVIDIA's files and the
game enabled DLSS, on an RTX card); dlss is the older form (true when upscaler is "dlss").
antialiasing: how edges are smoothed when upscaling is "off" (any other upscaling already smooths them); "auto" follows quality (TAA in
high and medium, SMAA there in a project created before November 2026; FXAA in low), "taa" is sharp in motion but needs a redraw every frame (it turns upscaling "native" on), "smaa" is sharp
with no trail, "fxaa" the lightest, "none" keeps jagged edges.
shadows: the player's shadow quality, for the sun and every light; "auto" (default) follows quality and the scene's shadow quality,
"off" removes every shadow (the cheapest, rays included). ray_tracing: shadows drawn with rays; "auto" uses them only on a dedicated
graphics card in medium and high quality, "on" forces them, "off" never. ray_tracing_available is true only when the card has it and
the game allows it (window ray_tracing); ray_tracing_heavy is true when "on" forces it where it is heavy (an integrated chip, low
quality): tell the player the picture may slow down. ray_tracing_cut is true when the renderer turned rays off because the graphics
card's memory is full (shadows come back from shadow maps); another ray_tracing or quality choice makes it try again.
indirect_light (true by default): light bounced by surfaces (a sunlit floor lights the walls, a room is lit through its window), ray
traced with a light cache; used only in high quality with ray tracing on, it costs about 1 to 2 ms.
game.set_graphics({quality?, upscaling?, upscaler?, antialiasing?, shadows?, ray_tracing?, indirect_light?}) -> bool (dlss = true|false still works). Changes only the fields given, from the next frame; false when nothing is
drawn. Not kept by itself: save the player's choice (game.save with {systems = false}) and set it again in on_start.

items.title: Modules and events (see modules_list)
items.text:
game.module_settings(module) -> table. The settings of a module for the whole game, as the user set them.
game.system(id, module) -> table or nil. The values of a module for this object: a module is placed on objects or groups, and each one has its own values (a boss and a skeleton do not hit alike). nil if the object does not carry it.
game.with_system(module, {hidden=false, asleep=false}?) -> {ids}. Every visible object carrying it; with hidden=true, hidden ones too (a zone is usually an invisible box); with asleep=true, those asleep far away in a large world too (see game.awake). They also carry the tag "@module": game.near(pos, radius, "@sante") finds the nearest ones.
game.system_owner(id, module) -> id or nil. Where the object gets that module from: the nearest object or group, itself or above it, on which the module is placed (itself if it carries it alone); nil if the module does not apply to it. A module placed on a group gives it to every piece inside (game.with_system returns each piece, never a group without a model); pieces with the same owner are one thing: one marker, one place, one counter. A piece with its own values for the module is its own owner.
game.emit(event, {fields}?). Announces an event: every listener runs now, in the order they subscribed, and receives the fields (an empty table if none).
game.on(event, function(fields) ... end). Listens to an event, usually in on_start. An error in a listener stops that listener's script only.
Modules talk only through events: listen to theirs, and send the ones they listen to. Your own scripts can use events too, with names of your own.
game.override(name, function(default, ...) ... end). Replaces a point a module offers (see its overrides in modules_info), from a script of your own: never edit a module's script. The function receives the module's own behavior first: call default(...) to keep it, and change only what you need. Several scripts, modules included, can override the same point: each receives the previous one as default, so always call default for the cases you do not handle. If one fails, the error is reported and the chain skips it.
Example: game.override("sante.degats", function(default, cible, brut, source, retenue) if game.has_tag(cible, "boss") then return 0 end return default(cible, brut, source, retenue) end)

items.title: Sound
items.text:
Files are WAV, MP3, FLAC or OGG: find them with assets_search and kind "sound". In game_run nothing is heard: the report lists what played.

game.sound(file, {volume=1, pitch=1, loop=false, fade=0, at=pos_or_id, min_distance=2, max_distance=40, group="effects"}?) -> handle. With at, the sound comes from that place, or follows that object: quieter far away, left or right of the camera. Without at, it is heard everywhere at the same level (a menu click, a fanfare).
game.stop_sound(handle, {fade=0}?)       game.music(file, {volume=0.6, fade=1, group="music"}?). One music at a time, looping: a new one crossfades.
game.stop_music({fade=1}?)

items.title: Sound mixer
items.text:
Every sound belongs to a group of the game's mixer (game settings, Sound mixer): music, effects, ambience, voice, ui, and those the user added. group names one by its id or its name ("ambience" or "Ambiance"); without group, a sound goes to effects and the music to music. Pick the group that fits: a looping fire or wind in ambience, a character's line in voice, a menu click or a pickup chime in ui. The mixer sets each group's volume, can mute it, and lowers one while another plays (ducking: music under voices). Do not lower a music by hand when a line plays: put the line in voice.

game.volume(group or "master", 0..1). The player's level, on top of the game's mix: for an options menu (the menu module does it).
game.mute(group or "master", true or false). Cuts a group, or all the sound, and brings it back (a cutscene without ambience).
game.muffle(group or "master", 0..1, {fade=0.5}?). Muffled like under water or behind a wall: 0 clear, 0.5 behind a door, 1 under water. A trigger rule can do it too.
game.sound_groups() -> {{id, name}, ...}. The mixer's groups in order, name in the player's language: for an options menu.

items.title: Videos
items.text:
Files are MP4, M4V or MOV (H.264 video, AAC sound): find them with assets_search and kind "video". The game counts their time step by step, from the length written in the file: in game_run nothing is seen, but they start, end and announce their end at the same step as on screen, and the report lists them (videos: file, fullscreen, seconds watched, end "finished", "skipped", "stopped" or "playing").

game.video(file, {skip=true, event=nil, pause=true, volume=1, group="voice"}?) -> handle. A full-screen cutscene, over the world and the HUD, with its sound: an intro, an ending, a story moment. Its sound goes to the voice group, so the music lowers under it; give another group of the mixer if it fits better. While it plays it takes the keyboard, mouse and gamepad: with skip, Escape, Enter, Space, a click, A or Start skip it. pause=true stops the world meanwhile. Starting another one replaces it.
When it ends (finished, skipped or stopped), the engine announces "video.fin" {video=handle, fichier=file, passee=true if skipped}, and also your event if given: game.on("intro_done", function(e) game.go_to("Village") end). This is how you chain what comes next.
game.hud_video(key, file, {x, y, w=0.3, h=0, loop=true, volume=1, group="effects", event=nil, alpha, align, parent}?) -> handle. A video inside the HUD (a screen in a menu, an animated portrait), like game.hud_image: h=0 keeps the video's real proportions. Calling it again with the same key and file keeps it playing; game.hud_remove(key) stops it. volume=0 for a silent one.
game.video_stop(handle)    game.video_playing(handle) -> bool    game.video_time(handle) -> seconds into the video, or nil once it ended (to time subtitles).
A video on an object of the world (a television) is not available yet.

items.title: Saving the player's progress
items.text:
game.save(slot, table) -> true, or false and a reason. slot: lowercase letters, digits, _ and -, such as "game1". The table holds text, numbers, booleans, vectors, lists and tables with text keys: the state of the game (level, position, items), not the whole world. 1 MB at most.
game.load(slot) -> table, or nil if there is none.     game.has_save(slot) -> bool     game.delete_save(slot)
Saves are kept between plays of the player's game. In game_run they stay in memory: your tries never touch the player's saves.
The systems keep their own state: game.save asks every script that defines on_save() for a table (its state: the inventory's items, the quests' progress, the shops' stocks, the dialogues' marks), and game.load gives each one back to its on_load(state). game.load called in on_start waits until every script has started. Do not save or re-add what a system keeps. The engine keeps the world too, in every scene visited: objects shown or hidden, solid or not, moved, turned, resized or pushed, destroyed (game.destroy) or copied (game.clone, game.pool), tags, lights, looping effects, decals, the active camera, timelines playing, joints, ragdolls, the vehicle driven, the player's speed and abilities. game.load puts each scene back as it was when saved; the player's own position is the game's to keep. {systems = false} as the last argument of game.save or game.load leaves them out (to read a save without resuming it).
A script of your own can do the same: function on_save() return {opened = opened} end   function on_load(state) opened = state.opened end. The state follows the rules of game.save; it is stored under the script's name.

items.title: Ending and debugging
items.text:
game.finish("won" or "lost", message?). Stops the simulation; the game shows the message and offers to play again. Only for a game that has an ending.
game.log(...). Shown in the report of game_run.
game.time() -> seconds                 game.dt() -> seconds per step           game.step() -> step number

items.title: Example of the syntax, not a model for your game
items.text:
A dog that follows the player, and coins to collect.

local gold = 0
function on_start()
  for _, id in game.with_tag("dog") do
    game.character(id, {idle="Idle", walk="Walking_A"})
  end
end
function on_update(dt)
  local player = game.player()
  for _, id in game.with_tag("dog") do
    local to = game.position(player) - game.position(id)
    if vector.magnitude(to) > 3 then game.walk(id, vector.normalize(to) * 2) end
  end
  for _, id in game.near(player, 1.2, "coin") do
    game.destroy(id)
    gold += 1
  end
  game.hud_text("gold", "Gold: " .. gold, {x=0.02, y=0.07, align="left"})
end

This page is generated automatically from the WorldMint code (engine/script/script_runtime.cpp (scriptApiReference)): it always matches the editor.

items.title: Game systems
items.text:
Systems are ready-made game rules that ship with the editor. You activate them in the Game tab (Systems section), then place them on objects or folders: see The Game tab. The agent can activate, place and set them for you.

System What it does Basic combat The player strikes ahead with a key, with the damage, reach and cooldown set on them. It hits what carries Health. For enemies that attack, add "Enemies". Building The player places pieces in the world: walls, floors, a campfire, any model. In building mode (B), a preview goes where they aim, on a grid or freely: with the view (the centre of the screen) when they play a character, with the cursor from above. A click places the piece and takes its cost from the inventory. A placed piece can be torn down, and gives back part of its cost. Crafting Recipes that turn what the player carries into something else: three wood and two stones make an axe. One crafts from a window (C), bare-handed or in front of a workbench: an object of the world carrying this system, such as a campfire or a forge, which allows its own recipes. Day and night Time goes by: the sun rises, crosses the sky and sets, then night falls, darker and bluish, and the day comes back. Broad daylight is the scene's light as you set it. The chosen lamps light up at night, and a clock can show. Decal An image projected on what lies under the object: a footprint, an impact, a stain, a puddle, a scorch mark, a sign painted on a wall. Create > Decal places an invisible box that carries it: the image covers its width and depth, and lies on the ground or the wall around its base. Dialogue A character who talks when used: their lines show one by one, with the player's answers as buttons. An answer leads to another line and can send an event, to which the Trigger system or a script reacts. Tests (an item carried, a mark, the talks already had) choose what they say. Enemies What carries this system patrols, chases the player when it sees them, and hits them in reach, with its own values: an early skeleton and a boss have neither the same speed nor the same damage. They walk around walls. Fog volume A local fog, limited to an area: the mist of a valley, an undergrowth, a marsh, the smoke of a cave. Create > Fog volume places an invisible box that carries it: it fills the box (or the sphere inside it) and fades out towards its edges. With volumetric fog (High or Medium quality), it catches the sun's rays and shadows. Its kind "Glowing air (rays only)" (Create > Glowing air) is an almost invisible air that only shows the sun's rays, like the dust of a forest. Gathering What carries this system is a resource to gather: a tree to chop, a rock to mine, a bush to pick. Each use is a hit; at the last one, the resource gives what it holds to the inventory, disappears, and grows back if wanted. Healing What carries this system gives health back to the player: a spring to touch, or a potion picked up into the inventory and drunk with a key, each with what it gives. Health Health and armor for the objects that carry it: the player, a group of skeletons, a boss, each with its own values. Shows nothing: add "Health bar" to see it. Health bar Shows the player's health on screen, as a bar and in numbers. Interaction The player uses with a key what carries this system: a door, a merchant, a lever. Shows the prompt, and leaves the effect to the game. Interface The look of the game's menus, buttons, lists and text fields: the colors of backgrounds, text and what is selected, the text size, the rounding of corners. Everything the game shows uses them, except what a script chooses itself. Inventory What carries this system can be picked up, and the player keeps it, grouped by kind. The game can give some, take some, and react to each change. Joint Links this object to another one, or to the world: a door on its hinges, a drawbridge, a wheel, a drawer, an elevator, a chandelier, a plank that gives way under a weight, a rope, a spring. With stops, a motor that opens and closes it, a breaking force. The object also carries Physics. Map A minimap in a corner of the screen, the player in the middle, and a big map of the whole scene with the M key, zoomed and moved with the mouse or the gamepad (triggers and stick). What carries this system shows on it as a marker: a shape and a color, or an image, and its name; always, once discovered up close, or only as a quest objective. Merchants, characters who talk and the objectives of quests in progress are marked by themselves. Menu The title screen when the game starts, and the pause with Escape: Resume, Options (in sections: sound, display with the graphics and, for a translated game, the language, controls), Quit. The game stops while the menu is open, and it takes the look of the Interface system. A game with the Multiplayer setting also has Host and Join there. Needs What the player needs to live: hunger, thirst, tiredness, or whatever the game wants. Each need goes down over time; at zero, the player loses health. It goes back up by eating or drinking what the inventory holds, at a source in the world (a well, a bed) carrying this system, or through a Trigger rule. Each need can be switched off without losing its settings. Particle effect Particles coming out of the object: a campfire, a torch, smoke, sparks, magic, rain or snow around the player. Choose the effect, its size, its colour and its amount; it loops or plays once. For an effect on its own, Create > Particle effect places an invisible box that carries it. Passage What carries this system leads to another scene of the game: a door into a house, a cave entrance, a level's exit. One arrives at the chosen object of that scene, after a fade to black. Physics The objects that carry it fall, roll, slide, and the player pushes them by walking into them: crates, barrels, a ball, rocks. Those that come at the player push back, by their mass: a rock knocks them aside, a ball bounces off. In water, they float, sink or stay in between, and drift with the water. Their shape wraps the model, or follows its outline. Placed on a folder, it applies to everything inside. Quest log The game's quests and their steps, which move on by themselves: on an event (a Trigger rule, a Dialogue answer, an enemy defeated), a Dialogue mark, items carried or items handed over. A finished quest can give a reward; a quest can also fail (an event, a mark, time running out) or be abandoned from the log, then be taken up again. A log opens with J, and a notification announces each new quest, each step and each end. Ragdoll An animated character that falls limp, like a rag doll: when it dies, under a hard hit, or when the Trigger asks. Its body is built on its own, from its skeleton. It can get back up, and its animation resumes smoothly. Shop A merchant who sells when used: a window with their items and prices, the player's money, and Buy and Sell buttons. The money is a kind of inventory item, such as "Gold". Sounds The game's noises, placed on what makes them: footsteps of characters (timed by their animation, and by the ground), hits given and taken, deaths, doors and chests being used, ambience of a fire or a river, an enemy's alert cry. Plus, for the whole game: music, fight music, pickups. Several files separated by commas: a random one each time. Stamina Placed on the player: running, jumping and striking tire them. Exhausted, they can only walk until they recover. Shows its bar under the health bar. Trigger "When… then…" rules without writing code: when the player enters a zone, uses a lever, when a boss dies… then a door opens, a chest appears, the game is won. With ready-made actions, and those written for this game. Vehicle Turns a model into a car, a motorbike or a boat you drive. A car: its wheels (chosen among its children, found by their name, or taken out of a one-piece model) spin, steer and follow the suspension. A motorbike: it stays upright, leans into turns and can fall over. A boat: its hull floats, measured on its model, an engine pushes it and a rudder turns it; it runs aground on land. The player gets in and out with the Use control, drives with the game's controls, on the keyboard or the gamepad, and the camera follows. Zone A zone that announces who enters and who leaves it: a pressure plate, a trap, a finish line, a goal. Place it on an invisible box, of the size you want. The game decides what happens.

In the Properties of an object or folder that carries the system, Systems section. A folder passes its values on to what it contains; an object can change a value for itself only.

Setting What it does Name in code Type Default Limits or choices Kind of joint How the object moves relative to what holds it: it turns around an axis (hinge), slides along an axis (slider), turns every way around a point (ball), stays in place until it breaks (fixed), or hangs at the end of a rope or a spring. type Choice in a list Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel) charniere: Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel)glissiere: Slider: slides along an axis (drawer, elevator)boule: Ball: turns every way (chandelier, pendulum)fixe: Fixed: holds in place until it breaks (plank, beam)corde: Rope: never goes further than a lengthressort: Spring: comes back to its length Attached to (empty: the world) The object that holds it: the cart of a wheel, the furniture of a drawer. Empty, it is attached to the world, where it stands: a door in a wall, a chandelier on a ceiling. autre Object of the scene (empty) Attachment point Where it is held, on its model's box: a door on one side, a drawbridge at the bottom, a chandelier at the top, a wheel in the middle. The point and the axis show in the 3D view when the object is selected. pivot Choice in a list In the middle centre: In the middlegauche: On the left side (−X)droite: On the right side (+X)bas: At the bottomhaut: At the toparriere: At the back (−Z)avant: At the front (+Z) Axisshown only if Kind of joint is “Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel)” or “Slider: slides along an axis (drawer, elevator)” The object's axis it turns around (hinge) or slides along (slider). Vertical for a door or an elevator, sideways for a drawbridge or a wheel, front to back for a drawer. axe Choice in a list Vertical (Y): a door, an elevator vertical: Vertical (Y): a door, an elevatorcote: Sideways (X): a drawbridge, a wheelavant: Front to back (Z): a drawer Stop on one side (degrees, 0 or less)shown only if Kind of joint is “Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel)” How far it turns one way, from where it starts: 0 for a door that opens one way only, −90 for a swing door. −180 and 180: it turns endlessly, like a wheel. angle_min Number 0 from -180 to 0 Stop on the other side (degrees)shown only if Kind of joint is “Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel)” or “Ball: turns every way (chandelier, pendulum)” Hinge: how far it turns the other way, 90 for a door. Ball: how far it swings from where it starts, in every direction; 180: no limit. angle_max Number 90 from 0 to 180 Travel backwards (m, 0 or less)shown only if Kind of joint is “Slider: slides along an axis (drawer, elevator)” How far it slides towards the back of the axis, in meters, from where it starts: 0 for a drawer closed at the start. course_min Number 0 from -100 to 0 Travel forwards (m)shown only if Kind of joint is “Slider: slides along an axis (drawer, elevator)” How far it slides towards the front of the axis, in meters: 0.5 for a drawer, 5 for a one-floor elevator. course_max Number 1 from 0 to 100 Length (m, 0: the starting one)shown only if Kind of joint is “Rope: never goes further than a length” or “Spring: comes back to its length” The length of the rope or spring, in meters. 0: the distance between the object and what holds it at the start. Attached to the world, the rope hangs from a point above the attachment point. longueur Number 0 from 0 to 100 Springiness (0: rigid)shown only if Kind of joint is “Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel)”, “Slider: slides along an axis (drawer, elevator)” or “Spring: comes back to its length” 0: the stops are hard. Above, they cushion like a spring: 1 bounces softly, 5 is firm. For a spring, its stiffness: 2 by default. rigidite Number 0 from 0 to 20 Motorshown only if Kind of joint is “Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel)” or “Slider: slides along an axis (drawer, elevator)” What makes it move on its own. To a position: it goes to its stop (open) or back to the other (closed), and the Trigger opens and closes it. At a steady speed: it turns or slides without stopping. Without a motor, the Trigger can still open and close it. moteur Choice in a list None: it moves when pushed aucun: None: it moves when pushedposition: To a position: open or closedvitesse: At a steady speed: a wheel, a mill Speed (degrees or meters per second)shown only if Kind of joint is “Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel)” or “Slider: slides along an axis (drawer, elevator)” ; shown only if Motor is “At a steady speed: a wheel, a mill” The motor's speed: in degrees per second for a hinge (360: one turn per second), in meters per second for a slider. Negative, the other way. vitesse Number 90 from -3600 to 3600 Motor strengthshown only if Kind of joint is “Hinge: turns around an axis (door, drawbridge, wheel)” or “Slider: slides along an axis (drawer, elevator)” The motor's strength (in newtons, or newton-meters for a hinge). The higher, the heavier the object it moves, and the more it resists a push: 500 for a door, 20,000 for an elevator carrying the player. force Number 500 from 0 to 1 000 000 Open at the start (motor to a position) With a motor to a position: it starts open (at its stop) instead of closed. The Trigger then opens and closes it. ouvert Yes or no no Breaking force (N, 0: unbreakable) Beyond this force, in newtons, the joint gives way and the object falls: a rotten plank 800 (the player breaks it by jumping on it), a footbridge 5,000. 0: it never breaks, except through the Trigger. rupture Number 0 from 0 to 10 000 000

items.title: Joint (articulation)
items.text:
Links an object to another one, or to the world, with a real physics joint: a door on its hinges, a drawbridge, a wheel on a cart, a drawer, an elevator, a chandelier, a pendulum, a plank that gives way, a rope, a spring. The engine runs it, without a script. The object also carries physique (added with it): give it a masse.

  • systems_attach it on the moving part (the door, not the wall), then systems_set:
  • type: charniere (turns around an axis), glissiere (slides along an axis), boule (turns every way around a point), fixe (holds until it breaks), corde (never further than a length), ressort (comes back to its length).
  • autre: the object that holds it (the cart of a wheel, the furniture of a drawer); empty: the world, where it stands.
  • pivot: where it is held on its model's box: centre, gauche (−X), droite (+X), bas, haut, arriere (−Z), avant (+Z). No coordinates: a door is held on one side, a drawbridge at the bottom, a chandelier at the top, a wheel in the middle.
  • axe (charniere, glissiere): vertical (a door, an elevator), cote (X: a drawbridge, a wheel), avant (Z: a drawer).
  • Stops: angle_min (−180 to 0) and angle_max (0 to 180) in degrees for a hinge, from where it starts (−180 and 180: it turns endlessly); angle_max is the swing cone of a boule (180: free); course_min / course_max in meters for a slider. longueur for a rope or spring (0: the starting distance; attached to the world, it hangs from that far above the pivot). rigidite: 0 hard stops, above: springy (a spring's stiffness).
  • Motor (charniere, glissiere): moteur aucun (moves when pushed), position (holds closed, goes to its far stop when opened), vitesse (turns or slides all the time at vitesse, degrees or meters per second); force its strength (500 for a door, 20000 for an elevator that carries the player); ouvert starts it open.
  • rupture: the force in newtons beyond which it breaks (800: a rotten plank the player breaks by landing on it; 0: never).
  • Open and close without code: a declencheur rule with action ouvrir or fermer and cible the door (a lever with interaction, a zone in front of the door). Action casser breaks it. A rule quand: casse reacts when it breaks.
  • Scripts: game.joint_open(id), game.joint_close(id), game.joint_break(id), game.joint(id) (kind, position: degrees or meters, broken). The engine announces articulation.cassee (cible, autre).
  • Examples: a door {"type": "charniere", "pivot": "gauche", "axe": "vertical", "angle_max": 100, "moteur": "position", "force": 800} with masse 30; a drawbridge {"type": "charniere", "pivot": "bas", "axe": "cote", "angle_min": -90, "angle_max": 0, "moteur": "position", "ouvert": true}; a chandelier {"type": "boule", "pivot": "haut", "angle_max": 30}; an elevator {"type": "glissiere", "axe": "vertical", "course_max": 5, "moteur": "position", "force": 20000} with masse 200.
  • Check with game_run: joints gives each one's angle or position now and the range it reached, and whether and when it broke.

items.title: Health bar (barre_de_vie)
items.text:
Shows the player's health on screen, from the health module (sante), which it activates if missing. The player must carry sante (systems_attach on the player): otherwise the bar never shows. It does nothing else, and is not placed on objects.

  • It draws the HUD keys barre_de_vie, barre_de_vie.fond and barre_de_vie.chiffres: do not reuse them.
  • Settings: position, width and height as fractions of the screen, color as #RRGGBB, and whether the numbers show.
  • It shows the player only. For a bar above enemies, say it is not available yet.
  • A full bar that never moves usually means nothing in the game sends sante.blesser to the player.

items.title: Several players
items.text:
One copy per player: each player sees their own health bar (the health of their own character, sante.change with cible = that player).
